title: 常用软件
content: 附录七：有用的软件 本附录介绍几款日常使用频率较高的软件，涵盖压缩、播放、下载、编辑、系统增强等方面。 7.1 压缩软件：NanaZip / WinRAR Windows 自带解压只支持 格式，遇到 、 等就无法处理。需要安装第三方压缩软件。 NanaZip：开源，基于 7‑Zip 开发，界面适配 Windows 11 现代风格，支持深色模式。可从微软商店安装，也提供 直接下载。功能完整，解压和压缩都够用。 WinRAR：经典压缩软件，支持创建 格式（商业算法）。安装后有 40 天试用提示，但可继续使用。如果需要向他人发送加密或分卷压缩包，用 WinRAR 或 7‑Zip 均可。 两款都可以满足日常使用，选一个装就行。 7.2 视频播放器：PotPlayer Windows 自带的“电影和电视”播放器解码能力有限，很多格式（如 、 、 ）无法打开。PotPlayer 启动快、解码全，几乎不用设置就能播放绝大多数视频文件。 说明：PotPlayer 并非技术上的最佳选择。更专业的用户可能会选择 MPV 配合自编译解码器，或者使用特定版本以支持杜比视界和 HDR 映射。但 PotPlayer 对普通用户来说足够稳定且易于使用。如果您已经能够自行配置复杂播放环境，本推荐对您无效，您的技术水平已超出本附录的受众范围。 7.3 BT 下载工具：qBittorrent 下载 BT 种子或磁力链接，推荐 qBittorrent。开源、无广告、功能完整。支持搜索插件、顺序下载、速度限制、IP 过滤等。 几种常见的下载链接类型： 种子文件（.torrent）：一个小文件（通常几十到几百 KB），里面记录了要下载的资源的元信息（文件名、分块哈希、Tracker 地址等）。下载软件打开种子后，根据其中的信息去连接其他用户下载数据。 磁力链接（magnet:?xt=urn:btih:...）：种子的“升级版”，不需要先下载 .torrent 文件。软件直接根据链接中的哈希值在 DHT 网络中查找资源。复制整段链接到 qBittorrent 即可添加任务。 ed2k 链接（ed2k://...）：电驴（eMule）协议的链接，用于老式 P2P 网络。现在资源较少，部分老资源库仍在使用。qBittorrent 不支持 ed2k，需要使用 eMule 或支持该协议的下载器。 几个设置建议： 添加公共 Tracker 列表（参考 ），可提高连接成功率。 限制上传速度（例如设为 1 MB/s），避免抢占带宽导致网络卡顿。 下载完成后做种一段时间（上传量达到 1:1 或 24 小时），这是 BT 分享精神的体现。 7.4 代码与纯文本编辑器：VS Code 即使不写代码，VS Code 也是一款值得安装的纯文本编辑器。它比记事本强在：语法高亮（打开 、 、 等文件时自动着色）、多标签、正则搜索、插件扩展（Markdown 预览、拼写检查等）。 安装后可以做两件小事： 设置字体：在设置中搜索 ，填入 ，并开启 以支持连字。 安装中文语言包：在扩展商店搜索“Chinese (Simplified)”。 以后打开任何配置文件、日志文件、脚本或笔记，都可以用 VS Code 查看编辑。 7.5 苹果设备图像扩展：HEIF / HEVC iPhone 拍摄的照片可能是 格式（HEIF），视频是 格式（HEVC/H.265）。Windows 默认无法打开或显示缩略图。 需要在 Microsoft Store 安装两个官方扩展： HEIF 图像扩展（免费） HEVC 视频扩展（来自设备制造商的版本，免费） 安装后即可在文件资源管理器中直接查看苹果设备拍的照片和视频。 7.6 终端增强：Windows Terminal CMD 和 PowerShell 自带的窗口较简陋：不支持多标签、字体渲染一般、复制粘贴别扭。Windows Terminal 是微软官方推出的现代终端，支持： 多标签页，可拆分窗格 GPU 加速渲染，字体清晰 自定义主题、背景图片、透明度 同时打开 PowerShell、CMD、WSL 的任意组合 安装后把它固定在任务栏，以后所有命令行操作都从这里进。 补充阅读 以下内容涉及相关软件的技术细节和替代方案，难度中等。可根据兴趣选择性阅读。 补充1：7‑Zip 命令行用法 7‑Zip 的核心是命令行版本 。很多自动化脚本（如批量解压、压缩备份）都依赖它。常用命令： 解压： 压缩： 测试完整性： NanaZip 安装后不默认提供命令行版本，如需使用可以从 7‑Zip 官网下载独立命令行程序。 补充2：PotPlayer 与硬件解码 PotPlayer 默认使用内置解码器，在播放 4K HDR 内容时可能占用较高 CPU。可以切换为显卡硬件解码： 右键画面 → 选项 → 滤镜 → 视频解码器 → 内置解码器 → 硬件解码（DXVA2 / D3D11）设为“自动”。 如果显卡支持，可开启“HDR 直通”（需要显示器支持）或“像素着色 HDR 转换”。 补充3：qBittorrent 搜索插件 qBittorrent 内置搜索功能，需要先安装 Python 并下载搜索插件（从官方 GitHub 仓库获取）。安装后可在程序内直接搜索各大资源站（需自行添加插件，默认不提供）。此功能涉及版权问题，使用需遵守当地法律。 补充4：VS Code 常用插件推荐 PDF Viewer：在 VS Code 内浏览 PDF 文件。 Remote - SSH：通过 SSH 连接远程服务器编辑文件。 补充5：Windows Terminal 的配置文件位置 Windows Terminal 的设置保存在 中（可通过下拉菜单 → 设置 → 左下角“打开 JSON 文件”）。可以直接编辑该文件以添加自定义配色方案、背景图片等。社区有很多现成的主题配置（如 、 ）。 补充6：HEVC 视频扩展的两种版本 Microsoft Store 中有两个 HEVC 扩展： HEVC 视频扩展（付费）：售价 7 元，由官方发布。 来自设备制造商的 HEVC 视频扩展：免费，但可能需要满足特定硬件条件（如安装了厂商提供的驱动）。绝大多数笔记本预装 Intel 核显驱动后会附带此扩展，可直接搜索安装。 如果安装免费版时提示“不符合安装条件”，可以尝试直接搜索“HEVC 视频扩展 设备制造商”的商店链接（通过搜索引擎获取）强行安装，通常也能成功。

title: 游戏
content: 附录八：游戏 讲了这么多，终于讲到最激动人心的部分了——。本附录介绍主流游戏平台的使用方法、账户安全、以及几个实用功能。 对于MacOS游戏，我会单开一个附录介绍。 目前我还没用过MacOS，不过很快就有机会实操了。 8.1 Steam Steam 是全球最大的数字游戏发行平台。大多数 PC 游戏都可以在这里买到。 8.1.1 找到官方网站 Steam 官网是 。国内搜索“Steam”时，可能出现一个叫“蒸汽平台”的网站（ ），那是腾讯代理的国服版本，游戏库和账号系统与全球 Steam 不互通，不建议使用。认准 域名。 如果这网站打不开，你可以借助下面介绍的 Watt Toolkit 加速访问 8.1.2 注册账户 注册时建议使用安全性较高的邮箱，例如 Outlook、Gmail 或 ProtonMail。QQ 邮箱被盗风险相对较高，Steam 账号一旦被盗，损失比较大。 你可以下载steam手机端用于2FA认证。 注册过程中可能遇到谷歌的人机验证（reCAPTCHA）。如果加载不出来，也可以借助下面介绍的 Watt Toolkit 加速访问。 8.1.3 Watt Toolkit（原名 Steam++） 这是一款开源免费的多功能 Steam 工具箱，可从 GitHub 或官网下载。主要功能： 网络加速：加速访问 Steam 社区、GitHub、谷歌验证码、Ubisoft Connect 等。 账号切换：快速切换已登录的多个 Steam 账号。 库存管理：直接管理游戏库存，编辑游戏信息（名称、封面、背景等）。 挂卡：自动挂机掉落 Steam 集换式卡牌。 完全免费，无广告，比很多收费加速器实用。 8.1.4 Steam 账户内容 Steam 点数：购买游戏会获得点数（每消费 10 元得约 100 多点）。点数可用于装饰个人资料（头像框、背景、动画贴纸）、购买聊天表情、给其他玩家的评测发“滑稽”等。 Steam 等级：通过合卡或消费提升等级。等级越高，好友上限增加，个人资料展柜更多。对普通玩家意义不大。 8.1.5 关于换区 不推荐将 Steam 账户切换到其他区域（如阿根廷、土耳其等低价区）。Steam 官方严厉打击跨区购买，轻则强制转回国区，重则封禁账户。国区本身已经是全球低价区之一，大多数游戏价格合理，不需要折腾。 8.1.6 家庭共享 Steam 家庭共享允许你和最多 5 个家庭成员共享游戏库。开启后，好友可以玩你库中的游戏，你也可以玩他的，前提是不同时在线玩同一款游戏（各玩各的不同游戏没问题）。 开启方法：Steam 设置 → 家庭 → 勾选“在此电脑上授权库共享”，然后勾选要共享的账户。 注意：部分游戏（尤其是需要额外第三方账号的）不支持共享；存档各自独立，不影响进度。 8.1.7 远程同乐 对于《双人成行》《胡闹厨房》这类本地多人游戏，远程同乐功能可以让你邀请好友在线游玩，无需好友购买游戏。 使用方法： 拥有游戏的人打开游戏。 在 Steam 好友列表中右键点击好友 → 选择“远程同乐邀请”。 好友接受后，画面会串流给对方，双人分屏游玩。 好友只需要稳定的网络和 Steam 账号，不需要购买游戏。 8.2 Epic Games 商店 Epic 是 Steam 的主要竞争对手，由《堡垒之夜》和虚幻引擎的开发商运营。它的最大特点是每周赠送免费游戏。 官网： 。可以用 Steam 账号登录，也可以单独注册。 免费游戏：每周四更新一款或多款免费游戏，领取后永久保留在库中。曾送过《GTA5》《文明6》《蝙蝠侠》等大作。建议下载 Epic 客户端，每周登录领一下，积少成多。 补充阅读 以下内容为 Steam 和 Epic 的进阶使用技巧。 补充1：Steam 退款政策 在 Steam 购买游戏后，如果游玩时间不超过 2 小时且购买时间不超过 14 天，可以申请无理由退款。退款会原路返回支付账户（或退到 Steam 钱包）。适合试玩后不喜欢的游戏。 退款路径：Steam 客服 → 选择游戏 → 我要退款。 补充2：Steam 愿望单与折扣通知 将游戏加入愿望单后，当游戏打折时 Steam 会发送邮件通知。大型促销（夏促、冬促、春节特卖）期间许多游戏折扣达到 2-5 折，建议等促销再入手。 补充3：Steam 云存档 Steam 默认开启云存档。游戏存档会自动同步到服务器，换电脑登录后存档自动下载。部分老游戏可能不支持。可以在游戏属性中查看和手动管理。 补充4：Epic 与 Steam 的互联 部分游戏支持跨平台联机（如《火箭联盟》《糖豆人》）。但 Epic 和 Steam 是两个独立平台，游戏库不互通。同一款游戏在两个平台都买了也无法共享进度（除非游戏本身支持跨平台存档）。 补充5：Epic 的优惠券与返利 Epic 有时会发放 10 美元优惠券（适用于 14.99 美元以上游戏），配合折扣可以极低价入手游戏。另外 Epic 有“Epic 奖励”返利计划，每笔消费返 5%（可用作下次购买抵扣）。 补充6：游戏激活码 从第三方网站（如杉果、Humble Bundle）购买的 Steam 激活码，在 Steam 客户端左下角“添加游戏”→“在 Steam 上激活产品”中输入即可入库。注意辨别来源，不要购买来路不明的黑卡码（可能会被回收甚至封号）。 补充7：Steam 大屏幕模式 Steam 内置大屏幕模式（控制器图标），界面针对手柄和电视优化，适合连接手柄在客厅游玩。也可用于在平板上串流游戏（Steam Link 应用）。

title: 技巧和名词表
content: 附录九：快捷键、小技巧与名词表 这个附录整理了一些你可能用得到的小技巧，还有一堆听起来很唬人的名词。不用急着全部记住，先有个印象就行。以后哪天遇到问题，或者看到哪个词觉得眼熟，翻回来查一查就好。 一、快捷键表 这些快捷键大部分在 Windows 里通用。用熟之后会比鼠标快很多。 | 快捷键 | 做什么的 | |--------|----------| | | 复制 | | | 粘贴 | | | 剪切 | | | 撤销上一步 | | | 重做（把撤销的那一步找回来） | | | 全选 | | | 保存 | | | 查找（在网页、文档里搜索文字） | | | 切换窗口（按住 Alt 再按 Tab 可以选择） | | | 打开任务视图，可以新建桌面 | | | 打开“此电脑”（文件资源管理器） | | | 显示桌面，再按一次恢复 | | | 锁屏 | | | 打开“运行”窗口 | | | 打开设置 | | | 打开搜索 | | | 打开快速链接菜单（下一节会细说） | | | 截图 | | | 直接打开任务管理器 | | | 打开剪贴板历史（需先在设置里开启） | | 或 | 打开表情符号面板 | | | 打开任务栏上第几个程序 | | | 窗口分屏（左右半屏、最大化、最小化） | | | 在文件资源管理器里新建文件夹 | | | 关掉当前窗口；桌面状态下按会弹出关机选项 | | | 重命名选中的文件 | | | 刷新 | | | 删除文件（会进回收站） | | | 彻底删除（不进回收站，想清楚再用） | 二、小技巧 2.1 右键 Windows 徽标键（Win + X） 在屏幕左下角的开始按钮上点右键，或者按 ，会弹出一个菜单。里面的东西都是系统自带的管理工具，比你去控制面板翻来翻去快得多。 | 菜单里的选项 | 是干什么的 | |--------------|------------| | 应用和功能 | 卸载不需要的程序 | | 移动中心 | 调亮度、音量、投屏 | | 电源选项 | 改睡眠时间、电源计划 | | 事件查看器（Event Viewer） | 看系统日志，蓝屏原因常在这里 | | 系统 | 看电脑配置（CPU、内存、Windows版本） | | 设备管理器（Device Manager） | 查看和更新驱动 | | 网络连接 | 看网卡、手动填 IP 地址 | | 磁盘管理（Disk Management） | 给硬盘分区 | | 计算机管理（Computer Management） | 整合了好几个管理工具 | | Windows PowerShell / 终端（Terminal） | 打开命令行 | | 任务管理器（Task Manager） | 看进程、看性能、关掉卡死的程序 | 这个菜单里的东西大部分需要管理员权限。平时排查问题的时候，这里是最快的入口。 2.2 文件资源管理器的选中技巧 在文件资源管理器（File Explorer，就是打开“此电脑”后看到的那个窗口）里，选中文件的时候有两个很常用的方式： 按住 再点文件：可以一个一个挑着选。比如你先点了一个文件，按住 Ctrl 再点另一个，两个都会被选中；再点一次其中某个，可以把它从选中里取消。适合“我要挑这几个，不要那一个”的情况。 先点一个文件，然后按住 再点另一个文件：会把这两个文件之间的所有文件（包括中间的那些）一次性全选中。适合“我要从 A 到 B 这一整段”的情况。 这两个可以配合用。比如先按 Shift 选一段连续的范围，再按住 Ctrl 选中几个分散的。 2.3 任务管理器里能看到 PID 打开任务管理器（Task Manager， ），点“进程（Process）”，你会看到一列表格。在表头那一行（显示“名称”“CPU”“内存”的那一行）上点右键，可以勾选更多列。其中有一个叫 PID。 PID（Process Identifier，进程标识符）：系统给每个正在运行的程序（进程）分配的一个编号，每个程序都不一样。 有什么用：有时候一个程序卡死了，但任务管理器里有好几个同名的，你分不清该结束哪一个。这时候看 PID 就能区分。另外有些命令行工具（比如 ）也需要用 PID 来指定要关掉哪个进程。 勾选方法：任务管理器 → 详细信息 → 右键点击表头 → 选择列（Select columns）→ 勾选“PID”。 2.4 Windows Terminal 与 PowerShell 7 Windows Terminal：一个现代的命令行窗口程序。比起传统的 CMD 黑窗口，它支持多标签页、可以分屏、字体渲染更清晰，还能自定义主题。附录七里介绍过，装好之后把它固定在任务栏，以后所有命令行操作都从这里进。Windows Terminal 本身只是一个“壳”，里面可以跑 CMD、PowerShell 或者任何其他命令行工具。 PowerShell 7：一个命令行工具。和 Windows 系统自带的 Windows PowerShell（版本 5.x）是两个版本，可以共存。它的命令更统一，功能更强，还能跨平台（Windows、Mac、Linux 都能用）。普通用户不一定需要装，但如果你以后写脚本或者跟着某些教程操作，可能会用到。 两者的关系：Windows Terminal 是“窗户”，PowerShell 7 是“窗户里坐着的那个人”。你打开 Windows Terminal，在里面可以新建一个标签页跑 PowerShell 7。 2.5 环境变量 环境变量（Environment Variable）：可以理解成系统里的一些“全局小纸条”。每张小纸条上写着一个名字和对应的值，任何程序运行的时候都可以看这些小纸条，知道去哪里找东西。 常见的有： PATH：记录了一堆文件夹路径。你在命令行里敲 ，系统会挨个去这些文件夹里找 。你安装 Python 或者 FFmpeg 之后想在命令行里直接运行，本质上就是把它们的安装路径加到了 PATH 里。 TEMP：临时文件放在哪里。 USERNAME：当前登录的用户名。 怎么改：右键“此电脑”→ 属性 → 高级系统设置（Advanced system settings）→ 环境变量（Environment Variables）。分“用户变量（User variables）”（只对当前用户生效）和“系统变量（System variables）”（对所有用户生效）。 你不需要现在就会改。但如果以后你在命令行里敲一个命令，提示“不是内部或外部命令”，你知道可能是 PATH 没配好，往这个方向去搜就行。 2.6 注册表 注册表（Registry）：Windows 的一个巨型配置数据库。你平时在设置里改的东西——桌面壁纸、开机启动项、文件夹选项——最终都会写到注册表里。 怎么打开： ，输入 ，回车。 里面长什么样：左边是“项”（Key，像文件夹），右边是“值”（Value，像文件）。几个最顶层的叫根键（Root Key）： ：当前用户的设置 ：整台电脑的全局设置 ：文件关联（比如 默认用记事本打开） 一个重要警告：改错注册表可能会让软件出问题，严重的时候系统都开不了机。动手改之前，一定记得备份：右键点你要改的那个项 → 导出（Export），存一个 文件。万一改坏了，双击那个文件就能恢复。 你不需要现在就会改。但以后你在网上搜到某个教程说“改注册表可以解决某某问题”，你知道注册表是干什么的，也知道改之前要先备份，这就够了。 2.7 组策略 组策略（Group Policy）：你可以把它理解成“注册表的图形化开关”。组策略把一堆相关的注册表修改打包成了一个个选项，你只需要选“启用（Enabled）”或者“禁用（Disabled）”，系统自动帮你改注册表，不用自己去翻。 怎么打开： ，输入 ，回车。（注意：Windows 家庭版默认没有这个功能。） 举个例子：你想禁用 USB 存储设备，防止别人插 U 盘拷你的文件。在组策略里找到“可移动存储访问”，选“拒绝所有权限”，启用了就行。如果让你自己去注册表里找对应的位置，可能找半天。 家庭版用户想用组策略的话，可以搜一下“gpedit-enabler”这种工具，但不保证稳定，也不一定要折腾。 2.8 内存管理相关 以下三个概念在任务管理器的“性能（Performance）”标签页里可以看到。 页面文件（Page File） 页面文件是硬盘上的一个隐藏文件（通常叫 ）。它还有一个名字叫 SWAP（交换文件）。当你的物理内存（RAM）不够用的时候，系统会把内存里暂时用不到的数据挪到这个文件里，把空出来的内存给当前需要运行的程序用。 可以理解成：你的桌子（内存）太小，放不下所有东西，就把暂时不用的资料先收到抽屉（硬盘）里，要用的时候再拿出来。硬盘比内存慢得多，所以如果系统频繁使用页面文件，电脑会明显变卡。 C 盘空间不足的时候，页面文件无法正常扩展，电脑就会卡顿。这也是为什么附录二里反复强调不要把 C 盘塞满。 已提交（Commit） 任务管理器里显示的“已提交”是一个总量，表示“系统已经承诺分给所有程序的内存总和”。这个数字可以大于你的物理内存——因为有一部分承诺是通过页面文件来兑现的。 打个比方：你手头只有 100 块钱现金（物理内存），但你的信用卡有 200 块钱额度（页面文件的空间）。你能“承诺”花掉的钱可以超过 100 块，只要最终从信用卡里补上就行。 当“已提交”的总量超过了物理内存 + 页面文件的总和，系统就会提示“内存不足”，甚至可能强制关掉一些程序。 分页缓冲池（Paged Pool）与非分页缓冲池（Nonpaged Pool） Windows 内核（Kernel，系统的核心部分）会给自己留一块内存，专门放一些关键数据。这块内存分为两种： 非分页缓冲池（Nonpaged Pool）：永远呆在物理内存里，不会被挪到页面文件。因为有些关键数据（比如处理硬件中断的）必须随时能用，不能等从硬盘读回来。 分页缓冲池（Paged Pool）：可以被挪到页面文件。里面放的是那些“需要的时候能等一下”的内核数据。 普通用户不需要关心这两个池的具体数值。但在任务管理器的性能页面看到它们的时候，知道“分页的可以挪到硬盘，非分页的必须留在内存”就够了。 2.9 硬件编解码器 硬件编解码器（Hardware Encoder/Decoder）：显卡（GPU）里面有一块专门的电路，用来做视频的编码或者解码。这块电路和显卡跑游戏的流处理器是分开的。 硬件解码（Hardware Decoding）：播放视频的时候，用显卡里这块专门电路来解码。CPU 几乎不用干活，功耗低，发热小，播放高码率 4K 视频也不会卡。 硬件编码（Hardware Encoding）：录屏、直播、导出视频的时候，用这块电路来压缩视频。速度快，对游戏帧数影响小。 软件编解码器（Software Encoder/Decoder）：用 CPU 来做这些事。CPU 虽然也能干，但效率比硬件电路低很多。播放 4K 视频或者导出视频的时候，CPU 容易跑满，电脑变卡，发热也大。 你实际会遇到的情况： 用 OBS 录游戏，编码器选 NVENC（NVIDIA 硬件编码）或者 QSV（Intel 核显硬件编码），就是让显卡硬件编码。对游戏帧数影响小。 播放一个高码率 4K 视频，CPU 占用很高，说明播放器没用上硬件解码。去播放器设置里找“硬件解码”或者“DXVA”选项，打开它。 任务管理器的“性能”页面里，GPU 那一栏通常会有“Video Encode”“Video Decode”两个小图，显示硬件编解码器的占用率。 2.10 磁盘性能相关 IOPS（Input/Output Per Second，每秒输入输出次数） 衡量硬盘处理“零散小文件”的能力。比如你打开一个有很多小图的文件夹、在游戏里加载场景、开虚拟机，这些场景下 IOPS 比顺序速度更重要。 机械硬盘（HDD）：几十到一百多 IOPS 普通 SATA SSD：几千到几万 IOPS 好一点的 NVMe SSD：几十万甚至上百万 IOPS 这也是为什么把操作系统装在固态硬盘上，开机速度、打开软件的速度会快那么多——不是因为顺序读写有多快，而是 IOPS 比机械硬盘高了几百上千倍。 MB/s 与 Mbps 这两个单位经常被弄混，尤其在测网速的时候。 MB/s（Megabyte per second，兆字节每秒）：你复制文件时看到的那个速度。1 MB/s 就是一秒传 1 兆字节的数据。 Mbps（Megabit per second，兆比特每秒）：宽带套餐里说的那个速度。比如 100 兆宽带，指的是 100 Mbps。 换算关系：1 MB/s = 8 Mbps。所以 100 兆的宽带，理论最快下载速度是 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB/s。 记住了：小写的 b 是比特（bit），大写的 B 是字节（byte），1 字节 = 8 比特。网速除以 8，才是你看到的下文件的速度。 MB/s 和 IOPS 的关系：这两个不是一回事。MB/s 是“一秒能传多少数据”，IOPS 是“一秒能处理多少个请求”。拷贝一个大电影文件，考验的是 MB/s；同时打开一千张小图片，考验的是 IOPS。一块好硬盘，两项都应该好，但价格也更贵。 2.11 留下印象即可 环境变量、注册表、组策略、页面文件这几个东西，你现在不需要会改，更不要乱动。但“留个印象”很重要： 以后装软件时命令行提示“不是内部或外部命令”——你知道可能是 PATH 的问题。 以后网上教程说“改注册表”——你知道那是什么，改之前要备份。 以后系统报“内存不足”——你知道可能是物理内存或者页面文件空间不够了。 以后电脑突然变卡，C 盘又红了——你知道可能是页面文件受影响。 以后播放视频卡顿或者 CPU 占用很高——你知道可能是没用上硬件解码。 以后测网速看到数字和下载速度对不上——你知道 Mbps 和 MB/s 要除以 8。 知道大概是什么东西、出了问题往哪个方向查，已经比绝大多数用户强了。 三、名词表 3.1 进程 进程（Process）：一个正在运行的程序。你打开一个浏览器、一个游戏、一个记事本，系统就给你创建了一个进程。每个进程有自己的内存空间，互不干扰。 在任务管理器里结束一个卡死的程序，本质就是杀掉它的进程。注意不要随便结束名字看起来像系统进程的东西（比如 ），可能让电脑出问题。 3.2 线程 线程（Thread）：一个进程可以有多个线程。线程是真正干活的人。 打个比方：进程是一个工厂，线程是工厂里的工人。一个工厂可以只有一个工人（单线程），也可以有多个工人同时干活（多线程，Multithreading）。多线程的好处是能同时做几件事——浏览器一边下载文件一边渲染网页，就是多线程的功劳。 任务管理器里的 CPU 占用率，其实是所有线程占用率的和。一个高负载的程序往往有好几十甚至上百个线程。 3.3 句柄 句柄（Handle）：一个整数编号，Windows 用它来指代某个资源（比如一个打开的文件、一个窗口、一个线程）。你打开一个文件，系统给你返回一个句柄；以后对这个文件的操作（读、写、关闭）都要通过这个句柄。 句柄泄漏（Handle Leak）：程序用完资源之后忘了关闭句柄，导致这个资源一直被占用。最常见的症状就是：你想删一个文件，系统提示“文件被占用”，但你已经关掉了所有可能打开它的程序。很可能就是某个进程的句柄没关掉。 可以用 Process Explorer 或者 LockHunter 这类工具查看是哪个进程占着不放。 3.4 更多名词速查 | 中文 | 英文 | 简单解释 | |------|------|----------| | 应用程序编程接口 | API（Application Programming Interface） | 程序之间互相调用的约定 | | 基本输入输出系统 / 统一可扩展固件接口 | BIOS / UEFI（Basic Input/Output System / Unified Extensible Firmware Interface） | 主板上的底层系统，负责开机和初始化硬件 | | 动态链接库 | DLL（Dynamic Link Library） | 一段可以被多个程序共用的代码 | | 驱动程序 | Driver | 让操作系统认识和控制硬件的“翻译官” | | 图形用户界面 | GUI（Graphical User Interface） | 就是你点来点去的那些窗口和按钮 | | 安全外壳协议 | SSH（Secure Shell） | 一种加密的网络协议，用于安全地远程登录另一台电脑 | | 命令行界面 | CLI（Command Line Interface） | 就是那个黑窗口 | | 内核 | Kernel | 操作系统的核心，管着硬件、进程、内存 | | 内存 | RAM（Random Access Memory） | 断电数据就没了 | | 只读存储器 | ROM（Read-Only Memory） | 一般用来存固件，用户改不了 | | 软件开发工具包 | SDK（Software Development Kit） | 开发某个平台需要的工具合集 | | 命令行解释器 | Shell | CMD 和 PowerShell 都算 Shell | | 通用唯一标识符 | UUID / GUID（Universally Unique Identifier / Globally Unique Identifier） | 一串很长几乎不会重复的编号，用来唯一标识某个东西 |

title: Welcome Letter
content: To Whom It May Concern — Being an Epistolary Address to the Young Graduate, on the Eve of a New and Unwritten Age It was the best of times, it was the worst of times — though those words were written of a distant revolution, they fit your own case with a curious and rather startling accuracy. For you have just closed one book, and now another lies open before you, its pages blank, its margins wide, its ink not yet dry. And between these two volumes — between the last examination and the first independent click of a mouse — there stands a machine. A laptop. A computer. A box of glass and silicon and quiet, humming mystery. Perhaps it arrived wrapped in cardboard and bubble‑wrap, a gift from parents who smiled as you tore the tape away. Perhaps you saved, week after week, from part‑time wages or New Year’s money, until the price became a number you could bear to part with. Perhaps it came second‑hand, passed down from an older cousin who said, with the solemnity of a prophet, “She’s got a few more years in her.” However it came to sit upon your desk, it is now yours. Yours alone. And you have not the faintest idea what to do with it. Do not blush at this confession. Do not lower your eyes. Every person who has ever touched a keyboard — every engineer, every designer, every gamer who has ever shouted at a lagging screen — was once exactly where you are now. They stared at the unfamiliar glow and felt the same small, honest fear: What if I break it? Let me tell you a secret. You will not break it. Not truly. Not in any way that cannot be undone. Modern machines are built with the patience of saints and the forgetfulness of goldfish. They have been dropped, drenched, buried under laundry, and still they rise again. The worst you can do — a mistaken deletion, a misplaced folder, a toolbar that multiplies like rabbits — is a small and fixable thing. There are no final mistakes here. There is only discovery, and the gentle art of learning what that curious button does. For eighteen years, you have lived in a world where questions came with answer keys. The teacher asked, the textbook replied, and the exam measured how well you remembered. But this machine has no answer key. It has no final exam. No one will stand over your shoulder and tell you that you clicked the wrong icon. The only authority in this new world is you. That is a terrifying thought. And also a glorious one. I wrote this guide because I remember the first time I held my own computer. I remember the weight of it, the smell of new plastic, the way the screen reflected my own uncertain face. I remember the voice that whispered, What if I break it? And I remember the quiet afternoon, weeks later, when I fixed something that I had broken — and felt, for the first time, not like a user, but like a person who understood. This book is not a textbook. You need not read it from the first page to the last, nor memorise its passages, nor fear its footnotes. Skim it. Leap about. Read the parts that speak to your present trouble — the file that will not open, the Wi‑Fi that will not connect, the question that you cannot quite put into words. Set it down when you grow weary, and take it up again when curiosity returns. I have tried to write as I would speak to a friend sitting across a table: plainly, sometimes bluntly, but always with the hope that you will leave with more than you brought. You will find here recommendations for software that does not steal your attention, systems for organising your digital life so that you are not forever searching, explanations of the words that sound like spells but are merely tools. You will find warnings against the traps that caught me and a thousand others — the unnecessary optimisations, the predatory downloads, the beliefs that sound wise but are only old. And you will find, if you look, a few invitations to wander down paths that lead to unexpected places. One last thing before you begin your journey. You are leaving a world where most questions had a single, correct, right‑hand‑column answer. The world inside this machine has many answers. Many tools. Many ways to accomplish the same small task. I will show you the ways that worked for me and for the thousands who came before. But you will, in time, find your own. That is not a failure of this guide. That is its only real purpose. So, dear graduate — dear friend I have never met — take a breath. The screen is dark, but it will not stay so. Place your fingers on the keyboard. Press the power button. Hear the fan begin its quiet whir. You have finished one chapter. Now another begins — unwritten, ungraded, and entirely yours. — A fellow traveller, who once stood where you now stand

title: Resources
content: Appendix 21: Resources This appendix shares some useful resources. For anything involving copyright issues, please use your own judgment. The content here is presented as‑is, without endorsement. Useful Sites and Software rutor.is: A Russian site with a wide selection of games, movies, and TV shows. It updates quickly and has a good variety. It is not difficult to use – you can figure it out with a little trial and error. FitGirl Repack: Specialises in highly compressed game repacks. If your internet connection is slow or your hard drive space is limited, her versions are worth considering – they are very small, and after installation, the games run perfectly. The official domain changes from time to time, so just search for the latest one. Kazumi: An app for watching anime. It is a powerful media player on its own, but you need to connect third‑party sources (e.g., Yinghua Dongman, DM84). Search for it yourself and follow the official guide. Once configured, watching online is very convenient. AnimeGarden: If you prefer not to stream or want to download anime music, this is a good place. It is a mirror of the Angel Anime forum – search and access are much faster than on the original site. It mostly provides magnet links, suitable for downloading with a torrent client. Baidu Tieba is also a surprisingly good resource. For obscure, old, or niche games – and fan translation patches – the forums (sub‑communities called "tieba") often have people who actually store and share them. Look for posts where the moderator or a member shares a cloud storage link; dig through the comments, and you will often find something useful. You do not need the standalone app – just use a browser. 3DM and Youmin Xingkong (GameStar) are long‑standing single‑player game sites with comprehensive resources. However, games downloaded from Youmin often come with pop‑up ads or a custom launcher – annoying, but the games still run. If that bothers you, check the comments to see if someone has posted a link to a "clean" or "portable" version. Basic Etiquette Before downloading anything from a forum or site, it is a good idea to read the comments. People often report things like "the link is dead" or "what is the extraction password?" After you finish downloading, if the forum requires a reply, do not just post "+3" to pad your count – say something useful, like "the link works" or "the download speed is decent." If you act like a leech for too long, eventually there will be no place left to borrow from. When you encounter someone who shares resources generously on a forum, on Tieba, or in a group – maybe they bought a game with their own money, uploaded it, maybe they spent time creating a fan translation patch, maybe they curated a collection of dozens of old games – do not just download silently. Post a reply. Say "thank you for sharing" or "you are a kind soul." It costs you nothing, but it makes the sharer feel appreciated. Potential Problems You May Encounter When downloading "learning edition" games (unofficial/repack releases), you may run into some odd things: Mojibake (garbled file names) : A mess of random characters. You may need a special tool to decode them. Split archives: A pile of , , files. You must download all of them before you can extract the game. Nested archives: You extract one archive, only to find another archive inside – and maybe another layer after that. Passwords: An extraction password is required. It is usually hidden in the post (e.g., behind a spoiler tag or in a comment). These annoyances are actually good learning opportunities. To get the game working, you will actively search for things like "how to decode mojibake file names" or "how to extract lz4 archives". As you search, you will discover that these problems are not that hard. The next time you run into them, you will already know what to do. A Delicate Matter If you are interested in Japanese games or ASMR, DLsite is a legitimate platform. There are many tutorials on Bilibili that walk you through creating an account, buying points, waiting for discounts, and using coupons. Supporting the creators is not expensive, and it gives you peace of mind. Avoid doing things you should not do. Be discreet and stay out of trouble. A Personal Recommendation: A Game I Truly Like Finally, allow me to indulge in a little personal bias – if you are comfortable with adult games, I highly recommend Alice in Cradle. In a nutshell, it is a side‑scrolling action RPG (ACT + RPG) , in the Metroidvania style. You play as Noelle, a young elf girl, exploring, fighting, and solving puzzles in a magical fantasy forest. The combat system revolves around spell casting – you combine button presses to unleash different spells. The story takes place in a world built on "mana", where elves, orcs, and demons coexist. The character design is thoughtful, the pixel art is exquisite, and the music is excellent. A word of warning: the game is R‑18 rated, with some adult content (e.g., defeat CG scenes). There is a "safe mode" in the settings that you can turn on. If this bothers you, look elsewhere. If it does not, you will find a doujin (indie) game that is genuinely well‑crafted in terms of gameplay. You can search for "Alice In Cradle" on Moegirl (Mengniang Baike) – the entry there is very detailed. On Bilibili, there is an official account and many guide videos. The game is still being updated, and a free demo is available for download. If you try it and end up liking it, then we share the same taste. One final thought There is no shortage of resources online. What matters is how you find them, how you use them, and how you treat the people who share them. Stay curious, stay polite, and that will serve you better than hoarding hundreds of gigabytes of files.

title: GameRecommendation
content: Appendix 22: Game Recommendations This appendix lists games I genuinely like, sorted by category. These are purely personal tastes – take them as suggestions, not gospel. I do not play competitive games, and my setup cannot handle the latest high‑spec blockbusters, so this list only covers games I can actually run, have played, and truly enjoyed. If your tastes align with mine, this may be useful. If not, treat it as a casual glimpse. Visual Novels (VN) Ever17 -the out of infinity- A classic sci‑fi mystery VN developed by KID and written by Kotaro Uchikoshi. The player is trapped in the underwater theme park "LeMU" and must escape before the 119‑hour countdown reaches zero. The story alternates between two protagonists (a teenage boy and a young man) across four character routes. The payoff comes at the end of the final route – a few minutes of revelations that recontextualise everything you thought you knew, leaving your scalp tingling. 9-nine- (Complete Series) An battle romance AVG from PALETTE, split into four episodes plus a finale. Set in the city of Batsubutsugawa after an earthquake gave rise to "artifacts" that grant supernatural abilities. Protagonist Shinji watches as the city's ordinary life unravels. The first two episodes are standard moe‑style paranormal battles. The third episode takes off, and by the fourth (Snow of the White Snow), the writer pulls the player themselves into the story in a way that is quietly devastating. The fourth wall of the visual novel genre is shattered, and you never even noticed it being built. ATRI -My Dear Moments- A short, all‑ages visual novel published by Aniplex.EXE. In a post‑apocalyptic world of rising seas, a boy named Natsuki salvages a robot girl, Atri, from the ocean floor. The high‑spirited "high‑performance robo‑daughter" greets him with "Master!" and fills their daily seaside life with warmth and laughter. But three diaries reveal the truth – all that cheerful everyday life is a setup for a farewell. In just eight hours, it tells a complete arc of meeting, bonding, parting, and a reunion spanning decades. Summer Pockets REFLECTION BLUE Key's long‑form, all‑ages crying game. Set on the island of Torishiro in the Seto Inland Sea. Protagonist Hairi goes to pack up his late grandmother's belongings and ends up spending his summer with the island's girls. "Summer", "nostalgia", and "memory" are the central themes. REFLECTION BLUE adds four new routes and a massive amount of new CG – it is the definitive edition and a culmination of Key's later work. eden\ An all‑ages visual novel from minori. No choices – a single, straight path. With Earth about to be destroyed, a super‑weapon "Felix" girl named Sion spends her final days delivering humanity's last evacuation ship. When the order comes to evacuate, the protagonist, Ryou, chooses to stay behind on the dying planet and accompany her to the very end. Presented in full cinematic widescreen, with music by Tenmon. It is about "goodbye", executed with absolute purity and romance. Triple‑A Games GTA5 Need I say more? Los Santos. The single‑player campaign's three protagonists (Michael, Trevor, Franklin) deliver a masterclass in love‑hate relationships. The online mode is a criminal empire that can swallow thousands of hours. GTA6 Confirmed by Take‑Two – scheduled for November 19, 2026, on PS5 and Xbox Series. Red Dead Redemption 2 One of the highest achievements in open‑world storytelling. 1899, the dying days of the American frontier. Arthur Morgan's struggle between loyalty to his gang and his own redemption. Slow‑paced, dense with detail, and capable of absorbing hundreds of hours. Rockstar co‑founder Dan Houser called it "the best work he's ever been part of". Cyberpunk 2077 A disastrous launch, reborn after two years. Night City's density and immersion are unique in open‑world games. Version 2.0 and the Phantom Liberty DLC rebuilt the game from the ground up – it is now what was promised. If you are new, play the base game first, then watch the spin‑off anime Edgerunners. It hits hard. Indie Games Disco Elysium A detective RPG with no traditional combat – everything is driven by dialogue and skill checks. You are an amnesiac detective tasked with investigating a hanged corpse outside the Whirling‑in‑Rags. Your stat points go into things like "Inland Empire", "Hand/Eye Coordination", and "Encyclopedia" – each skill is a voice in your head, and they argue with each other. The script won a Hugo Award, the only game ever to do so. Save often – you can die in very strange ways. Rain World You are a slugcat, trying to survive in a fully simulated ecosystem of ruins. Every creature has its own behavioural logic – they hunt you, are hunted by apex predators, migrate, sleep, fight. They do not care about you. The game is brutally hard, with a vertical learning curve. But once you cross that threshold, you will find one of the most profound works ever made about the transition from prey to predator. It started with a Metacritic score of 59, but the devs kept updating for seven years. Today it sits at 94% positive on Steam, with the massive expansion Downpour and a 2025 DLC, The Watcher. Öoo A caterpillar is swallowed by a giant bird. You must escape before you are digested. Your only tool is a bomb that regenerates infinitely – blast your way through obstacles, trigger mechanisms, and even launch yourself higher with the explosion. About 2–3 hours long, completely wordless. Made by three Japanese indie developers working together. The art style resembles Animal Well. It achieved overwhelming positive reviews on Steam in its first week. Noita Every pixel has its own physical properties – burning, melting, exploding, conducting electricity. You wander through procedurally generated caves collecting wands, then combine spells like programming: split on trigger, delayed cast, projectile modifiers – almost any combination works, including ones that instantly kill yourself. No saves. One life. Back to the start. Lobotomy Corporation Project Moon's first game. You play the manager of a facility that extracts energy from "Abnormalities" – creatures born from humanity's collective subconscious. Each Abnormality has its own escape mechanics and handling logic. Your employees will die, and they will die horribly. This is where the game's massive urban fantasy world begins. Library of Ruina Continues from the ending of Lobotomy Corporation. Angela builds a library in the ruins, inviting "guests" to visit – those who lose become books. The card‑battle system revolves around "emotion levels": instead of just playing whatever you draw, you accumulate emotion through clashes, and your hand is reshuffled every turn. This is where Project Moon's storytelling truly opens up. Limbus Company Project Moon's third game, and their first cross‑platform title. You play the manager of a bus, dragging 12 sinners (all familiar faces from the Lobotomy Corporation era) through the City to collect golden branches. Turn‑based combat with real‑time clash decisions. Still updating. osu! An open‑source, community‑driven rhythm game. Four modes (standard, taiko, catch the fruit, piano). Player‑made beatmaps are the core. The entry barrier is low, but the skill ceiling is absurd – playing the same map hundreds of times is normal. Casualties: Unknown A brutal cave‑exploration survival game. You are a prisoner sent to an alien planet to retrieve lost cargo, exploring 11 layers of caves. Its standout feature is a comprehensive limb and cardiovascular simulation – wounds need bandaging, infections need treatment, blood loss must be managed. Your mood affects your survival odds; excessive pessimism makes everything worse. Three playable characters with different playstyles, 300 discoverable items, and adjustable loot rates in the main menu. Still in demo, but already very enjoyable and punishing. Highly recommended for the curious. Outer Wilds Very good. Very moving. Very healing. A game you can only truly play once. Mods Many games have modding communities. Search Nexus Mods – it is the world's largest game mod sharing platform. Almost every popular game has user‑created mods there. It is free; you just need to create an account to download. The free download speed is slow, but it works.

title: Git
content: Appendix 23: Git This appendix introduces the basics of Git. Git is a version control tool that records every change you make to your files, allowing you to return to any previous version at any time. Whether you are writing a thesis, code, or any kind of document, Git saves you from the endless cycle of "final.doc", "finalv2.doc", "finalv2really.doc", and "finalv2reallythistimefor_real.doc". 23.1 Why Use Git? When writing a thesis, you have probably experienced something like this: Then your supervisor says: "I think the structure of the first draft was better – can we go back to that?" You are left searching through a dozen files, afraid to delete the wrong one. Git solves this. It records every change, and you can revert to any historical version at any time. You only ever need one file – no more creating multiple copies. What Git gives you: Every change is logged; you can always see what was modified and when. Reverting to any previous version is just one command away. You can create "branches" to experiment safely, without affecting your main version. When collaborating with others, no one accidentally overwrites someone else's work. 23.2 Installing Git Windows: Visit , download the installer, and follow the default options. After installation, search for "Git Bash" in the Start menu – if a command‑line window opens, you are good to go. macOS: Open Terminal and type . If Git is not installed, macOS will prompt you to install the Command Line Tools – follow the instructions. Linux (Ubuntu/Debian): After installation, open a terminal (Git Bash on Windows, Terminal on macOS/Linux) and set your name and email (these are just for tracking who made changes; you can use anything): 23.3 Initialising a Repository ( ) Git turns a folder into a repository, storing all version history inside that folder. How to do it: In File Explorer, create a dedicated folder for your thesis, e.g., . Right‑click the folder → select "Git Bash Here" (if you have Git installed). In the terminal, type: You will see a message like . That folder is where Git keeps all its history. Do not touch it. From now on, any changes you make inside the folder can be recorded by Git. 23.4 Your First Commit A "commit" is a snapshot of all your current files, saved into Git's history. Scenario: You have just finished the first chapter of your thesis and want to save a checkpoint. Steps: Add the file to the "staging area" – this tells Git "I want to save these files": To add all files in the current folder at once: Commit with a message (use to add a short description of what you changed): Now your first chapter has a version record. Whenever you reach a milestone, repeat + . Viewing history: This lists all commits, each with a hash (like ), author, date, and commit message. 23.5 Checking the Status At any time, type: This tells you: Red files: modified but not yet ed. Green files: added but not yet ted. Clean working directory: all changes are committed. Get into the habit of running often – you will always know exactly where you stand. 23.6 Branches: Experiment Without Fear Branches are Git's most powerful feature. Think of them as parallel universes. Scenario: Your supervisor says, "Try restructuring Chapter 3, but I am not sure if it will work – just give it a try." You do not want to break your existing version, but you want to experiment. How to do it: Create a new branch from the current version: This creates a branch called "experimental-changes" that is identical to your current main branch (often called or ). Switch to the new branch: Or do both in one command: Make any changes you like and commit them freely. Even if you mess up, your main branch remains untouched. To switch back to the main branch: Your files will revert to the main branch state; all experimental changes are safely stored in the "experimental-changes" branch. List all branches: The branch with a next to it is the one you are currently on. 23.7 Merging: Bringing Experimental Work Back If your experimental changes turned out well and your supervisor approves, you can merge them back into the main branch. How to do it: Switch back to the main branch: Perform the merge: Git will incorporate all the changes from the "experimental-changes" branch into the main branch. If both branches changed the same line of the same file, Git will flag a conflict. You will need to resolve it manually – Git marks the conflicting sections in the file with , , and . Choose which version to keep, delete the markers, then save, add, and commit. If the experiment fails: Just delete the branch – the main branch is unaffected: 23.8 Real‑World Scenario: Your Supervisor Edits Your Thesis Your supervisor says, "I made some edits to Chapter 3" and sends you a revised file. You overwrite your old file with the new one. How can Git show you exactly what your supervisor changed? How to do it: Before overwriting, ensure all your changes are committed ( should be clean). Replace the old file with the new one your supervisor sent. Use to see the differences: This shows every line that changed – green for additions, red for deletions. After reviewing, commit the changes: If your supervisor sends multiple revisions: Repeat the steps each time. Git preserves the history of every version, so you can always go back. 23.9 Going Back in Time: What If You Regret a Change? Scenario: You have been working for three days and realise the direction is wrong. You want to go back to the version from three days ago. View the history and find the hash of the version you want (the first few characters are enough): Go back to that version: Your files will revert to that state. If you want to continue working from there, create a new branch. For a more drastic "go back" (discard all subsequent changes): ⚠️ Warning: permanently deletes all later changes. Think twice before using it. 23.10 Quick Command Reference | Command | What it does | |---------|---------------| | | Initialise a new repository | | | Add a file to the staging area | | | Add all changes to the staging area | | | Commit the staged changes | | | Show the current status | | | Show the commit history | | | Show a concise history (one line per commit) | | | Show unstaged changes | | | Show staged but uncommitted changes | | | List all branches | | | Create a new branch | | | Switch to a branch | | | Create and switch to a new branch | | | Merge the specified branch into the current branch | | | Delete a branch | | | Switch to a specific historical version | | | Permanently revert to a specific historical version | Extended Reading The following sections cover more advanced Git usage. Come back when you need them. Extended 1: The File Some files should not be tracked by Git – for example, temporary build files, system caches, or large binaries. Create a file in the root of your repository and list the files or patterns you want to ignore: Git will automatically ignore these files and they will not appear in . Extended 2: Amending the Last Commit If you just committed but realise you made a typo in the message or forgot to include a file: This modifies the most recent commit without creating a new one. title: Appendix0
content: Appendix 0: To the Friend Who Walked Beside Me in the Half‑Dark — A small note of thanks, tucked inside a technical manual, for someone who might just recognise these moments Before I begin talking about hard drives and memory modules, about file systems and firewalls and all the cold, orderly things that live inside a machine, I need to say something about something that lives outside it — something warmer, far less orderly, and quietly important to me. This isn't a chapter of instruction. It has no diagrams, no command lines, no troubleshooting steps. If I'm honest, it's a letter. A letter slipped between the pages of a book about computers, where a certain friend of mine might come across it one day. I've written this guide for many people — classmates who've never owned a laptop, friends who click and hope, strangers who will download the file and forget it by morning. But this appendix is for one specific friend. Someone with a tight ponytail that swings when she walks — a walk that is determined and slightly sideways, as if the pavement is a friend she's in a hurry to greet. That person is you. You've always been a quiet person — not the shy kind of quiet, but the kind that's comfortable in silence. You speak when you have something to say, and you don't feel the need to fill every gap. I've always been more restless, more talkative, the one who starts conversations or makes jokes. And somehow, we fit. Over the years, I've learned that with you I can just be myself — no performance, no guarding. Two friends doing homework — or pretending to — in a pavilion. I remember those PE afternoons as a different kind of peace. Tucked in the pocket park between the teaching buildings — a little bamboo grove with a wooden pavilion — we'd escape during the sports period. The morning session, at eleven, brought sun almost directly overhead, so bright you had to squint, carving sharp shadows from the roof onto your shoulders. The afternoon session, at half past three, came with slanting light through the gaps between the buildings, stretching the tree shadows and soaking the whole park in honey. While others ran and shouted, we'd slip into that pavilion with our homework and sit side by side. We said we were doing homework. But we always ended up talking. You talked about your cat — that long‑haired, white‑and‑orange creature you called "Juzhang." It took me a second to realise it was a pun on "bureau chief." You said it with that little upward tilt of your mouth. You told me how he hid under your bed when strangers came, how he only crept out long after the door was closed. Then one day, you said he'd crawled into a donut‑shaped box, and you'd tilted it upright, leaving just the opening. I reached my hand in — and touched a patch of warm, impossibly soft fur. He didn't scratch, didn't run. I stroked his head, behind his ears, under his chin. He started to purr, and after a while he even leaned forward to sniff my fingers. When I pulled my hand out of the box, we looked at each other and you smiled. You said he would "learn from his mistake" and never crawl in there again. That small, ordinary afternoon stayed with me, because it was a good one — the kind you have with an old friend where nothing much happens, and that's the point. In the pavilion, we often finished only a couple of problems in an entire class, or left a whole worksheet half‑done. The sunlight moved slowly across the pages — from the tip of your pen to the back of my hand, then from my hand to the scattered pile of erasers and pen caps between us. Sometimes we'd leave the pavilion and walk a few laps on the track. One lap, two laps. The red cinder crunching under our shoes. Our shadows — bunched into small dark puddles under the eleven o'clock sun, or stretched long in the half‑past‑three light — fell side by side on the red track. No hidden meaning. Just two shadows, two people, a shared silence. I also remember visiting your home and listening to you play the piano. Before you sat on the bench, you'd glance at me and say, in that small, shy voice, "I'm not very good at it." Then you'd press the soft pedal with your left foot and keep it there — the one that moves the hammers closer to the strings, making the sound gentle and distant, as if from another room. You also used the sustain pedal whenever you felt the piece needed "a bit of maestoso flavour." You'd hold it down and let the notes bleed into one another, staying in the air an extra second. When you hit a wrong note, you'd stop, frown, and start again. I'd sit on the chair nearby, pretending to look at my phone, but really I wasn't looking at anything. I was listening — those hesitant, honest notes, softened and blurred by the pedals. They were yours, and I was glad to be there as your friend. And there's something else I've come to value more than I can easily say. You've accepted my imperfections — the clumsy, not‑good‑enough parts of me that I try so hard to hide — and you've never made me feel small for them. More than that, you've accepted my moods, those small, nameless highs and lows I can't always explain. Sometimes I don't say anything at all, but you still notice. In our whole class, you're the one who can tell whether I'm truly happy or just pretending. You never pry. You never try to "fix" me. You're simply there. And when I'm ready to talk, you listen. I've been able to tell you things I could never say to anyone else for fear of being laughed at or misunderstood. With you, they're just my words. No polishing, no defence. I'm not writing this manual because of a grand, dramatic feeling. I'm writing it because I wanted a way to say thank you for that. There are many things I'd like to tell you, but most of them are best left to the kind of quiet understanding we've always had. So I'm putting this here, in an appendix that might, to anyone else, read as a series of small, unremarkable memories. I don't think about you every morning or every night. That would be a different kind of story. But I do know this: in the moments we sat in that pavilion during PE, walked slowly around the track, or when you pressed the pedals and played an imperfect but whole piece — I felt lucky to have you as a friend. Not a dramatic or overwhelming luck, just a steady, quiet one. I can't promise what the future holds, or that our paths won't diverge. But I can say that however long you walk beside me — through the pocket park, through a sun‑lit track or a shadowed one, through these strange, lengthy pages — I'll be grateful. Grateful for six years of friendship, for everything you've taught me about patience and acceptance, and for the fact that someone like you crossed my path. With steady friendship, Yours, who remains deeply thankful for those afternoons

title: Office
content: Appendix 10: Office This appendix covers the core features of Microsoft Office's three main components: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. You'll rely on them throughout college for writing papers, delivering presentations, and working with data. I'm focusing on Microsoft Office (specifically Office 365). WPS Office works similarly but has minor differences in behavior. I recommend Office 365—though if your instructor explicitly requires WPS for your thesis (which is rare), it's safer to follow that rule, because format handling between MS Office and WPS can be subtly, almost mysteriously, inconsistent. Opening an MS Office document in WPS (or vice versa) can shift margins, line spacing, or font rendering. Before submitting your final draft, always open it in the software your instructor uses and double‑check the layout. In the next appendix I'll introduce LaTeX, which is even more powerful for academic typesetting—most universities provide a LaTeX thesis template anyway. Part 1: Word Word is a document‑editing tool. You'll use it for papers, resumes, assignments, and more. Below are the features that actually matter. 1.1 Styles A Style is a predefined bundle of formatting—font, size, bold/italic, color, paragraph spacing, and so on. Many people write by selecting text and manually tweaking the font size, bolding, and line spacing as they go. That works for a one‑page memo, but for a thesis with dozens of pages and multiple heading levels, it's tedious and a nightmare to revise. The right way: define your styles first, then apply them. Word comes with built‑in styles like "Heading 1", "Heading 2", and "Normal". Right‑click any style → Modify to set its font, size, line spacing, and before/after paragraph spacing. Once you change a style definition, every piece of text using that style updates automatically. Benefits: Consistent formatting everywhere—no more "this heading is Songti size 16, that one is Heiti size 15". Fast updates—change the style once, and the entire document reflects it. Enables automatic table of contents generation (via the References feature). 1.2 Page Breaks vs. Line Breaks When you need to start a new page (e.g., each thesis chapter on a fresh page), many people hammer the Enter key until they reach the next page. That's fragile—any small edit earlier will break the layout. The proper methods: inserts a Page Break. Everything after the cursor moves to the next page. The break stays fixed regardless of edits above. inserts a Line Break (not a paragraph break). Enter creates a new paragraph with spacing between them; just moves to the next line without starting a new paragraph—useful for addresses, poems, or any place where you want a new line but no extra gap. 1.3 Layout The Layout tab controls the overall page appearance: Margins: the blank space around your document. Theses usually have strict margin requirements (e.g., top 2.5cm, bottom 2.5cm, left 3cm, right 2cm). Use "Custom Margins" for precise values. Orientation: Portrait vs. Landscape. If a table is too wide to fit, you can make that single page landscape by choosing "Apply to this section" in Page Setup. Columns: split a page into two or more columns—handy for newsletters or pamphlets. 1.4 References The References tab is your thesis‑writing powerhouse. Table of Contents: As long as you've used heading styles (Heading 1, 2, etc.), click "Table of Contents" and Word generates one instantly. Page numbers update automatically when the document changes—just click "Update Table" if you add or remove headings. Footnotes and Endnotes: Footnotes appear at the bottom of the current page. Insert a superscript number in the main text, and the note sits at the page bottom—great for supplemental comments. Endnotes appear at the end of the document—sometimes used for references. Citations & Bibliography: Click "Insert Citation" → "Add New Source", fill in author, title, year, etc. Word formats the citation for you. At the end of your document, click "Bibliography" to auto‑generate the reference list. Different journals/schools require different styles (APA, MLA, Chicago, etc.)—just pick the one you need from the "Style" dropdown. Captions: After inserting a figure, table, or equation, select it and click "Insert Caption" to add numbered labels (Figure 1, Table 1, etc.). Combine with "Cross‑reference" to write "as shown in Figure 1" in your text—clicking it jumps to the figure. If you insert a new figure in between, all numbers update automatically. 1.5 Review The Review tab is heavily used during college—especially when your instructor marks up your paper. Comments: Select some text and click "New Comment"—a bubble appears on the right. Instructors can write things like "logic unclear here" or "add a reference". After you address it, you can "Reply" or "Resolve" the comment. Track Changes: When you turn this on, every edit (deletions, insertions, moves) appears in colored markup. Your instructor sees exactly what you changed, and you see their edits. The markup stays until you accept or reject each change. Compare: You have two versions of a paper and want to know what's different? Click "Compare", select the original and the revised document, and Word generates a side‑by‑side comparison highlighting every change. 1.6 Important Settings in Word Options Click File → Options to open the Word Options dialog. A few settings are worth knowing: General → User Interface Options: Change the color scheme to "Dark Gray" or "Black" to reduce eye strain during long writing sessions. Display: "Always show these formatting marks on screen": I recommend checking "Tabs", "Spaces", and "Paragraph marks". You'll see gray dots (spaces) and pilcrow signs (paragraph breaks) that help debug misalignment. Never change the document page color: Some people set a green or dark background for comfort, but your final reader (instructor, journal reviewer) sees plain white paper. If you pick light‑colored text on a dark background, it may become invisible on white. Keep the default, or at least check how it looks before printing/submitting. Save: "Save AutoRecover information": defaults to 10 minutes. For critical documents, you might shorten it to 5. "Default file format": choose . is the older format with limited compatibility. Embed fonts: if you use a non‑standard font, recipients without it will see a fallback font and the layout may break. Check "Embed fonts in the file". Note that some fonts have license restrictions that prevent embedding. Advanced: Image fidelity: Word compresses inserted images by default to save space. If you need high‑quality figures (e.g., for a printed thesis), go to "Image Size and Quality" and set "Default resolution" to "High fidelity". Cut, copy, and paste: When pasting from a webpage, you often bring along unwanted formatting (background colors, weird fonts). Under "Pasting from other programs", choose "Keep Text Only" so you get clean plain text. Show document content: you'll find options like "Show background colors and images in Print Layout view". Add‑ins: these extend Word's capabilities—for example, Zotero (reference manager) installs an add‑in here so you can insert citations directly. If an add‑in slows Word down or causes errors, you can disable it here. 1.7 DOTM Templates .dotm is the Word template format that supports macros. Normal documents are , templates are , and macro‑enabled templates are . A template is like a mold. Create a resume template with margins, styles, headers, etc., save it as . Every time you double‑click it, Word generates a new document that inherits all settings—the original template remains untouched. Some universities provide a thesis template with pre‑set formatting and maybe automation scripts (e.g., one‑click figure number checks). If it's , you'll be prompted to "Enable Macros" when opening—you need to allow that to use the full functionality. Where to place templates: Word looks for templates in . Put yours there, then they appear under File → New → Personal. Word Further Reading Extra 1: Styles and Table of Contents linkage When generating a TOC, Word only picks up "Heading 1", "Heading 2", and "Heading 3" by default. If you use custom styles (e.g., "Level 1 Heading"), you must manually map them via References → Table of Contents → Custom Table of Contents → Options → assign the appropriate outline level. Extra 2: Section Breaks A Section Break is more powerful than a page break. After inserting one, each section can have independent margins, headers/footers, and page orientation. Example: your preface and TOC use Roman numerals, while the main body uses Arabic numerals—you need a section break between them. How to insert: Layout → Breaks → Next Page (Section Break). Extra 3: Document Page Color The "Never change the document page color" option in Word Options is aimed at people who write in dark mode. Windows 11's dark mode can make Word appear black‑on‑white, but the actual document background remains white. If someone changes the font color to a light shade while in dark mode, it may become unreadable on a white background for the instructor. Staying with the default is safest. Part 2: Excel Excel is a spreadsheet tool for handling data, performing calculations, and creating charts. Many people just type into cells and dread formulas. Part 3: PowerPoint PowerPoint is a presentation tool. You'll use it for college reports, course presentations, thesis defenses, research talks, and project showcases. Many people think PPT is just "putting text on slides", but it's really about information design—how to organize content, emphasize key points, and guide your audience. This section covers the essentials and practical tips. 3.1 Where to Start 3.1.1 What Goes on a Slide For a slide that conveys a complete idea, include at least: A title: the core question or conclusion for that page— not something vague like "Overview" or "Part 1". Body: supporting evidence or bullet points, preferably in short phrases rather than full sentences . Notes/footer (optional): data sources, page numbers, dates—adds clarity. Important: Don't copy‑paste entire paragraphs from a Word document onto a slide—it creates a painful reading experience. In Word, you need complete sentences to explain. In PPT, the audience reads the slide while you speak, so the on‑screen content should be concise—keywords and short phrases. One slide = one core idea. If it doesn't fit, move it to the next slide or delete it. —Nobody wants to read a wall of text projected on a screen. 3.1.2 Information Hierarchy Your slide should have a clear visual priority that guides viewers from most important to supporting details. Unlike Word, where linear reading is typical, PPT benefits from a visible structural anchor. You can place the current section title in a corner of each slide to keep the audience oriented. General guidelines: Font size directly signals importance. Avoid having multiple headings at nearly the same size on one page. Use bold/color only for the most critical words— never bold entire paragraphs . In body text, use short sentences and bullet points for easy scanning. 3.1.3 Basic Operations For Office 2016 and newer, the layout is largely consistent. Here are the core areas you'll use for 90% of everyday tasks. Interface When you create a new presentation, you'll see a dense ribbon at the top with tabs like "File", "Home", etc.—this is the ribbon, where most slide operations live. On the left, a thumbnail strip shows each slide. Here you can: Right‑click a slide to copy or delete it. Right‑click empty space to insert a new slide or add a section. Drag slides to reorder them. The center area is your editing workspace for the current slide. You might see a vertical toolbar on the right—this could be OfficePLUS, a Microsoft‑sponsored add‑in for the Chinese market. If you find it intrusive, you can disable it via Add‑ins. The most common operation: Insert Almost everything you add to a slide lives under the Insert tab. Insert a text box: Insert → Text Box → choose "Horizontal" or "Vertical", then drag on the canvas to create a box and type. This is one of the most frequent actions—aside from title and content placeholders, you'll often need additional text boxes for custom content. Also, put each distinct piece of text in its own text box—it makes positioning much easier later. Insert a picture: Insert → Pictures, or simply drag an image file directly into the PowerPoint window. To resize without distortion, hold while dragging a corner handle . Insert a shape: Insert → Shapes—choose arrows, rectangles, circles, lines, etc. Drag on the canvas to draw. After drawing, you can change fill color, outline, and even double‑click the shape to add text inside. Insert a table: Insert → Table—drag in the grid to select row/column count, or click "Insert Table" to enter numbers manually. You can also copy a table from Excel and paste it here. Insert a chart: Insert → Chart—choose column, line, pie, etc. A mini Excel sheet pops up—enter your data there, and the chart updates live. At the far right of the Insert tab, you'll find "Header & Footer"—use it to add slide numbers, dates, or footer text consistently across all slides. Much faster than doing it manually per slide, and you won't miss any. You can also do this via the Master (see 3.2). The most common operation: Modify Click any element on a slide (text box, picture, shape, chart) to select it—then you can modify it. Edit text: click inside a text box, cursor appears—type or delete. Select the text, then use the Home tab to change font, size, bold/italic/underline, color, etc. Remember: font size is a direct way to show hierarchy—title, body, and auxiliary text should have clear size tiers. Oh, and avoid the built‑in WordArt effects—they rarely look professional. Edit a picture: double‑click the image to enter the Picture Format tab. Here you can adjust brightness/contrast, crop (including crop to shape), remove background (Office 2016+ can do one‑click background removal—we'll cover it in 3.4.2), and add borders/shadows. All image adjustments live here. Edit a shape: select a shape → Shape Format tab → change fill color, outline color/thickness, shape effects (shadow, glow, etc.). If a shape is blocking text, right‑click → "Send to Back" or "Bring to Front" (or move step‑by‑step) to adjust layering. Move and resize: drag an element to reposition. Drag corner handles to scale proportionally (hold ) ; drag edge handles to stretch in one direction (use sparingly—it often distorts). Undo: Click the curved arrow at the top‑left, or press Ctrl + Z, to step back. PPT supports multiple undo levels—experiment freely. View modes Besides the default "Normal" view (editing area on top, thumbnails on left), PPT offers other views accessible from the bottom‑right: Normal view: everyday editing—most used. Slide Sorter: thumbnails tiled, great for reordering, bulk deletion, or copying slides. Hold Ctrl to select multiple slides, then apply "Hide Slide" or delete in bulk. Reading View: like a slideshow but in a window—quick preview of the finished look without going full‑screen. Slide Show To present, press (start from beginning) or (start from current slide). Press to exit. Saving your file This is the most important yet most overlooked step. After creating a new file, press or click the floppy‑disk icon at top‑left to save. Build a habit: hit Ctrl + S every few minutes . PPT can crash—unsaved changes are gone forever. The default format is —the standard. If your recipient uses an older Office version (pre‑2007), you might need to save as (compatibility mode), but nowadays almost everyone supports . On first save, confirm the "Save as type" dropdown says "PowerPoint Presentation (.pptx)", not template or show format. You can enable , but earlier versions of Office may require the file to be stored in OneDrive for that to work. WPS Office users can enable it without that restriction. Once you master these basics, you can start building a full presentation. Next, use the Master and Layout system to enforce consistency and avoid manual duplication. 3.2 The Slide Master This is a crucial PowerPoint feature that most beginners never touch. It's like Styles in Word: change it once, and every slide using that layout updates instantly. What Is the Slide Master The Slide Master is the underlying "blueprint" for each slide. Anything you add or change on the Master automatically appears on all slides using that layout. Use it to control: Fonts (what font and size for headings vs. body) Placement of title and content placeholders Page numbers and dates Fixed elements (e.g., school logo, institution name) Background color or image A Practical Example Suppose you're making a 20‑slide class presentation and manually insert the school logo in the top‑right corner of each slide. Later, your instructor says to move it to the bottom‑left—now you have to edit all 20 slides manually, risking missing one. Using the Master, you insert the logo once in the top‑level Master, and every slide reflects the change instantly. How to do it: View → Slide Master. The left pane shows a set of Master and layout thumbnails. The topmost (largest) controls all layouts. On a specific layout (e.g., "Title and Content"), add your logo, adjust fonts, etc. After closing the Master view, all slides using that layout update automatically. Best practice: Set up your Master before you start creating content—fonts, colors, logo placement. If you already have dozens of slides with manual overrides, changing the Master later can cause conflicts and messy results. 3.3 Themes and Layouts Themes A Theme is a coordinated visual package—font combinations, color palettes, background styles. In the Design tab, you can change the entire presentation's look with one click. Office built‑in themes: usable, but many are overly flashy and not suitable for academic presentations. Custom themes: it's better to build one based on your university's official colors (from the logo). Go to Design → Variants → Colors → Customize Colors, set Accent 1–6 to your preferred palette—then all charts and shapes in the presentation will follow these colors. Recommendation: Avoid downloading fancy commercial templates with heavy backgrounds and decorative graphics. For academic talks and defenses, keep the background clean and text legible—no distractions. Layouts Layouts are predefined page structures under the Master. They tell PowerPoint "where the title goes, where the body goes, and whether there's a picture placeholder." Common layouts: Title Slide: for the cover—large title and subtitle only. Title and Content: the workhorse content page—title plus body/chart area. Section Header: for chapter transitions. Blank: fully custom—good for full‑page images or your own diagrams. Comparison: two content areas side‑by‑side for contrast. Tip: Don't start every slide from "Blank" and manually add text boxes. Instead, when inserting a new slide, choose a suitable layout and just fill in the content. This keeps positions consistent and makes future Master‑based changes much easier. 3.4 Working with Pictures and Shapes 3.4.1 Key Points Maintain proportions: When resizing, hold Shift and drag a corner handle to keep the original aspect ratio. Never stretch one‑dimensionally—faces get squashed, charts become distorted. A slightly smaller image is fine; a deformed one ruins the layout. Pictures should serve your point: Don't add random decoration. Every image should have a reason—to prove a conclusion, show a result, or illustrate a process. 3.4.2 Cropping and Background Removal PowerPoint's built‑in cropping is more powerful than you might think: Crop to ratio: Select the image → Picture Format → Crop → Aspect Ratio—quickly crop to 1:1, 16:9, etc., to make multiple images uniform. Crop to shape: Crop into circles, rounded rectangles, etc.—great for team photos or icons. Remove Background: Select the image → Picture Format → Remove Background. For simple backgrounds, you don't even need Photoshop. Double‑clicking an image automatically takes you to the Picture Format tab —all cropping and adjustment tools are there. 3.4.3 SmartArt and Shapes SmartArt turns boring bullet lists into visual diagrams with one click: Process (sequential steps with arrows) Hierarchy (organizational charts) Cycle (closed‑loop processes) Relationship (side‑by‑side, radial, Venn, etc.) Pro tip: Select an existing bullet list, then go to Home → Convert to SmartArt and pick a graphic—it's faster than starting from scratch. Caution: Don't overuse SmartArt just because it's shiny. Many default styles come with garish 3D effects and extra lines that clutter the slide. Stick with "simple" style SmartArt, remove unnecessary shadows and bevels—clear communication wins. 3.5 Charts and Data Presentation 3.5.1 Inserting a Chart PPT charts embed a mini Excel spreadsheet. When you insert a chart, a data sheet pops up—edit the numbers there and the chart updates live. Supported types: column, line, pie, scatter, area, etc. Choose based on what you want to convey: Compare sizes → column chart Show trends → line chart Show proportions → pie chart ( keep it under 5 slices ) 3.5.2 Chart Design Principles Common pitfall: Copy‑paste a chart directly from Excel into PPT—it brings along cluttered gridlines, multi‑color legends, and tiny decimal numbers. Projected on a big screen, the back row can't read a thing. What we usually do: Remove clutter: gridlines, duplicate axis titles—strip them out. Keep only essential data labels. Highlight key data: color the most important bar differently (e.g., grey for all classes, red for your own class). Keep others muted—contrast draws attention. Eliminate legends when possible: if there's only one data series, you don't need a legend—delete it so the audience sees the trend directly. Make fonts big enough: axis numbers and labels should be no smaller than 12pt . Principle: Think from the audience's perspective—"What do I want them to understand from this slide?" Then use color, annotations, and magnification to guide their eyes. Don't just dump raw data and call it done. 3.6 Animations and Transitions 3.6.1 Animations PowerPoint's animation system is surprisingly capable—modern hardware handles it smoothly, so "laggy PPT" is often a myth. The simplest use is to control progressive disclosure—reveal one bullet point per click so the audience doesn't read ahead. Click → appear → you explain → next click. If you don't want to spend much time on animations but still want some liveliness: Fade Wipe (left‑to‑right or bottom‑to‑top) Appear Animations to avoid: Bounce, spin, spiral fly‑in—they make academic presentations look cheap. Don't animate every single element on a slide. How to set: select an element → Animations tab → pick an entrance effect. Use the Animation Pane on the right to adjust order and trigger ("On Click" is the most common). Remember: Animation serves your talk, not to show off how fancy your PPT can be. If you're replaying an animation just for the cool effect, it probably should be removed. If you want to go deeper into PowerPoint animations , we'll cover that in 3.6.3 to 3.6.5. 3.6.2 Slide Transitions Transitions are the effects when moving from one slide to the next. If you don't want to invest much time: Recommended: Fade, Push (clean and professional). Avoid: Airplane, Ripple, Origami—overly complex. Stick with one subtle transition throughout. You can also set all to "None" and only use "Fade" once for section breaks—gives nice rhythm. For a deeper dive into transitions , see 3.6.6. 3.6.3 Animation Speed (for PowerPoint, not WPS) This and the next two subsections assume you're using PowerPoint (not WPS Presentation) and want to dig into the animation details . In the Animation Pane (Animations tab > Animation Pane), you can see all animations on the current slide. Double‑click one to open its detailed settings—you'll find "Smooth Start", "Smooth End", and "Bounce End" sliders. Adjusting these creates smoother acceleration/deceleration curves, as shown: As for duration, 0.5–1 second is a good range for most element entrances/exits. 3.6.4 Animation Timing Open the Animation Pane—you'll see a timeline of all animations ordered by click triggers. The logic is straightforward (example): You can also double‑click an animation, switch to the "Timing" tab, and set "Repeat" to loop it. Multiple animations on one element: select the element, then in the Animations tab click "Add Animation" to append more—you'll see them stacked in the Animation Pane. This allows effects like moving and rotating simultaneously. Special animations: Audio and video playback/stop are also treated as animations—you can edit them in the Animation Pane to start or pause at specific times. For audio, after selecting the audio icon, go to the Playback tab and enable "Play across slides" so it continues when you advance. 3.6.5 Animation Triggers Select an element, then below the Animation Pane button you should see a "Trigger" button. In the dropdown under "On Click of", you can choose another element—meaning the animation plays when that specific element is clicked. Combined with 3.6.4, you can trigger multiple animations in sequence. 3.6.6 Page Transitions (continued) PowerPoint's "Transition" refers to the effect applied when entering the current slide, not when leaving it. Morph Transition Microsoft 365 (or Office 2016+) provides Morph. It works by detecting the same object on two slides with different positions, sizes, or rotations—then automatically interpolates the movement. Practical uses: Zoom from a thumbnail to a full‑scale image. Animate chart elements smoothly between data sets. Move a highlight box gracefully across a process diagram. ... To use: duplicate a slide, modify the object on the second slide, then apply Transition → Morph to the second slide. 3.7 Alignment and Layout Techniques This is the fastest and most effective way to improve your PPT's visual quality. Many messy presentations aren't due to ugly colors or missing animations—they're caused by misaligned elements and uneven spacing. 3.7.1 Alignment Basics Select multiple objects (text boxes, images, shapes), then under Picture Format or Shape Format → Align: Left / Center / Right align Top / Middle / Bottom align You can also enable Gridlines and Guides (View → check "Guides") to drag out reference lines. "Looks about aligned" is usually not aligned—use the tools. 3.7.2 Distribution Basics When you have three icons or text boxes that need equal horizontal spacing, dragging manually never gets it right. Select them, then use "Distribute Horizontally" or "Distribute Vertically" under Align—spacing becomes exactly equal. Note: Align first, then distribute—doing it in reverse can mess things up. 3.7.3 Grouping Group multiple elements (e.g., an icon and its label) so you can move and position them as one unit. Select them and press . To edit an individual element later, click inside the group—or press to ungroup. 3.7.4 Spacing (optional deep dive) If you want fine‑tuned layout details, read on—otherwise skip to 3.8. Spacing greatly affects visual comfort. Generally, for a top‑left title, make the left margin slightly smaller than the top margin —it stabilises the page: For content centered on the slide, positioning it slightly above the geometric center makes it feel more balanced: If you use multiple stacked rounded rectangles, try to match their corner radii: 3.8 Presentation and Delivery Tips 3.8.1 Presenter View Using Presenter View is a must‑have skill for college defenses and talks. When connected to a projector, your laptop shows a special interface while the audience sees the full‑screen slide. You can see: The current slide A preview of the next slide (helps with transitions) Your notes (visible only to you—great for talk prompts) A timer Enable it: Slide Show → check "Use Presenter View". If you have a second display, it usually activates automatically. Newbie tip: Always test Presenter View on the classroom computer before your defense. Older projectors may mirror your screen directly, exposing your notes to the audience—you'll need to set Windows display mode to "Extend" to avoid that. 3.8.2 Rehearse Timings If you need to speak without notes or have a strict time limit (e.g., a 5‑minute competition talk), use Slide Show → Rehearse Timings. Run through your presentation naturally—PPT records your time per slide and total duration. You can later save these timings for auto‑advance. 3.9 Exporting and Compatibility Save Formats : default—use this for everyday work. : legacy format (Office 97‑2003)—not recommended. : if you only need to share the presentation for viewing (not editing), export to PDF—it guarantees layout fidelity across any device. Font Issues The classic disaster: You carefully tuned fonts and layout on your own machine. On the classroom computer, everything turns to宋体 (SimSun) and the formatting falls apart. Why: The classroom computer doesn't have your custom font installed. Solutions: File → Options → Save. Check "Embed fonts in the file". Choose "Embed only the characters used in the presentation" (smaller file) or "Embed all characters" (if the recipient needs to edit). Caveat: Some fonts are licensed and cannot be embedded—you'll get an error. In that case, select the text box, right‑click "Save as Picture" or "Convert to Shape"—the text becomes an image that preserves the look without relying on the font. Video and Audio If you insert a video, make sure to copy the video file along with your PPT, or test whether embedding works. Recommendations: Use MP4 format for best compatibility. Do a full playback test on the target computer beforehand—check both picture and sound. 3.10 Closing Thought: Shift Your Mindset Move from "this slide looks empty, let me add some decoration" to "what format will help my audience understand my point fastest?" PPT is not about showing how much you know—it's about helping others understand your perspective. In fact, if you can strip away the redundant and highlight the essential, your slides already beat the majority. Extra: VBA Macros VBA (Visual Basic for Applications) is Office's built‑in programming language. You can write scripts to automate repetitive tasks. Open the VBA editor: What VBA Can Do Batch process Word documents: Change the margins of every Word file in a folder to 2.5cm all at once. Manually, you'd open each document and click through dozens of dialogs—with a VBA script, one click does hundreds. Excel automation: Merge data from 12 monthly spreadsheets into one master sheet. Write a loop that opens each file, copies data, and pastes into the summary. PowerPoint batch operations: Add a company logo to the top‑right corner of all 200 slides. Recording Macros The easiest way: click the "Developer" tab → "Record Macro" → perform your steps (e.g., set margins, change fonts) → "Stop Recording". Excel automatically converts your actions into VBA code. You can replay it anytime. Note: Recorded macros generate verbose code (it records every click, including unnecessary ones). Still, it's a great learning tool—record something, inspect the generated code, and then tweak it. Security , , are macro‑enabled files. Office will prompt "This file contains macros" when you open them. Only enable macros from trusted sources (e.g., school‑issued, colleagues). Macros can delete files or format drives—they're essentially small executable programs. Viewing and editing macros**: opens the VBA editor—you can see all modules and code. Even if you're not a programmer, you can often recognize basic logic (like "open", "copy", "paste" in plain English).

title: LaTeX
content: Appendix 11: LaTeX This appendix introduces the basics of LaTeX. LaTeX is a typesetting system designed for academic papers, especially good for mathematical formulas and references. If you plan to publish papers or write a thesis, you will likely encounter it. This appendix uses Shanghai Jiao Tong University's thesis template (SJTUThesis) as an example to show how to write LaTeX documents with VS Code. Please note: The content below is for reference only. Always follow the specific formatting requirements given by your university instructors or journal guidelines. The goal is simply to help you get familiar with LaTeX. 11.1 What Is LaTeX? LaTeX (pronounced "lah-tekh" or "lay-tekh") is different from Word. Word is "what you see is what you get" – you type, and it immediately shows the formatted result. LaTeX is "what you think is what you get" – you write code (a markup language), then compile it to produce a PDF. Advantages: Formatting is automatically consistent – no accidental mixing of fonts or sizes Mathematical formulas look beautiful References are automatically numbered and sorted Long documents (dozens or hundreds of pages) rarely become sluggish Disadvantages: There is a learning curve; you will need to look things up when errors occur You must compile to see the result, unlike Word's live update Many science and engineering departments require theses and journal papers to be typeset in LaTeX. Your university may provide a template (e.g., the document class), and you simply fill in your content. 11.2 Setting Up the Environment: TeX Distribution + VS Code To write LaTeX, you first need a "compilation environment" – a TeX distribution. The most common one is TeX Live (works on Windows, Linux, and macOS). 11.2.1 Installing TeX Live Download the TeX Live ISO file from Tsinghua University's TUNA mirror. Extract or mount the ISO, then run (Windows) or (Linux/macOS). Choose "full installation" (scheme-full) to avoid missing packages later. The installation may take about half an hour. After installation, open a command line and type . If you see version information, the installation succeeded. Additional note: About latexmk and Perl (Windows users) The compilation tool is a Perl script. TeX Live comes with its own Perl interpreter ( ), so normally works right after installation. If you get a "command not found" error when typing , it means TeX Live's directory is not in your system PATH. You can re‑run the installer and check "Add to PATH", or add it manually (see Appendix 9 for environment variables). 11.2.2 Installing VS Code and the LaTeX Workshop Extension If you have not already installed VS Code, do so first (see Appendix 7). Once installed, go to the Extensions Marketplace, search for LaTeX Workshop, and install it.
