This extension provides syntax highlighting, automatic compilation, forward/backward search, and more. 11.2.3 Configuring VS Code (Optional but Recommended) Open VS Code settings ( ), search for , and change the default compilation recipe to . This will automatically compile whenever you save a file. Alternatively, place a file in your project folder: 11.3 A Real Template: SJTUThesis Shanghai Jiao Tong University's thesis template, SJTUThesis, is a complete LaTeX project. You can find it on GitHub ( ). Download and unzip it, then open the folder in VS Code. You will see several files and folders. 11.3.1 First Step After Downloading: Try to Compile The three most common problems on the first compilation Problem 1: Missing fonts Many university templates require SimSun, SimHei, and Times New Roman fonts. Windows comes with these fonts, so no issue there. macOS users may need to install SimSun manually (copy it from a Windows machine, or use a command like ). Linux users – I trust you can figure it out. Problem 2: Missing packages If the compilation error says , you are missing a package. Install it using TeX Live's : If is not found, run it as administrator (Windows) or with (Linux/macOS). You may need to switch to a different mirror – see the TUNA mirror documentation. Problem 3: Encoding errors An error like usually means the file is not saved as UTF-8. In VS Code, click the encoding indicator at the bottom‑right, then choose “Save with Encoding” → UTF-8. 11.3.2 Main File Structure | File/folder | Purpose | |-------------|---------| | | The master file – the "skeleton" of your thesis. It includes chapters via | | | Configuration: your name, thesis title, department, etc. | | | Reference database (BibTeX format) | | | Holds the chapter files, e.g., , | | | Holds image files | | | The template's style file (generally you do not need to modify it) | 11.3.3 The Skeleton of When writing your thesis, you will only need to edit the chapter files under and the personal information in . The master file usually does not need to be touched. 11.4 How to Write Content 11.4.1 Chapters and Headings Inside a chapter file (e.g., ): Write your text directly. A blank line indicates a paragraph break. 11.4.2 Mathematical Formulas (Basics) Inline formulas are wrapped in : Displayed equations (with numbering) use the environment: Common symbols inside formulas: Superscripts and subscripts: , Fractions: Square roots: , Summation: Integration: Greek letters: , , , , , etc. 11.4.3 Mathematical Formulas (Intermediate) Multi‑line equations (align environment) When an equation is too long to fit on one line, or you need to align at equal signs, use the environment: marks the alignment point (usually placed before the equal sign), and ends a line. To suppress numbering on a particular line, add before : Matrices Use (parentheses), (square brackets), (vertical bars), etc.: Ellipses: (horizontal), (vertical), (diagonal): Piecewise functions (cases environment) 11.4.4 Figures Place your image files in the folder (PDF, PNG, or JPG are recommended). Then insert a figure in a chapter file: tells LaTeX that the figure can be placed here, at the top of a page, at the bottom, or on a separate float page. LaTeX automatically chooses the best position. centres the figure. sets the figure width to 80% of the text width. sets the caption; the figure number (e.g., “Figure 3.1”) is generated automatically. defines a label so you can reference it in the text: . Note: Do not use spaces or Chinese characters in image file names or paths, otherwise LaTeX may not find them. Use English names like . Subfigures (side‑by‑side figures) When you need to place two or more images side‑by‑side with separate (a), (b) captions, use the package: Make sure to load the package at the beginning of the document: . University templates usually already include it. 11.4.5 Tables Writing tables in LaTeX can be somewhat tedious. A practical approach is to use an online tool (like Tables Generator) to generate the code and then paste it. Here is a simple three‑line table example: The package provides , , and . The template should already load it. Long tables that span multiple pages (longtable) If you have a very long table (e.g., several pages of experimental data), a normal + cannot break across pages – the table will be cut off at the page boundary. In this case, use the package: differs from ordinary tables in that it can break across pages, and the header is repeated at the top of each page. The downside is less flexible float placement, but for long tables it is the only practical option. 11.4.6 References (Basics) References are stored in a file in BibTeX format. A sample entry (from ): In the body of your thesis, cite it: After compilation, the reference list is automatically generated where appears. Citation numbers and the list formatting follow the required standard (e.g., GB/T 7714 for Chinese theses). Important notes on the field: Separate multiple authors with (not commas): LaTeX uses to distinguish authors, automatically producing “Li, X. D., Zhang, Q. H., & Ye, J. L.” or “Li et al.” as needed Do not write – the whole string would be treated as a single author 11.4.7 References (Intermediate) Where to get BibTeX entries for Chinese publications CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure): On the article detail page, look for “Export” → “BibTeX” → copy the content. However, CNKI‑exported BibTeX often has problems (e.g., missing between authors, incorrect format). After exporting, manually check and fix: Check : if it shows , change it to Check : it should be , not Check journal name: CNKI sometimes puts the journal name in instead of – move it if needed Google Scholar: Below the search result, click “Cite” → “BibTeX” and copy directly. The quality is generally better than CNKI. Recommended workflow: Use Zotero (free reference manager). With the browser plugin, you can capture references with one click. Zotero automatically recognises the fields, and you can export a file. Zotero also integrates with Word/LaTeX, greatly reducing manual entry errors. Why references might not show up If after compilation you see in the text, or the reference list is empty, the compilation order is likely wrong. The correct sequence is: → generates auxiliary files → processes the file → writes references into the document → resolves cross‑references (optional but recommended) With VS Code’s LaTeX Workshop using the recipe, this order is handled automatically. If you use the command line, run: automatically detects how many passes are needed and whether is required. 11.4.8 Three Common Pitfalls for Beginners Pitfall 1: Blank lines causing paragraph indentation In LaTeX, a blank line means a paragraph break. If you have two consecutive lines of text separated by a blank line, the second paragraph will have an indented first line (as is customary in Chinese typography). Many people do not want this indentation and manually add – but doing that for every paragraph is tedious. The correct approach: For Chinese theses, first‑line indentation is usually required, so you do not need to change anything. If you really need a paragraph without indentation (e.g., for a figure caption), write just before that paragraph. If you want to disable indentation globally, add in the preamble, but this will deviate from most university formatting requirements – not recommended. Pitfall 2: Abusing to force line breaks Using inside a regular paragraph forces a line break but does not create a new paragraph. The next line will not have indentation, and line breaks may appear in odd places. Wrong: Right: Let LaTeX wrap lines automatically. If you genuinely need a line break without a new paragraph, use . If you want a new paragraph, use a blank line. Pitfall 3: Figures not showing Missing figures usually have three causes: Wrong path: but the folder is named (missing the ‘s’) – case sensitivity also matters Spaces or Chinese characters in the file name: → rename to Unsupported format: When compiling with , supported formats are PNG, JPG, and PDF. If you use , PDF is the most reliable. As a rule, use PDF (especially for vector graphics) Debugging tip: Look at the compilation log (in VS Code, LaTeX Workshop’s “LaTeX Compiler” output window) and search for . 11.5 How to Compile 11.5.1 Compiling in VS Code Press (or click “Build LaTeX project” in the left sidebar) – this triggers automatic compilation. After a successful build, is generated. LaTeX Workshop uses the recipe by default, which handles multiple passes and references automatically. If compilation fails: Open VS Code’s “Output” panel ( ), then choose “LaTeX Compiler” from the dropdown menu Look for error messages in red, and search online for the error text See the Extended Reading section for common error messages and solutions 11.5.2 Compiling from the Command Line If you prefer the command line, navigate to the project folder (where is) and run: If you get a “command not found” error for , the Perl environment is not set up correctly. Refer back to the extra note in section 11.2.1. If you prefer not to use , you can manually run the steps: Note: The command handles references. Some older templates use instead (command: ). The modern version of SJTUThesis uses . 11.5.3 Using the Template’s Built‑in Compilation Script Many LaTeX templates provide a (Linux/macOS) or (Windows). For SJTUThesis: Windows: double‑click , or run it from the command line Linux/macOS: run in the terminal (requires to be installed) 11.6 A Minimal Example Below is a “minimal paper fragment” that does not rely on any complex template. Copy it into a file and try compiling it. Compiling this produces a PDF document with formulas, section headings, automatic numbering, etc. Extended Reading The following content covers more advanced LaTeX topics. Refer to it when you outgrow the basics. Extended 1: What Are Packages (Macros)? LaTeX’s functionality is extended through “packages”. When you write at the beginning of your document, you are loading a package for mathematical formulas. Commonly used packages: : inserting images , : advanced mathematical features : setting page margins : generating hyperlinks and bookmarks : three‑line tables : multi‑page tables : subfigures (side‑by‑side figures) : algorithm environments Extended 2: Reference Management Tools If you have many references, consider using dedicated reference management software such as Zotero (free) or JabRef. They allow you to import reference entries from journal websites with a single click and then export a file. Zotero also has a plugin (Better BibTeX) that generates stable citekeys and can integrate directly with VS Code or Overleaf. Extended 3: Common Compilation Errors and Solutions | Error message | Likely cause | Solution | |---------------|--------------|----------| | | An undefined command was used | Check spelling, or load the required package | | | Missing package | | | | Encoding issue | Save the file as UTF‑8 | | | Forgot to load the package | Add , or change to | | | Didn't run | Run then recompile | | appears in the text | Incorrect citation label | Check that the key in matches the key in the file | | Figure not shown; only the file name appears | Unsupported format or wrong path | Check the file name (no spaces or Chinese characters); try PDF format | Extended 4: Forward and Inverse Search Forward search: In the file, hold and click on a line – you jump to the corresponding location in the PDF. Inverse search: Double‑click a line in the PDF – you jump back to the corresponding line in the file. LaTeX Workshop supports forward search by default. Inverse search on Windows may require extra configuration (setting SumatraPDF as the default PDF viewer). For beginners, this is not essential. Extended 5: Template Document Class ( ) and Configuration ( ) The style of the SJTU template is written in . Ordinary users do not need to modify it. Only if you are creating a document class from scratch would you need to write a file. For a thesis, using the template provided by your university is the safest approach. Extended 6: Overleaf – Online LaTeX Editor If you do not want to install TeX Live locally, you can use an online LaTeX editor – for example, Overleaf ( ), or Chinese alternatives like TeXPage or SJTU LaTeX Document Assistant. You simply register an account, upload a template (or choose one from the template library), and write LaTeX in your browser with real‑time preview. This is an excellent way for beginners to get started quickly. Comparison between Overleaf and a local environment: | Feature | Overleaf | Local (TeX Live + VS Code) | |---------|----------|----------------------------| | Installation cost | Zero – register and use | Download 4–5 GB, ~30 minutes to install | | Compilation speed | Depends on server load | Depends on your computer (generally faster) | | Offline use | No | Yes | | Chinese template support | Need to upload fonts | Fonts managed by the OS | | Collaborative editing | Native support | Needs Git or other tools | For beginners, it is recommended to start with Overleaf to get your first document working, then decide whether to install a local environment.

title: OpenSource
content: Appendix 12: Open Source This appendix introduces the basic concepts of open source software, common open source licenses, and a few noteworthy open source projects. This material is not essential for everyday computer use, but it is good to understand – much of the computers, phones, and internet you use today are built on open source software. 12.1 What Is Open Source Open source means that a piece of software's source code is open to everyone. Anyone can view, modify, and distribute that code. The opposite of open source is proprietary software – the source code is not public. Users can only run the compiled program; they cannot see how it works or modify it. Windows, Microsoft Office, Photoshop, and Steam are all proprietary software. Open source does not mean free of charge. Many open source programs are indeed free to use, but the core meaning of "open source" is about freedom – freedom to use, to study, to modify, and to share. Some open source products are sold (e.g., enterprise editions or paid support). 12.2 Free Software vs. Open Source Software These two terms are often used interchangeably, but their underlying philosophies differ slightly. Free Software is a concept promoted by the Free Software Foundation (FSF) , founded by Richard Stallman in 1985. Here "free" refers to freedom of speech, not free beer. The FSF emphasises the ethical dimension: users should have control over the software, not the other way around. Open Source Software emerged a bit later (1998) and focuses more on technical advantages: opening the source code leads to better quality, higher security, and faster iteration. The term deliberately avoids the ideological language of "free software", making it more palatable to businesses and the commercial world. In practice, the two overlap heavily – most free software is also open source, and vice versa. But in spirit, the FSF is more "hardcore", emphasising user rights and ethics, while the open source movement is more pragmatic, focusing on collaboration and efficiency. 12.3 Open Source Licenses An open source license specifies what others can do with your code and what conditions they must follow. Different licenses vary significantly, and choosing the wrong one can create legal risks. 12.3.1 Permissive Licenses These licenses place few restrictions on users. You can take the code, use it, modify it, and even release your modified version as closed source (without sharing your changes), as long as you retain the original copyright notice. MIT License: One of the simplest licenses. It says only two things: keep the copyright notice, and don't hold the author liable. Many small Node.js and Python projects use it. Apache License 2.0: Similar to MIT, but adds a few clauses: it explicitly grants patent rights (to avoid certain patent traps) and requires you to state which files you modified. Projects from the Apache Software Foundation – such as Hadoop and Kubernetes – use this license. BSD License: Very similar to MIT. There are several variants (2‑Clause, 3‑Clause, 4‑Clause). The differences involve whether you can use the author's name for advertising and whether all derivative works must retain the original author's information. FreeBSD and early versions of the Go language use BSD licenses. 12.3.2 Strong (Copyleft) Licenses These licenses require that your modifications and derivative works must also be open sourced under the same license. GPL (GNU General Public License) : The most famous copyleft license. If a piece of software uses GPL‑licensed code, then the entire software must be released under the GPL. The Linux kernel, Git, and the GCC compiler all use the GPL. GPLv2: The version used by the Linux kernel. GPLv3: Released in 2007, adding provisions about patents and anti‑circumvention. Some projects (including the Linux kernel) consider v3 too strict and stick with v2. LGPL (Lesser GPL) : A relaxed version of the GPL. If you only link to an LGPL library (e.g., use a or ), your own code does not need to be open source. However, if you modify the library itself, those modifications must be open sourced. Often used for function libraries such as GTK and parts of FFmpeg. AGPL (Affero GPL) : The GPL has a loophole: if you run GPL code on a server and users only interact with it over the network (without receiving a copy of the software), you are not required to release your code. AGPL closes this loophole – providing a service over the network counts as distribution, so you must open source your code. Early versions of MongoDB used the AGPL. 12.3.3 Which One Should You Choose? | Your goal | Recommended license | |-----------|---------------------| | Let anyone use the code, even in closed‑source commercial products | MIT / Apache 2.0 | | Ensure the code and all derivatives remain forever open source | GPL | | You are writing a library – allow others to link to it without forcing their code open | LGPL | | You offer a network service and don't want someone to take it, tweak the UI, and sell it closed‑source | AGPL | Choosing a "wrong" license is not a disaster – you can change it later. However, if you use GPL‑licensed code in your project, your code must be released under the GPL. This is a legal requirement, not a suggestion. 12.4 Mirror Sites A mirror site is a replica of a large software repository or open source project. Because the original servers are often outside China, access can be slow and unreliable. Universities and companies inside China set up mirrors that synchronise regularly with the original sources, allowing domestic users to download at high speed. Some of the best‑known mirrors in China: Tsinghua University TUNA Mirror: Large, fast‑updating, and comprehensive. Many of the software download links recommended earlier in this guide come from here. USTC (University of Science and Technology of China) UTSC Mirror: Similarly long‑standing and broad in coverage. Shanghai Jiao Tong University SJTUG Mirror: One of the download locations for the SJTUThesis template. Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Huawei Cloud : They also run open source mirrors, focusing on operating systems and development tools. How to use: Different package managers have different methods for changing the mirror source. I recommend searching on your own. Example search query: 12.5 Notable Open Source Software You may not have used the following open source applications, but they run quietly behind the scenes in many industries. It's enough to know their names and what they do. 12.5.1 The Linux Kernel Linux is an open source operating system kernel, released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. It is not a complete operating system like Windows, but the lowest‑level core of the system – managing hardware, processes, memory, and the file system. Android – the OS on your phone – runs on the Linux kernel. More than 70% of the world's servers run Linux. Routers, smart TVs, car infotainment systems, ATMs, supercomputers – the vast majority run Linux. Without Linux, the internet as we know it would not exist. 12.5.2 GIMP GIMP (GNU Image Manipulation Program) : An open source image editing application, often described as the "open source alternative to Photoshop". It is very powerful – layers, filters, masks, paths, colour adjustments – all present. The interface is different from Photoshop and requires some learning. Suitable for people who do not want to pay for Photoshop but need to edit images occasionally. 12.5.3 LibreOffice LibreOffice: An open source office suite, comprising Writer (documents), Calc (spreadsheets), Impress (presentations), Draw (drawing), and Base (databases). It is compatible with Microsoft Office formats ( , , all open). The interface is a bit rougher than Office, but it is the standard default on Linux systems. If you do not want to subscribe to Office 365, give it a try. 12.5.4 Krita Krita: An open source digital painting application, aimed at illustrators and concept artists. Its brush engine is very powerful, supporting pressure sensitivity, stabilisation, and brush smoothing. The comic features (storyboarding, speech bubbles) are also mature. The difference from GIMP: GIMP is more like Photoshop (general image editing), while Krita is more like Procreate / Painter (dedicated drawing). Many animation studios use it. 12.5.5 Blender Blender: An open source 3D creation suite. Modelling, sculpting, materials, rendering, animation, video editing, compositing – it does everything. Once dismissed as "amateur software", it is now an industrial‑grade tool that can compete with Maya and 3ds Max. The Hollywood animated film Spider‑Man: Into the Spider‑Verse used Blender, and some promotional videos for Arknights and Genshin Impact were made with Blender. The learning curve is steep, but it is completely free. 12.5.6 VLC VLC: An open source multimedia player. Similar to PotPlayer, but VLC is cross‑platform (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS). It can play almost any video format without requiring extra codecs. Small footprint, fast startup, and can also act as a network streaming client. We recommended PotPlayer earlier; VLC is a good alternative. 12.5.7 7‑Zip / NanaZip 7‑Zip: An open source compression tool. NanaZip, recommended earlier, is a modernised interface for 7‑Zip. The core 7z format achieves higher compression ratios than ZIP. Its command‑line version is used in many automation scripts. 12.5.8 FFmpeg FFmpeg: An open source command‑line tool for audio and video processing. It is the Swiss Army knife for video professionals. You can use it to convert formats, cut clips, merge videos, extract audio, burn subtitles. OBS, VLC, YouTube, and Netflix all use FFmpeg behind the scenes. It was mentioned earlier in the video processing section. 12.5.9 OBS Studio OBS (Open Broadcaster Software) : An open source tool for live streaming and screen recording. Compared to the paid XSplit, OBS is no less capable and is completely free. It supports multiple scenes, multiple sources, filters, and streaming. Many game streamers and online course recorders use it. Its configuration was covered in Chapter 4. 12.5.10 VS Code VS Code: Microsoft's open source code editor. Recommended in Appendix 7 – with plugins, it can do almost anything. Although developed by Microsoft, the code is open source (MIT license). Some joke that "Microsoft is now one of the largest open source contributors" – Azure documentation, TypeScript, .NET Core are all open sourced. 12.5.11 osu! osu!: An open source music rhythm game. Players click, drag, and spin along with the music. There are four modes (standard, taiko, catch the fruit, piano). The community is very active, with millions of user‑made beatmaps. It has excellent tablet support – many people play it with a drawing tablet. The game itself is free and open source, sustained by donations and paid skins. 12.6 A Final Thought The computer you use today – opening a browser (Chromium engine), watching videos (FFmpeg decoding), chatting (Linux servers forwarding messages), browsing forums (hosted by Nginx or Apache) – all of it runs on open source projects. You may never need to read a single line of kernel code, nor submit a pull request to any project. But knowing that these things exist, knowing where they came from and under what rules they operate, will deepen your understanding of the digital world. They are not perfect, but without them, today's world would not look the same. 12.7 Creative Commons Licenses (CC) Creative Commons (CC) is not a software open source license. It is a set of public licenses for creative works – articles, images, music, videos, blog posts, courseware, Wikipedia entries, and more. The goal is to allow creators to proactively declare "how others may use my work", instead of defaulting to "all rights reserved". 12.7.1 Why CC Licenses Exist Traditional copyright defaults to "All Rights Reserved". You draw a picture and upload it. If someone wants to share it, translate it, or turn it into a wallpaper, legally they must ask your permission first. In practice this is very inefficient: many authors are unreachable, or they would not mind sharing but have never explicitly said so. CC licenses provide a standardised set of "Some Rights Reserved" statements. A creator can clearly tell everyone: you may copy, share, modify, and even commercially use my work, as long as you meet my conditions (e.g., attribution, non‑commercial use). 12.7.2 The Four Core Elements All CC licenses are built from combinations of the following four conditions: | Icon | Abbr | Condition | Meaning | |------|------|-----------|---------| | | BY | Attribution | You must credit the author, the work's title, and the license. All CC licenses include BY. | | | SA | ShareAlike | Modified works must be released under the same license. Similar to GPL's copyleft. | | | NC | NonCommercial | Only non‑commercial uses are allowed. Commercial use requires separate permission. | | | ND | NoDerivatives | You may copy and share, but not modify, adapt, or create derivatives. | 12.7.3 The Six Main CC Licenses Combining the above conditions gives six common licenses, from most permissive to most restrictive: | Abbreviation | Full name | Conditions | What is allowed | |--------------|-----------|------------|------------------| | CC BY | Attribution | BY | Any use (including commercial), can modify, can release derivatives under a different license. | | CC BY-SA | Attribution-ShareAlike | BY + SA | Any use, can modify, but derivatives must use the same license. Wikipedia uses this. | | CC BY-NC | Attribution-NonCommercial | BY + NC | Can share and modify, but non‑commercial only; can change the license. | | CC BY-NC-SA | Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike | BY + NC + SA | Non‑commercial only, can modify, but derivatives must use the same license. | | CC BY-ND | Attribution-NoDerivatives | BY + ND | Can share (including commercially), but cannot modify. | | CC BY-NC-ND | Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives | BY + NC + ND | Most restrictive. Can only share as‑is, no modifications, no commercial use. | 12.7.4 CC0 and the Public Domain There is also a special version: CC0 (Public Domain Dedication) . A creator who chooses CC0 dedicates their work to the public domain – they waive all copyright rights. Anyone can use, modify, or commercially exploit the work without attribution and without any conditions. CC0 is not one of the "six licenses". It is a separate "no copyright" declaration. Some images on Unsplash, OpenStreetMap data, and certain academic databases use CC0. The public domain refers to works whose copyright has expired (e.g., the author died more than 70 years ago – varies by jurisdiction) or has been voluntarily waived. All CC licenses (including CC0) are logically "copyright‑based open permissions", whereas the public domain is "no copyright" – legally even more absolute. 12.7.5 License Versions CC licenses have gone through several versions: 1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, and 4.0. 4.0 is the latest (released 2013) . It fixes many legal issues, is more international, and is easier to interoperate with other licenses. When choosing a license, prefer version 4.0. Some older works may be marked 3.0 or 2.5 – those are still legally valid, but their porting to different jurisdictions may vary. 12.7.6 Typical Choices for Different Scenarios | Your goal | Recommended license | |-----------|---------------------| | You wrote a popular science article and want it widely read – you don't mind others adapting it into videos or even selling it, as long as you are credited | CC BY | | You drew an illustration – others may use it as wallpaper or print it on T‑shirts, but cannot sell those items | CC BY-NC | | You wrote a technical tutorial – others may translate, modify, and republish it, but the translated version must also be open (similar to GPL) | CC BY-SA | | You took a photo – others may use it freely, but they cannot crop out your watermark or alter it beyond recognition | CC BY-ND | | Your thesis is uploaded to the university repository – you want it to be downloadable and shared, but not modified or sold | CC BY-NC-ND | | You took a casual snapshot and truly don't care if someone uses it on a commercial poster | CC0 | 12.7.7 How to Find CC‑Licensed Works Images: Flickr's "Advanced Search" lets you filter by CC license. Unsplash images are mostly CC0 or similar terms. Wikimedia Commons files all have clear CC labels. Music: Free Music Archive (FMA), Jamendo. The YouTube Audio Library also has a CC category. Text: Wikipedia (CC BY‑SA). Some articles on Medium (look at the footer). Courseware: MIT OpenCourseWare (CC BY‑NC‑SA). Some resources from Chinese university MOOCs. 12.7.8 A Friendly Reminder CC licenses are legal tools based on copyright. They are effective in China as well (Chinese copyright law recognises the granting of partial rights through licenses). However, keep in mind: Works marked NC (NonCommercial) cannot be sold. What counts as "commercial"? Using them in internal company training, printing them on products for sale, putting them behind a paywall – all of these are commercial uses. Works marked ND (NoDerivatives) cannot be translated, remixed, or adapted. Simple copying and sharing is fine. If you fail to meet a condition (e.g., forget to provide attribution), your permission to use the work automatically ends – unless you obtain separate permission from the author. In addition to the human‑readable deed (a summary) and the machine‑readable metadata, every CC license has a full legal code. In case of disputes, the legal code governs.

title: Mrakdown
content: Appendix 13: Markdown This appendix introduces what Markdown is and how to use it. Markdown is a lightweight markup language that lets you write documents in plain text and then convert them to clean, formatted HTML. It is much simpler than Word and much nicer to look at than Notepad. This appendix covers only the most basic syntax. For more detailed tutorials, please visit . 13.1 What Is Markdown? Markdown is a plain‑text markup language. Instead of using your mouse to click a "bold" button, you just add a few symbols around your text. For example: Markdown files usually have the extension. You can open and edit them with any text editor (Notepad, VS Code). After writing, you can convert the file to HTML, PDF, Word, or other formats. What can you do with Markdown? Write README files (the project descriptions you see on GitHub are almost all Markdown) Write blog posts (many static blog systems such as Hexo, Hugo, and VuePress use Markdown) Take notes (Obsidian, Typora, and Notion all support Markdown) Write technical documentation (many open source projects use Markdown for their docs) In fact, all the content of this site was written in Markdown Markdown's biggest feature is that it is plain text – you can open it on any computer without worrying about layout breaking, unlike files. The syntax is extremely simple; you can learn it in ten minutes. 13.2 Basic Syntax Below is the most commonly used Markdown syntax. For a more complete reference, see the "Basic Syntax" section on markdown.com.cn. 13.2.1 Headings Use to indicate a heading. The number of symbols indicates the heading level. Always put a space after the . 13.2.2 Paragraphs and Line Breaks Separate paragraphs with a blank line. If you only want a line break (without starting a new paragraph), add two spaces at the end of the line, then press Enter. 13.2.3 Emphasis 13.2.4 Lists Unordered lists: Use , , or , followed by a space. Ordered lists: Use a number followed by a period, then a space. The numbers do not have to be sequential – Markdown will renumber them automatically. 13.2.5 Links 13.2.6 Images 13.2.7 Blockquotes Use to indicate a blockquote. You can nest them ( ). 13.2.8 Code Inline code: Wrap the code with backticks (the key above Tab, to the left of ). Code blocks: Wrap the code with three backticks. You can specify a language for syntax highlighting. ~markdown ~ 13.2.9 Horizontal Rules Use three or more , , or on a line by themselves. 13.2.10 Tables Use to separate cells and to separate the header from the body. 13.2.11 Task Lists Use for incomplete tasks and for completed tasks. 13.3 Extended Syntax Standard Markdown is fairly basic. Extended syntax adds more useful features: strikethrough, automatic links, footnotes, definition lists, Emoji, highlighting, subscripts, superscripts, and more. However, not all Markdown renderers support extended syntax. Examples of common extended syntax: For a detailed explanation of extended syntax, see the "Extended Syntax" section on . 13.4 What Tools Can You Use? VS Code: Install the extension. You can preview, generate tables of contents, and export to HTML. Typora: A dedicated Markdown editor that is "what you see is what you get" – you type the syntax, and it shows the rendered result in real time. Clean interface, good for beginners. Obsidian: A knowledge management tool that supports Markdown. Great for building a personal note archive. Any text editor: Even Notepad works, though you will not get preview. 13.5 A Final Thought Markdown is not a replacement for Word – for complex layouts, exact margins, or academic references, you should still use Word or LaTeX. But for everyday notes, documents, READMEs, and blog posts, Markdown is the most hassle‑free way to write. You do not need to memorise all the syntax. Just remember for headings, for bold, , and . That is enough. Look up the rest when you need it.

title: Color
content: Appendix 14: Color This appendix introduces the basic concepts of color – gamut, color space, color accuracy, and calibration. If you only use your computer to watch videos, play games, and edit your own photos, you probably won't need this knowledge. But if you start doing design work, photo retouching, or video editing, and need to share your work with others or send it to print, understanding these concepts will help. 14.1 The Most Important Thing You Need to Know If you are not delivering final work to someone else (e.g., sending to a client, printing, submitting to a publication) – if you are just using your computer for games, watching videos, or editing your own photos – then whether your screen's colors are "accurate" simply does not matter. Use whatever looks comfortable to you. Color management is a rabbit hole. Unless you make a living from color (graphic design, retouching, video color grading, printing), you do not need to go deep. If you ever need it later, just knowing that it exists and knowing which direction to search is enough. 14.2 Gamut and Color Space 14.2.1 What Is Gamut? Gamut is the range of colors that a device (a monitor, printer, projector) or a color standard can reproduce. The human eye can see many colors, but different devices can only cover a portion of them. Common gamut standards: | Gamut | Coverage (relative to human vision) | Main use | One‑sentence explanation | |-------|--------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------| | sRGB | About 35% | Web, ordinary monitors, Windows default | The most universal "safe" gamut. Almost every device displays it correctly. | | DCI-P3 | About 45% | Digital cinema, Apple devices, HDR video | Wider than sRGB, especially in reds and greens. | | Display P3 | About 45% | Apple displays | Based on DCI-P3, but with the same white point as sRGB for better compatibility. | | Adobe RGB | About 50% | Professional photography, printing | Enhanced cyan and green to cover the CMYK print gamut. | | Rec. 709 | Almost identical to sRGB | HDTV | sRGB's "TV version" – slightly different white point and gamma. | | Rec. 2020 | About 75% | 4K/8K UHDTV | One of the widest gamuts available; almost no consumer display can fully cover it. | 14.2.2 Three Names, Essentially the Same Range sRGB, Rec.709, and Rec.601 have nearly identical color ranges. The differences: sRGB: For computer monitors, the web, consumer digital cameras Rec.709: For HDTV – white point is the same as sRGB, gamma curve is slightly different Rec.601: Standard for SDTV, now largely replaced by Rec.709 For ordinary users, you can treat them as the same thing – the "common small gamut". The vast majority of images and videos you see online are in sRGB or Rec.709. 14.2.3 OKLAB: Why It Exists Traditional color spaces like sRGB and P3 are not mathematically "uniform". What does that mean? In sRGB, a numeric change of 10 might look large in dark areas but barely noticeable in bright areas. OKLAB is a newer color model designed so that the same numeric change produces the same perceptual change for the human eye. OKLAB is mainly used inside color conversion algorithms (for example, converting an sRGB image to P3 without introducing a color cast). Ordinary users do not need to work with it directly, but you can remember: if you see a piece of software that supports OKLAB, it handles color more scientifically. 14.2.4 Why So Many Gamuts? Different industries have different needs. Printing requires coverage of CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black), hence Adobe RGB. Cinema needs a wider dynamic range and vivid reds/greens, hence DCI-P3. Television has evolved from SDTV to HDTV to UHDTV, giving us Rec.601, Rec.709, and Rec.2020. For ordinary users, sRGB is the safest. If you create a very vivid image on a wide‑gamut monitor and send it to a friend who uses a normal sRGB monitor, they will see less saturated colors. Conversely, when someone sends you an sRGB image and you view it on a wide‑gamut monitor without proper color management, the colors will be incorrectly "stretched" and look oversaturated. This is why many designers switch their monitors to sRGB mode when editing. 14.3 Monitor Gamut Coverage When buying a monitor, you will see specs like "99% sRGB coverage" or "95% DCI-P3 coverage". What do these numbers mean? Gamut coverage: What percentage of a given gamut this monitor can actually display. 99% sRGB means the monitor can show 99% of the colors inside the sRGB triangle; the remaining 1% cannot be shown. Gamut volume: The ratio of the monitor's total color area to the area of a reference gamut. It is possible to have "120% sRGB volume" – but that does not mean accurate color, because the extra 20% may be in entirely wrong directions. For ordinary users: A monitor that covers 100% sRGB is already very good for daily use. Wider gamuts (P3, Adobe RGB) are not necessary unless you have a specific need (e.g., editing HDR video, doing print design). 14.4 Color Accuracy: ΔE (Delta E) ΔE (Delta E) is a number that measures how "accurate" a color is. The smaller the ΔE, the smaller the difference between the displayed color and the standard reference color. | ΔE range | Meaning | |----------|---------| | ΔE 5 | Color cast is clearly visible to the naked eye | Monitor ΔE values are usually quoted as "average ΔE". For example, "average ΔE < 2" means most colors are fairly accurate, but some colors (e.g., deep blue) may be off by more. For ordinary users: Do not obsess over ΔE. When you are gaming, you do not care whether "this red is the exact sRGB red". As long as colors are not wildly wrong (e.g., white looking pink), you are fine. 14.5 Calibration Devices and Calibration If you truly need accurate color (for example, you have taken a design job and the client requires no color deviation), then you need calibration. 14.5.1 What Is a Calibration Device? A colorimeter (or spectrophotometer) is a small, mouse‑sized piece of hardware. You attach it to your screen, it measures the colors your screen actually displays, and then it generates an ICC profile for your operating system. Once Windows loads this profile, it adjusts the output signal to make the screen more accurate. Common calibration device brands: Datacolor Spyder: Common models include Spyder X, Spyder 5. Suitable for ordinary users and photography enthusiasts. Calibrite (formerly X-Rite) : More professional – e.g., ColorChecker Display, i1Display Pro. Many studios use these. 14.5.2 Calibration Steps Connect the calibration device to your computer and install the accompanying software (or use the open‑source DisplayCAL). Let your monitor warm up for at least 30 minutes (so colors stabilise). In the software, set your targets: white point (usually D65, i.e., 6500K), brightness (120 cd/m² for a typical indoor environment), gamma (choose 2.2 for sRGB/Rec.709). Attach the device to the center of your screen and run the measurement. The software will display a series of colors, and the device reads them one by one. When the measurement finishes, the software generates an ICC profile and tells Windows to load it. Take this with a grain of salt – I researched this information; I have never used one myself. If you really need calibration, it is best to ask the vendor for advice. 14.5.3 When Do You Need Calibration? You just bought a new monitor: Factory calibration is not always accurate, and it drifts over time. Professional users calibrate every 1–2 months. You changed your graphics card or reinstalled your OS: The system's color configuration may have been lost. You notice two screens look different: For example, your laptop screen and an external monitor clearly do not match. You are sending work to print: Printing has strict color requirements. Without calibration, the printed result may be wildly off. 14.5.4 When Do You NOT Need Calibration? You only game and watch videos: Not needed. You use a built‑in laptop screen: The hardware quality of laptop screens is limited. Calibration will not improve it much, and it is not worth the expense. You occasionally edit photos, only to post on social media: Not needed. No one on social media is comparing your photos against a color checker. You do not own a calibration device: You can rent one (available on platforms like Taobao for a few dozen RMB per day) or borrow from a friend. Buying one costs anywhere from a few hundred to over a thousand RMB – if you only need it once, renting is more economical. 14.6 When Color Management Is Important vs. When It Is Not 14.6.1 When You Must Take Color Management Seriously Design work delivered to a client: If a blue that looks great on your screen looks purple on the client's screen, your final payment may be at risk. Printing: A screen and a piece of paper are completely different media. Without color management, the printed output will look nothing like what you see on screen. Video color grading delivered to a platform (Bilibili, YouTube, etc.) : If you set the wrong color space, the platform will re‑encode the video and the colors will shift. Product photography (Taobao, e‑commerce) : If the color of a garment is inaccurate, customers will receive items that look different from the photos, leading to high return rates. 14.6.2 When You Can Ignore Color Management Playing games: Not needed. Watching videos and movies: Not needed. The video is already graded; you are seeing what the director intended (as long as your monitor is not terrible). Editing your own photos, only to post on social media or keep on your phone: Not needed. Your friends use different brands of phones, each with different screen colors – no matter how accurately you calibrate, the colors will look different on their screens. Relax. Coding, writing documents, taking online classes: Color has nothing to do with the content. Not needed. 14.6.3 One‑Sentence Summary If you are not delivering work to others – if it is just for your own enjoyment – do not bother with color management. Spending your energy on content is far more valuable than spending it on color accuracy. 14.7 Windows Color Management: Why It Is More Complicated Than on Mac Let me briefly explain this. Many people say "Mac colors are accurate, Windows colors are a mess". The reason lies in the different designs of the two systems: macOS: System‑level, mandatory color management. Regardless of the application (even old software that does not support color management), macOS maps color data to the display's actual gamut at the system level. Combined with Apple's factory‑calibrated screens, it is accurate out of the box. Windows: Applications are on their own. Programs that support color management (Photoshop, Lightroom, Chrome/Edge) handle colors correctly. Programs that do not support it (older games, old screenshot tools, some image viewers) simply send their color values directly to the screen. If you have a wide‑gamut screen, colors in those applications will appear oversaturated. This difference does not affect ordinary users. But if you need accurate color and do not want to tinker, a Mac is indeed the more hassle‑free choice. Extended Reading The following sections involve mathematical calculations and deeper principles of color spaces. They are more advanced. Skim them first, and come back later when you need them. Extended 1: The CIE 1931 Chromaticity Diagram In 1931, the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) defined the CIE 1931 XYZ color space, which forms the foundation of all modern colorimetry. It is a horseshoe‑shaped diagram of human color perception. The x and y axes represent chromaticity (color, without brightness). Any gamut can be drawn as a triangle inside this horseshoe – the three vertices are the coordinates of that gamut's red, green, and blue primaries. sRGB, DCI-P3, and Rec.2020 are all different‑sized triangles inside this horseshoe. Extended 2: Gamut Coverage vs. Gamut Volume – The Mathematical Difference Coverage: The area of overlap between the monitor's gamut and the reference gamut, divided by the area of the reference gamut (a percentage). Coverage cannot exceed 100%. Volume: The total area of the monitor's gamut divided by the area of the reference gamut (a percentage). Volume can exceed 100% (meaning the monitor's gamut is wider than the reference). A monitor might claim "120% sRGB volume", but if that extra 20% volume lies in wrong directions, the monitor may still be inaccurate when displaying sRGB content. High volume does not necessarily mean good – coverage is a better indicator of accuracy for a given gamut. Extended 3: CIE Lab vs. OKLAB CIE Lab (also called CIELAB, Lab) is a color space defined by the CIE in 1976. It was designed to be "perceptually uniform" – but later research found that it is still not very uniform, especially in the blue region. OKLAB (proposed in 2020) improves uniformity, particularly in blue and cyan areas. OKLAB is currently one of the better color spaces for color conversion algorithms (e.g., converting from P3 to sRGB). Adobe Photoshop, Blender, and OpenColorIO have started to support OKLAB. Extended 4: White Point and Color Temperature The white point determines the coordinates of "white" on the chromaticity diagram. Common white points: D65: 6500K, corresponds to midday sunlight. sRGB, Rec.709, and Display P3 all use D65. D50: 5000K, slightly yellowish. The standard for the printing industry (because printing paper itself is not pure white). Original DCI-P3 white point: 6300K, slightly different from D65. Display P3 changed the white point to D65 for better compatibility with sRGB. Color temperature is measured in Kelvin (K). Lower values look more yellow/red (warm), higher values look more blue (cool). The "warm", "standard", and "cool" settings on a TV adjust the white point. Extended 5: How Calibration Data Is Stored The ICC profile generated by a calibration device is a file containing a CLUT (Color Lookup Table) . When Windows loads this profile, the graphics card applies the table when outputting signals: . This process requires GPU and OS support. Some older games may bypass color management entirely, making the calibration ineffective. Extended 6: Using a Wide‑Gamut Monitor for Everyday Work If you have bought a wide‑gamut monitor (e.g., covering 95% DCI-P3) but mainly use Windows, here is some advice: Switch your monitor to sRGB mode** via its on‑screen display (OSD) menu. This makes the monitor internally compress the wide gamut down to sRGB, so all applications (including those that do not support color management) show correct colors. If you truly need the wide gamut (e.g., for editing HDR video), enable color management inside your editing software, but switch back to sRGB mode for everyday use. Alternatively, only enable wide‑gamut mode when you are certain you need it. Use sRGB mode the rest of the time – no fuss.

title: VideoANDAudio
content: Appendix 15: Audio and Video This appendix introduces basic concepts and common tools for audio and video processing, including codecs, container formats, bitrate, OBS recording settings, and video editing software choices. The extended reading section covers FFmpeg command‑line usage and deeper technical concepts. 15.1 Codecs An encoder compresses raw audio or video data into a specific format. A decoder decompresses that data back into a playable signal. 15.1.1 Video Codecs | Name | Common encoders | One‑sentence explanation | |------|----------------|---------------------------| | H.264 / AVC | (software), (NVIDIA), (Intel) | Best compatibility – almost every device can play it. | | H.265 / HEVC | (software), (NVIDIA), (Intel) | Same quality as H.264 but smaller file size. | | AV1 | , (software) | Even higher compression, good for streaming. | Note: requires an NVIDIA GPU; requires an Intel iGPU. Not every computer has them. Software encoding vs. hardware encoding: Software encoding ( , , ): Better quality, smaller files, but uses the CPU heavily and is slow. Good for archiving and high‑quality encodes. Hardware encoding ( , ): Very fast (5‑10× faster than software), but slightly lower quality at the same bitrate. Good for screen recording, live streaming, and fast exports. 15.1.2 Audio Codecs | Name | Common encoder | One‑sentence explanation | |------|----------------|---------------------------| | AAC | | The most universal audio format today – almost every video uses it. | | MP3 | | Older format, good compatibility, but worse quality than AAC at the same bitrate. | | FLAC | | Lossless compression, large file size – good for archiving and listening to music. | | Opus | | Newer technology, excellent quality and compression; some older devices do not support it. | 15.2 Container Formats A container format is the "box" that holds video, audio, and subtitles. The same H.265 video can be put into an or into an . | Container | Characteristics | |-----------|-----------------| | MP4 | Most universal – almost every device plays it. Downside: usually can only hold one video track, one audio track, and one subtitle track. | | MKV | Very powerful – can hold multiple audio tracks, multiple subtitle tracks, and chapter information. If damaged, only the last few seconds are corrupted (the rest remains recoverable). | | MOV | Apple's QuickTime format, also supports multiple tracks. Good for exchanging files between Apple devices and Windows. | 15.3 Bitrate Bitrate is the amount of data used per second of video, measured in kbps (kilobits per second) or Mbps (megabits per second). Higher bitrate → better quality → larger file. CBR (Constant Bitrate) : The bitrate stays the same throughout. Suitable for live streaming. VBR (Variable Bitrate) : Simple scenes get a lower bitrate; complex scenes get a higher bitrate. Better quality at the same average bitrate. CRF (Constant Quality) : The encoder automatically allocates bitrate to keep the quality roughly constant for every frame. The most hassle‑free option for everyday encoding. 15.4 OBS Recording Settings 15.4.1 Basic Settings Output mode: Advanced → set output to "Output to file" Container format: Choose MKV (reason: if OBS crashes or your computer loses power during recording, MKV will only corrupt the last few seconds; MP4 will become completely unreadable) Encoder: If you have both an Intel iGPU and a discrete GPU → choose QuickSync HEVC (uses the iGPU to encode, does not compete with your games for GPU resources) If you have only an NVIDIA GPU → choose NVENC HEVC If you have only an AMD GPU → choose AMD AMF HEVC (good luck) 15.4.2 Recommended Settings | Resolution | Bitrate | Frame rate | Keyframe interval | B‑frames | |------------|---------|------------|-------------------|----------| | 1080p | 35 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 seconds | 3 | | 4K | 90 Mbps | 60 fps | 3 seconds | 3 | Games lack motion blur – every frame is a sharp instant capture. When the camera moves quickly, details can break up easily. Therefore, game recording requires higher bitrates than normal video. About B‑frames: B‑frames (bidirectional predicted frames) improve compression efficiency but increase encoding latency. Setting them to 3 is a good balance between quality and compatibility. 15.4.3 Administrator Privileges For some full‑screen games, if OBS cannot capture the game window, right‑click the OBS icon and select "Run as administrator". 15.5 Editing Software 15.5.1 Adobe Suite Premiere Pro: Video editing – one of the industry standards. After Effects: Visual effects, compositing, motion graphics. Audition: Audio editing, noise reduction, mixing. Adobe software is subscription‑based. You can download a trial version from Creative Cloud, then – without opening the software – immediately run AdobeGenP to activate it. I am not providing copies. This touches on copyright issues, so please use your own judgement. 15.5.2 DaVinci Resolve A professional editing and color grading tool from Blackmagic Design. The free version is already extremely powerful – editing, color grading (used by Hollywood movies), Fairlight audio, and Fusion effects all integrated. If you care about color accuracy, this is often a better choice than Premiere. 15.5.3 Open‑Source Alternatives If you do not want to pay for software and do not want to deal with piracy, these three open‑source tools are worth trying. Clypra Clypra is a modern open‑source video editor built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, Rust, and FFmpeg, released under the MIT license. Its goal is to replicate the paid features of CapCut's international version for free. Because it does not use Electron (which consumes lots of memory), it starts faster and uses fewer resources than similar tools. Core features: Multi‑track professional timeline with drag‑and‑drop editing and frame‑level trimming Real‑time audio waveform display for easy beat‑matching Filmstrip preview for quick content navigation Text subtitles and titles with custom fonts Project management and auto‑save, with 100 levels of undo/redo Supports MP4, MOV, MKV, AVI (video) and MP3, WAV, AAC (audio) Cross‑platform: Windows, macOS, Linux Not yet implemented: AI auto‑subtitles, transition/effect libraries, colour grading, green screen keying (these are under development). Who it is for: Short‑form video creators, beginners, people who do not want to pay for CapCut. Basic editing is already usable. Website: Search GitHub for Audacity Audacity is a long‑established, easy‑to‑use open‑source multi‑track audio editor and recorder, released under GPLv3. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Core features: Multi‑track editing with unlimited tracks Import/export of WAV, AIFF, MP3, OGG, FLAC, and more (can support MOV, M4A, etc. via FFmpeg) High‑quality recording (up to 24‑bit / 96 kHz) Built‑in effects: noise reduction, EQ, compressor, limiter, and more Vocal remover (using phase cancellation to separate vocals from accompaniment) Supports VST2/VST3, LV2, and Audio Unit plugins Nyquist scripting for custom audio processing (using a Lisp dialect) Who it is for: Podcasters, music hobbyists, recording beginners, people who need occasional audio cleanup. It is the "Notepad of audio editors" – not fancy, but it can do a bit of everything. Website: Ardour Ardour is a free and open‑source digital audio workstation (DAW) that competes with Pro Tools, Logic, and other professional software. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux. The current version is 9.0. Core features: Recording and MIDI composition: multi‑channel simultaneous recording (24+ channels), unlimited tracks and busses Non‑linear editing: non‑destructive editing with unlimited undo/redo Professional mixing: floating‑point mixing architecture, sends and returns, automation Extensive plugin support: AudioUnit, LV2, VST2/VST3, LADSPA Highly flexible signal routing: any channel to any other channel Video sync: sample‑accurate synchronisation, suitable for film and game sound design Advanced MIDI editing (new in 8.0): chord editing, quantisation, velocity maps, etc. Clip Launching mode (new in 7.0): Ableton Live‑style loop playback System requirements: 2 GB RAM recommended, ~600 MB disk space. Who it is for: Music producers, heavy‑duty podcasters, film/game audio professionals, anyone who needs serious depth in audio. The learning curve is steep, but its depth is unmatched by Audacity. Website: 15.5.4 Comparison and Recommendations | Software | Main use | Complexity | Paid equivalent | Recommended for | |----------|----------|------------|-----------------|------------------| | Clypra | Video editing | Medium | CapCut | Short‑form creators, beginners | | Audacity | Audio editing / recording | Low | Adobe Audition (basic parts) | Podcasters, voice recording, quick fixes | | Ardour | Full‑featured DAW | High | Pro Tools, Logic | Music production, professional mixing | 15.6 HDR and Color Management (Recap) From Appendix 14, we know that color management on Windows is finicky. HDR video editing is even more so: HDR10: The baseline HDR standard, 10‑bit colour depth, static metadata. Supported by most HDR monitors. Dolby Vision: A more advanced standard with dynamic metadata (per‑frame brightness information). Requires licensing on both the hardware and software sides. HLG: An HDR standard for broadcast TV. No metadata needed and is backwards‑compatible with SDR displays. If you have serious HDR editing needs, a MacBook Pro is currently the most hassle‑free choice (XDR screen, 1600 nits peak brightness, system‑level colour management). The time cost of wrestling with HDR on Windows can far exceed your expectations. Extended Reading The following sections cover FFmpeg command‑line usage, the inner workings of I/P/B frames, encoder tuning, and hardware detection. Come back when you need them. I will cover FFmpeg in more depth in the main book – stay tuned. Extended 1: FFmpeg Command‑Line Tool FFmpeg is an open‑source command‑line audio and video processing tool. Almost every audio/video software uses it under the hood. Converting formats, cutting clips, burning in subtitles – all can be done with a single command. Installation Download the Windows pre‑built package from ffmpeg.org. Extract it, then add the folder to your system PATH. Open a command prompt and type to confirm it works. Common Commands Format conversion: Video cutting (start at 1 minute 30 seconds, take 45 seconds): Parameter explanation: start time, duration, do not re‑encode (copy the streams directly). Putting before performs a fast seek (based on keyframes); putting it after performs an accurate seek (decodes every frame). Encode to HEVC (software) : Use NVIDIA hardware encoding (if your GPU supports it): Use Intel iGPU hardware encoding (if your iGPU supports it): Extract audio: means "no video stream"; sets the audio bitrate. Download an m3u8 video (online stream) : Batch Processing Here is a simple Windows batch script ( ): For more complex tasks, use PowerShell 7 (which supports for parallel processing) or Python with . The power of FFmpeg is that – apart from tasks that require real‑time preview (e.g., colour grading) – almost everything else (rough cutting, transcoding, concatenation, filtering) can be done with it. Extended 2: I‑frames, P‑frames, B‑frames – Detailed Explanation Video compression does not store every frame as a full image. Instead, it stores the differences between frames. I‑frame (Intra‑frame) : Stores a complete frame. Largest size, fastest to decode. These are the "full images" in the video. An I‑frame appears every so often (controlled by the "keyframe interval" setting). P‑frame (Predicted frame) : Stores only the differences from the previous frame. Medium size. Decoding requires referring back to a previous I‑frame or P‑frame. B‑frame (Bidirectional frame) : Stores differences from both the previous frame and the next frame. Smallest size, highest compression, but slowest to decode. Why cutting at a non‑I‑frame causes corruption: P‑frames and B‑frames only store "changes", not full images. If playback starts at a P‑frame or B‑frame, the decoder does not know what the previous frame looked like, so it guesses – resulting in broken blocks on the screen. When cutting without re‑encoding, cuts can only be made at I‑frames. To cut at an arbitrary frame, re‑encoding is required. Extended 3: Encoder Speed Presets The parameter for x264/x265 ranges from to . Slower presets give better quality (at the same bitrate). For daily use, or is fine. Beyond , the gains are marginal. : Extremely fast encoding, low quality, large files : Default, balances speed and quality : About 50% slower than medium, saves 5‑10% bitrate : Very slow, diminishing returns For NVENC, the options range from (fastest) to (slowest, best quality). Default is . At , quality improves noticeably, but encoding speed drops significantly. Extended 4: AV1 Encoders Compared libaom-av1: The reference AV1 encoder. Best quality, but extremely slow (encoding 1 second of video can take minutes to tens of minutes). libsvtav1: Developed by Intel. Much faster (hundreds of times faster than libaom) and still delivers very good quality. For everyday AV1 encoding, use libsvtav1. Extended 5: 2‑pass Encoding The first pass analyses the video, recording the complexity of each frame. The second pass then allocates bitrate accordingly – giving more bits to complex scenes and fewer bits to simple scenes. This is useful when you need to hit an exact file size (e.g., a file size limit for uploading to a website). For daily use, CRF is sufficient; 2‑pass is not needed. Extended 6: Dolby Audio Formats – Details AC‑3: The older Dolby Digital audio format. The DVD era standard. Supports 5.1 channels, typical bitrate 448k or 640k. E-AC‑3 (Dolby Digital Plus) : Dolby's lossy surround sound format. Supports 5.1 and 7.1 channels. Commonly used by streaming platforms (Netflix, Disney+, etc.). Typical bitrate 192k–768k. File extension may be . TrueHD: Dolby's lossless surround sound format. Common on Blu‑ray discs. Large file size; requires HDMI or eARC for direct passthrough. Supports up to 7.1 channels. Extended 7: Hardware Encoder Support Detection There is a tool on GitHub called HwCodecDetect that detects which hardware encoders and decoders your computer supports, and up to what resolution. It produces a report listing support for NVENC, QSV, AMF, VAAPI, VideoToolbox, and other interfaces. Extended 8: Pitfalls of FFmpeg Stream Copy does not re‑encode – it is very fast and lossless. However, when cutting video, if the start point is not an I‑frame, FFmpeg will start copying from the previous I‑frame. This means the resulting clip will start a few hundred milliseconds earlier than you intended. How to handle this: Accept the small error (usually less than half a second, often acceptable) Or re‑encode just the beginning part: first cut a rough range with , then re‑encode the head section accurately Extended 9: FFmpeg Filter Chain Example

title: Photography
content: Appendix 16: Photography This appendix introduces basic photography concepts – white balance, ISO, shutter speed, aperture, focal length, dynamic range – as well as professional camera apps for phones, the usefulness of RAW format, and some simple post‑processing ideas. Even if you only take casual snapshots, a little extra knowledge never hurts. 16.1 The Exposure Triangle: ISO, Shutter Speed, Aperture The brightness of a photo is determined by three things: ISO (sensitivity), shutter speed, and aperture. They are like three valves on a water tap, together controlling how much light reaches the camera. ISO (sensitivity) ISO is how sensitive the camera sensor is to light. A lower number (e.g., ISO 100) means less sensitivity, cleaner and sharper image quality. A higher number (e.g., ISO 3200) means more sensitivity – you can take brighter photos in very dark conditions – but at the cost of noise (grain) appearing in the image. Everyday advice: Use low ISO (100–400) when light is good for the best quality. Only raise ISO when it is genuinely dark. Shutter speed Shutter speed is the duration of exposure. A fast shutter speed (e.g., 1/1000 second) freezes moving subjects (birds in flight, racing cars). A slow shutter speed (e.g., 1/30 second or slower) captures motion blur (light trails from cars at night, silky water). Safe shutter speed: When shooting handheld, do not go slower than roughly "1 / (equivalent focal length)". For a 50mm lens, stay above 1/50 second, otherwise camera shake will blur the photo. Phone lenses have shorter equivalent focal lengths (around 24–28mm), so a safe shutter speed is around 1/30 second. Aperture Aperture is the size of the opening in the lens. It controls how much light enters and also affects depth of field (background blur). Wide aperture (small number, e.g., f/1.8) → more light, more background blur. Good for portraits and close‑ups. Narrow aperture (large number, e.g., f/8) → less light, everything in focus. Good for landscapes and group photos. Aperture on phones: The main cameras on most phones have a fixed aperture – you cannot change it. The "portrait mode" on phones does not adjust aperture; it uses software to simulate blur. So you do not need to worry about aperture values on a phone – just understand the concept. How the three work together A photo with the same overall brightness can be taken with many different combinations of settings. For example: wide aperture + fast shutter speed = narrow aperture + slow shutter speed. Choose based on what you need – want background blur? Use a wide aperture. Want everything sharp? Use a narrow aperture. Want to freeze motion? Use a fast shutter speed. Want light trails? Use a slow shutter speed. 16.2 White Balance White balance (WB) makes sure that white objects look white in a photo, regardless of the colour of the light illuminating them. Our eyes are very clever: under a yellow desk lamp, we still see a white piece of paper as white – our brain automatically compensates. A camera does not. Without adjusting white balance, a photo of white paper taken under yellow light will look yellow-ish. Cameras usually have Auto White Balance (AWB), which works well in most situations. But if you find your photos looking too yellow or too blue, you can manually select a WB mode (daylight, cloudy, tungsten, fluorescent, etc.) when shooting, or adjust the temperature slider afterwards in software like Lightroom. 16.3 Focal Length and Equivalent Focal Length Focal length (measured in mm) determines how wide or zoomed‑in your view is. Smaller numbers → wider view (wide‑angle). Larger numbers → narrower view, bringing distant objects closer (telephoto). Ultra‑wide (14–24mm): landscapes, architecture – grand, sweeping views. Standard (35–50mm): roughly the field of view of the human eye – street photography, everyday scenes. Telephoto (70mm and above): distant subjects – birds, people, the moon. Equivalent focal length: Phone sensors and standalone camera sensors (mirrorless/DSLR) have different sizes. A lens marked "24mm" on a phone will show a different field of view than a 24mm lens on a full‑frame camera. To make comparisons easy, the industry uses "full‑frame equivalent focal length". You do not need to memorise the formula – just remember that a phone's main camera is typically around 24–28mm equivalent (wide‑angle), and what phone makers call "telephoto" might be around 70mm equivalent or longer. 16.4 Minimum Focus Distance Every lens has a limit to how close you can get to a subject and still focus. If you move too close, the camera will refuse to focus – you have exceeded the minimum focus distance. Macro photography (flower stamens, insects) requires a lens that can focus very close. Ordinary lenses have minimum focus distances of a few tens of centimetres. If you want to try macro on your phone, check if it has a "macro mode" or "super macro", or buy a clip‑on macro lens. 16.5 Focus Peaking Focus peaking is a manual focus aid. When you turn the focus ring, areas that are in focus are highlighted with coloured dots (red, yellow, or white). The densest area of dots is where the sharpest focus lies. When to use it: When shooting macro, starry skies, or still life (e.g., product photography), autofocus may hunt or miss. Switch to manual focus, turn the ring while watching the peaking overlay, and stop when the dots are brightest – much more reliable than relying on your eye alone. Most mirrorless cameras and some phone pro modes support this. 16.6 Dynamic Range Dynamic range is the range between the brightest and darkest parts that a camera can capture at the same time. A high‑dynamic‑range scene: a portrait against a bright sky. The sky is very bright, the face is much darker. If the camera's dynamic range is insufficient, either the sky will be blown out (pure white) or the face will be too dark (details lost). The "HDR mode" on phones does this: the camera takes several exposures in quick succession (one for the highlights, one for the shadows, etc.) and merges them into a single photo where both the bright sky and the dark face are visible. Modern computational photography often runs this process automatically in the background – you do not need to turn on an HDR switch. When to use it: Sunrises and sunsets, backlit portraits, scenes with bright windows and dark interiors – any time the contrast is very high, HDR (if not already automatic) will help significantly. 16.7 Professional Camera Apps for Phones The built‑in camera app on most phones hides most controls; you just press the shutter button. If you want manual control over ISO, shutter speed, white balance, and focus, and want to shoot RAW, install a third‑party camera app. On iPhone: Halide Mark III Halide is a well‑known professional camera app. The latest version is Mark III. Manual control over all parameters (ISO, shutter speed, white balance, focus) Can shoot RAW (also supports Process Zero, which bypasses Apple's automatic processing) Now includes a Photo Lab editor for editing RAW photos Price: I am not sure – I have never used an Apple device. (But a friend of mine uses Halide often.) On Android: ProShot, Open Camera Android's openness allows for more third‑party camera apps. ProShot: DSLR‑style interface, manual control over ISO, shutter speed, white balance, focus, RAW support. Considered one of the best manual camera apps on Android. Paid. Open Camera: Open source, free, powerful. Supports manual controls, RAW, HDR, noise reduction, and more. If you do not want to spend money, this is the best choice – completely sufficient. Camera FV‑5: Another classic manual camera app, supports long exposure and RAW. Paid. When to use these apps: Shooting landscapes (manual focus to infinity), capturing light trails (slow shutter speed manually), shooting RAW for later editing – any time you want full control over your photo. 16.8 RAW Format 16.8.1 What Is RAW? By default, phones and cameras save photos as JPG (or HEIF). These are finished products – white balance, sharpening, noise reduction, and colour style are all baked in. There is very little room for editing afterwards. RAW is the unprocessed data straight from the sensor. It retains all the brightness and colour information as it was captured, without any processing. White balance can be changed freely, exposure can be pulled back by several stops, shadow details can be brightened – the editing flexibility is enormous. 16.8.2 Why Does RAW Look Grey and Flat? When you first open a RAW photo on your computer or phone, it often looks greyish, low‑contrast, and desaturated. This is normal. It is not "broken". It is because the RAW file has not gone through the camera's internal colour and contrast processing. You need to use software like Lightroom, Photoshop, or another RAW processor to "develop" it – adjust exposure, contrast, saturation, curves, etc. This process is called demosaicing or developing. 16.8.3 High Megapixel Counts on Phones and RAW Phones today boast 48MP, 64MP, or even 108MP sensors, but the RAW you get is often only 12MP or 16MP. This is not the phone lying to you – it is how the sensors work. Most high‑megapixel phone sensors use Quad Bayer (or even 16‑cell) designs. In normal shooting, adjacent pixels are merged into larger "super‑pixels" to get better light capture and image quality. A 48MP sensor, when quad‑merged, outputs a 12MP photo. Even when you shoot RAW, many phones output the merged 12MP RAW (for example, iPhone's ProRAW defaults to 12MP from the merged output). This is not a bad thing – a 12MP merged RAW usually has better image quality than a full 48MP RAW, because individual pixels on a tiny sensor are very small and prone to noise. If you truly need full resolution RAW (e.g., for large prints), look in your camera app for an option like "Full resolution RAW" or "Unbinned RAW". But in most cases, the 12MP merged RAW is perfectly adequate. 16.9 RAW vs. Straight‑out‑of‑Camera JPG | Format | File size | Editing flexibility | Best for | |--------|-----------|---------------------|----------| | JPG / HEIF | Small | Very limited – small brightness adjustments maybe, but white balance is mostly fixed | Everyday snapshots, social media, when you do not plan to edit | | RAW | Large | Huge – exposure can be pulled ±2 stops, white balance can be changed freely | When you want to do serious editing, colour grading, printing, selling photos | Conclusion: For casual photos, JPG is fine. But if you think "I might want to edit this later", or if the scene has very high contrast (backlighting, night scenes), shoot a RAW copy as well – disk space is cheap, but a missed moment is gone forever. 16.10 Colour Grading – Ideas and Tools Lightroom (LR) Lightroom is the most mainstream and beginner‑friendly photo editing software. It is available on mobile and desktop. A Creative Cloud Photography plan (which includes Photoshop) gives you access. The mobile version's basic features (exposure, contrast, saturation, curves) are free. A simple editing workflow (using Lightroom mobile as an example) : Import the RAW (LR will automatically enter the "develop" mode) In the "Brightness" section, adjust exposure, contrast, highlights, and shadows (pull down the bright sky, lift the shadow details) In the "Colour" section, adjust white balance (temperature, tint) and saturation Apply a preset or manually adjust the curve (an S‑curve is a simple way to increase contrast and add "pop") Finally, add a little sharpening and noise reduction – do not overdo it Two important reminders: Your screen colour needs to be trustworthy: You spend time carefully adjusting colours, only to find that your own screen was off – and the photo looks completely different (often grey and flat) on someone else's phone. This is a classic beginner trap. If your computer or phone screen seems too warm or too cool (compare it with another device), go into its settings and turn off "vivid mode", "dynamic colour enhancement", or similar options. The safest approach is to trust a device you know is accurate (like an iPad) or a friend's phone. Mobile LR presets ≠ desktop LR presets: The same preset file can look different when applied in Lightroom mobile versus Lightroom desktop – because the two use different colour spaces and rendering engines. If you tweak a preset on your phone and want to use it on your computer, test it side‑by‑side first and be ready to make small adjustments. Everyone has their own style There is no single "correct" way to colour grade. Some people like rich, saturated, punchy colours. Others prefer muted, cool, desaturated tones. Some only work in black and white. It is up to you. Look a lot (at good photos, at colour charts), edit a lot (pull curves, adjust HSL sliders), and over time you will develop your own feel. Extended Reading The following sections go into deeper technical details. Come back when you need them. Extended 1: Technical Principle of Pixel Binning Quad Bayer sensors arrange four same‑colour pixels in a 2×2 array. In normal shooting, these four pixels are merged into one "super‑pixel", outputting a lower‑resolution image. However, each super‑pixel has four times the light‑gathering area of a single tiny pixel, resulting in much higher signal‑to‑noise ratio. When high resolution is genuinely needed (e.g., in excellent light), the sensor can perform a remosaic to output the full 48MP. Some phones also use different gain (ISO) levels on the different sub‑pixels and merge them later, improving dynamic range in a single shot (a kind of "HDR‑in‑one"). Extended 2: Fine‑tuning White Balance Auto white balance can be fooled by a scene dominated by a single colour (for example, if you stand in front of a large red wall). If your photos have a colour cast, you can manually set a grey point: in Lightroom or another RAW processor, use the white balance eyedropper to click on an area that should be neutral grey or white (e.g., a piece of concrete, a white wall, a white piece of paper). The software will correct the global colour temperature based on that sample. Extended 3: Dynamic Range vs. Latitude Dynamic range is the range between the brightest and darkest light levels that a sensor can capture in a single exposure. Latitude is how much you can later brighten underexposed areas or darken overexposed areas in a RAW file without introducing excessive noise or artefacts. They are related but not identical. A sensor with high dynamic range usually has good latitude – you can lift shadows by 2–3 stops without ruining the image. Extended 4: How Computational Photography Affects RAW Modern phones' RAW files are no longer "pure" RAW in the traditional sense. iPhone ProRAW, for example, starts with RAW data but then incorporates multi‑frame information from Deep Fusion (it has already merged several exposures at different brightness levels in the background). The benefit is that ProRAW's dynamic range in challenging scenes far exceeds what a traditional RAW would have. The cost is that it already carries some "computational" fingerprints – it is not the rawest of raw data. Android manufacturers' "RAW" implementations vary – some are also multi‑frame DNGs.
