If you truly want the most unprocessed sensor output, you may need to use a third‑party app and disable all multi‑frame enhancements. Extended 5: Colour Space Settings in Lightroom Lightroom's working space on the desktop is typically ProPhoto RGB (very large). However, for photos you export to share with others, you should convert to sRGB – the most universal colour gamut, which almost every screen can display correctly. If you edit a photo on a wide‑gamut screen, then export it as ProPhoto RGB or Adobe RGB and send it via WeChat or upload it to a website, the colours will appear dull and grey on most viewers' devices. Remember to select sRGB when exporting.

title: Security
content: Appendix 17: Privacy and Security This appendix introduces the basic principles of network communication (HTTPS, TCP, TLS), password managers, two‑factor authentication (2FA), and some easily overlooked privacy habits. It does not go deep into technical details, but it will help you understand "how data travels through the network" and "how to prevent your accounts from being stolen." 17.1 How Data Travels Through the Network: TCP, TLS, HTTPS When you open a website (for example, ), three things happen behind the scenes: a connection is established, an encrypted channel is created, and data is transmitted. 17.1.1 TCP: Establishing a Reliable Connection TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is responsible for delivering data reliably from one end to the other. It first breaks the data into small packets, numbers each packet, sends them out, and waits for an acknowledgement before sending the next. If a packet is lost, TCP resends it. Think of it this way: TCP is like sending a registered letter – each letter has a tracking number, the recipient must sign for it, and if it is lost, you send another copy. The advantage is reliability; the downside is that it is slower because of all the back‑and‑forth acknowledgements. The difference from UDP: UDP is like sending a postcard – you drop it in the mailbox and forget about it, with no confirmation of receipt. The advantage is speed; the downside is that packets may be lost. Video calls and online games often use UDP (losing an occasional frame is tolerable, but high latency is not). 17.1.2 TLS: Locking the Data TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the "S" in HTTPS. It adds an encryption layer on top of the TCP connection. The data you send is encrypted into ciphertext before it leaves your computer and is only decrypted when it reaches the server. Any intermediate node (router, ISP, Wi‑Fi hotspot) sees only gibberish and cannot read the content. The TLS handshake works roughly like this: Your computer and the server greet each other and agree on an encryption algorithm. The server presents a digital certificate (to prove "I really am Baidu"). Both sides generate a shared session key (known only to the two of you). All subsequent communication is encrypted with that key. This is why it is relatively safe to log into your online banking or type passwords on public Wi‑Fi – the data is encrypted, so even if someone intercepts it, they cannot decrypt it. 17.1.3 HTTPS: HTTP + TLS HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the protocol browsers and servers use to transmit web page content. However, HTTP transmits everything in plain text, meaning anyone can eavesdrop. HTTPS is HTTP with TLS encryption. How to tell if a website uses HTTPS: There is a small padlock icon next to the address bar. Click on it to see the certificate information. 17.2 Password Management 17.2.1 Why You Need a Password Manager Most people use the same password for every website. If just one of those websites has a database breach (which happens often), hackers will try that password on your email, WeChat, Alipay – a technique called credential stuffing. A password manager helps you: Generate a strong, random password for each website (e.g., ) Automatically fill in login forms (no need to remember or type) Sync your passwords across your phone and computer 17.2.2 Firefox Built‑in Password Manager If you use Firefox, its built‑in password manager is sufficient for many people. Enable sync: Register for a Firefox account, then turn on sync in the settings – your passwords, bookmarks, and history will be synced (encrypted) to your other devices (phone, another computer). View / manage passwords: Settings → Privacy & Security → Saved Logins. Here you can view, delete, or export your passwords. Master Password: It is strongly recommended to set a Master Password. By default, Firefox saves your passwords encrypted, but if you are logged into Windows, anyone who opens Firefox can see all your saved passwords. Setting a Master Password means you will need to enter it once per session when opening Firefox or viewing passwords. Path: Settings → Privacy & Security → Use a Master Password. Downside: The Firefox password manager only works inside the Firefox browser. If you use other browsers or mobile apps, it cannot help you. 17.2.3 Cross‑Platform Password Managers If you need something that works across browsers and apps, consider these: Bitwarden: Open source, free (premium is $10 per year). Supports Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and has browser extensions for everything. You can also self‑host (not recommended for beginners). This is currently the safest choice for individual users. KeePass: Local storage only – the database file stays on your own machine. Very powerful, but the interface looks dated. You need to sync the database file manually (e.g., using cloud storage). 1Password: Paid. You can read this blog post – it is very well written. 17.2.4 Things You Must Never Do ❌ Write your passwords on a sticky note and attach it to your monitor. ❌ Send password screenshots over WeChat or QQ. ❌ Use "remember password" in your browser without also setting a Master Password (anyone who sits down at your computer can see them). ❌ Use the same password for every website. 17.3 Two‑Factor Authentication (2FA) 17.3.1 What Is 2FA? 2FA (Two‑Factor Authentication) adds an extra layer of protection on top of your password. When you log in, besides entering your password, you also need to enter a dynamically generated 6‑digit verification code (usually changing every 30 seconds). Even if someone steals your password, they cannot log in without that code. The most common form of 2FA is TOTP (Time‑based One‑Time Password) . The principle is: you and the server share a secret key, and you both generate a 6‑digit number based on the current time. Because time does not lie, both sides calculate the same number. 17.3.2 Microsoft Authenticator Microsoft Authenticator is one of the better 2FA tools. It is free on mobile phones and supports cloud backup (requires a Microsoft account). Important: You must remove 2FA associations before switching phones This is a big trap many people fall into when they change phones. Suppose you have used Microsoft Authenticator to set up 2FA for several accounts – Google, GitHub, Steam, your university email. You buy a new iPhone and use Apple's "quick transfer" to migrate your data. After the migration, Microsoft Authenticator is copied over, but the 2FA secrets are not migrated. TOTP secrets are stored in a special way that a simple "copy app data" does not include them. To make matters worse, if your accounts are cross‑dependent – for example, you need a GitHub code to log into Google, and a Google code to log into GitHub – after switching phones you cannot log into either, creating a loop. The correct procedure: Before switching phones, log into every website that has 2FA enabled. Go to the account security settings and turn off 2FA (or "remove this device"). Confirm that all accounts have been disassociated, then set up your new phone. On the new phone, reinstall Microsoft Authenticator. Re‑enable 2FA for each account one by one (scan the QR code or manually enter the secret key). What if you have already switched phones? : Most websites provide recovery codes – when you first enabled 2FA, the site gave you a set of codes or words to write down or print. Use one of those recovery codes to log in, then re‑bind the 2FA. If you have lost the recovery codes as well, you must contact the website's customer support, prove your identity (ID card, photo holding your ID, etc.), and wait for them to remove 2FA for you. This process can take days or even weeks. Therefore, whenever you enable 2FA on any account, store the recovery codes safely (print them out, or save them somewhere other than that phone). 17.3.3 Which Accounts Are Worth Enabling 2FA On? Email: Your Gmail, Outlook, school email – because many sites send password reset links to your email. If your email is compromised, all your other accounts are at risk. Apple ID / Google account / Microsoft account: These are the keys to your phone. Steam: Your game library has real value, and recovering a stolen Steam account is a pain. GitHub: If you are a computer science student, your code repositories could be deleted or malicious code could be inserted – the consequences are severe. Password manager: Bitwarden, 1Password, etc. – if they support 2FA, enable it. Not recommended: Small forum accounts that you almost never log into and would not care about if lost. 17.3.4 Backup Options for 2FA Aside from Microsoft Authenticator, here are a few other choices: 2FAS: Open source, supports iOS/Android, has cloud backup (via iCloud/Google Drive), clean interface. Recommended. Aegis (Android only): Open source, supports backup to a local file (encrypted and then stored in cloud storage), very powerful. 17.4 Some Easily Overlooked Privacy Habits 17.4.1 Do Not Let Your Browser Save Credit Card Information Chrome/Edge will ask if you want to save your credit card information for auto‑fill later. It is convenient, but if someone opens your browser (or if your computer is remotely controlled), they can see your full card number, expiration date, and even the CVV (in some versions). Suggestion: Do not save it. Typing 16 digits yourself is not that slow. 17.4.2 Public Wi‑Fi Public Wi‑Fi in coffee shops, airports, and hotels can be malicious hotspots (someone sets up a fake hotspot named "Starbucks Wi-Fi"). Once you connect, they can capture your HTTP traffic. Protection measures: Avoid typing passwords on public Wi‑Fi whenever possible. If you must use it, try to visit only HTTPS websites (the padlock icon will be green). The safest approach is to use your phone's hotspot or connect through your own proxy/VPN. 17.4.3 Screen Lock Many people do not set a screen lock on their computer (in Windows, press to lock). In a dormitory, lab, or library, you walk away for a minute to get water, and someone else can sit down at your computer and read your WeChat, email, or thesis draft. Suggestions: Windows: Settings → Accounts → Sign‑in options → add a PIN or password. Develop the habit: when you step away, press . Extended Reading The following sections cover HTTPS certificates, TLS handshake details, and some fundamental cryptographic concepts. They are more advanced. Come back when you need them. Extended 1: Digital Certificates and Certificate Authorities The certificates used in HTTPS are issued by a CA (Certificate Authority) . Your operating system and browser come with a built‑in set of trusted CA root certificates (e.g., DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, GlobalSign). When you visit , the server presents a certificate. The browser checks whether the certificate was issued by a trusted CA, whether the domain name on the certificate matches the domain you are visiting, and whether the certificate has expired. Only if all checks pass will the browser establish a TLS connection. This also explains why "downloading a root certificate from an unknown source" is dangerous – once you install a malicious CA certificate, an attacker can forge valid certificates for any website, and your browser will show it as "secure". Extended 2: TLS 1.2 vs. TLS 1.3 TLS 1.3 is faster by one round trip (RTT). TLS 1.2 requires two handshakes (about 2 RTT) before it can start transmitting data. TLS 1.3 streamlines the handshake (1 RTT, and even 0 RTT for session resumption). It is also more secure – it removes outdated cryptographic algorithms (such as RSA key exchange and CBC mode) and requires Forward Secrecy for key exchange. Most mainstream browsers and servers now support TLS 1.3. Extended 3: How Password Managers Encrypt Data The password database stored by a password manager is encrypted (typically using AES‑256). The decryption key is derived from your master password. The master password is never stored on any server – services like Bitwarden and 1Password use a zero‑knowledge architecture: the server stores only the encrypted data blob; without your master password, even they cannot decrypt your vault. This is also why "forgetting your master password" is usually unrecoverable – there is no "forgot password" button. Extended 4: Time Synchronisation Issues with TOTP TOTP relies on your device having an accurate clock. If your phone's time is off by more than 30 seconds from the standard time, the generated codes will be invalid. Enabling "auto‑set time" on your phone usually avoids this problem. If you find your codes are consistently rejected, go to your device settings and calibrate the time. Offline devices (e.g., hardware tokens) also have internal battery‑powered clocks that drift over the years and may need to be resynchronised. Extended 5: Storing Recovery Codes The recovery codes (usually 8‑10 words or a string of numbers) that a website gives you when you enable 2FA are lifesavers. Storage recommendations: Print them out and keep them in your wallet (not recommended to store them on your computer desktop). Store them in your password manager (Bitwarden allows notes for 2FA recovery codes). Store them in an encrypted notes app (e.g., Standard Notes, Joplin). Do not store them in your phone's photo gallery (if your phone is lost, everything is lost). Extended 6: Phishing Sites and the HTTPS Misconception HTTPS ≠ the website is trustworthy. Phishing sites can also obtain a free Let's Encrypt certificate and show a padlock icon in the address bar. Seeing a padlock only tells you that "communication with this website is encrypted", not that "this website is legitimate". How to tell: check the domain name spelling – is it or ? Make sure it is exactly the same domain you always use.

title: SSHandNATTraversal
content: Appendix 18: SSH and NAT Traversal (Intranet Penetration) This appendix explains what SSH is, how to use it, and how to access your computer from outside when it does not have a public IP address (often called "intranet penetration" or "NAT traversal"). It does not go deep into theory. The main goal is to prevent you from being completely lost when you need to connect to your university's computing lab to run simulations. 18.1 What Is SSH? SSH (Secure Shell) is an encrypted network protocol used to securely log into another computer remotely. Why SSH is needed: In the past, people used telnet for remote login. However, telnet sends all data (including passwords) in plain text. Anyone who can capture network traffic in the middle can steal your password. SSH encrypts the entire communication – anyone in the middle sees only gibberish. What SSH can do: Log into a remote server (replacing telnet) Securely transfer files (SFTP, SCP) Forward tunnels (push traffic from other, less secure protocols through an encrypted SSH channel) Run remote commands ( ) When you might use SSH at university: Connecting to your department's Linux server to do assignments or run experiments Connecting to a university computing cluster (supercomputing centre) Connecting to a Raspberry Pi, NAS, or other device on your lab network Connecting from your dormitory to a lab computer (often combined with NAT traversal) 18.2 How SSH Differs from Other Protocols | Protocol | Encryption | Typical use | |----------|------------|--------------| | Telnet | Plain text | Old‑style remote login (no longer recommended) | | SSH | Encrypted | Remote command line, file transfer | | RDP | Encrypted | Windows Remote Desktop (graphical interface) | | VNC | Optional | Remote desktop – not encrypted by default | | VPN | Encrypted | Whole network traffic goes through a tunnel | | HTTP | Plain text | Websites | | HTTPS | Encrypted | Websites (encrypted version) | Quick summary: For command‑line remote access, use SSH. For a graphical Windows desktop, use RDP. To tunnel all network traffic from your whole computer, use a VPN. 18.3 Windows Built‑in OpenSSH Windows 10 and 11 come with an OpenSSH client built in. You do not need to install third‑party software like PuTTY. Check if it is installed: Settings → System → Optional features → search for "OpenSSH Client". If it is not there, click "Add a feature". Basic usage (in CMD, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal): The first time you connect, you will be prompted to confirm the server's fingerprint (its public key). Type and press Enter – after that, you will not be asked again. Common parameters: to specify a port (default is 22) to specify a private key file (used for passwordless login) To exit an SSH session: Type or press . 18.4 Passwordless Login (SSH Keys) Typing a password every time is annoying, and automation scripts cannot easily handle interactive password entry. You can set up passwordless login. Generate a key pair on your local computer: Press Enter all the way through (it is a good idea to set a password to protect your private key). This creates two files in the directory: : your private key (never share this) : your public key (this goes on the server) Upload the public key to the server: After entering your password once, subsequent connections will not require a password. Why ed25519? It is faster, more secure, and uses shorter keys than RSA. Some older systems may not recognise it – in that case, use . 18.5 Aliases and the SSH Config File If you connect to several servers, typing every time is tedious. You can set up aliases in . Example content: After that, you only need to type to connect. 18.6 NAT Traversal (Intranet Penetration): What If You Have No Public IP? Most home broadband connections do not have a public IPv4 address. University lab and dormitory networks are typically the same – your computer does not have a standalone public IP, so people from outside cannot connect directly to you. What is NAT traversal? NAT traversal (often called "intranet penetration") refers to techniques that allow external networks to access devices on an internal network. The principle is that your computer actively connects to a server that does have a public IP (a relay). Outside users then reach your computer through that relay server. University scenarios: You are in your dorm and want to connect back to your dorm computer from outside (home, the lab, your internship company) to retrieve files. You are in the lab and want to connect from your dorm to the lab server to run code. You have created a simple webpage and want to temporarily show it to classmates, but you do not want to buy a server. FRP is currently the most popular self‑hosted tunnelling tool. It is open source, free, written in Go, and supports TCP, UDP, HTTP, and HTTPS. However, you need your own server with a public IP (a VPS) to run the FRP server component. If you do not want to buy your own server, you can use public services. Two recommendations: Openfrp: Has a free tier (speed‑limited to 12 Mbps, 2 tunnels). Supports TCP/UDP/TLS/HTTPS. Suitable for game hosting, remote desktop, temporary website testing. cpolar: Feature‑rich and well‑suited for many scenarios. Supports HTTP/HTTPS/TCP. The free tier provides a domain name that changes daily – good for temporary debugging. Other public services (Ngrok, Natapp, SAKURA FRP, etc.) are also available – they work out of the box without requiring your own server. Note: Most domestic public services require real‑name verification. This is a compliance requirement. 18.7 University Lab SSH Jump Servers Many university labs or supercomputing centres do not allow direct public SSH logins. Instead, you must first log into a jump server (bastion host) , and from there log into the internal lab server. Typical workflow: (jump server) On the jump server, (internal lab server) If you find two steps annoying, you can configure in your : After that, typing logs you directly into the lab server in one step. 18.8 Summary | Scenario | Recommended solution | |----------|----------------------| | Remote server management | SSH key‑based passwordless login + config aliases | | Access between computers on the same local network | Direct SSH using the internal IP address | | Access a device without a public IP from outside | Openfrp / cpolar / self‑hosted FRP | | Windows Remote Desktop (graphical) | Forward RDP through an SSH tunnel, or directly forward port 3389 using a NAT traversal tool | | University jump server | Use in your SSH config | SSH is capable of far more – port forwarding, proxy jumping, and other advanced features. However, for daily use, knowing , setting up passwordless login, and understanding how to do NAT traversal is already enough.

title: RemoteTransfer
content: Appendix 19: Remote File Transfer (Between Phone and Computer) This appendix introduces several ways to transfer files between a phone and a computer. No data cables, no hunting through confusing folder names in your phone's file manager. Pick the method that suits your needs. 19.1 Why Is Transferring Files So Annoying? Common methods for transferring files between a phone and a computer each have their own frustrations: WeChat / QQ: Compresses images, blocks large files, and you must be logged into the same account on both devices. USB cable: You have to find the cable, plug it in, select the right mode on the phone, and then dig through a bunch of folders with cryptic names. Bluetooth: Slow and prone to disconnecting. Cloud storage: You upload first, then download – a long detour, often with speed limits. There are better ways. The methods below are ordered by how strongly they are recommended. 19.2 Snapdrop: The Most Hassle‑Free Option Snapdrop is a web‑based local network file transfer tool. No software installation required, no login needed. As long as your phone and computer are on the same Wi‑Fi network, you can transfer files by opening a browser. How to use: Connect both your phone and computer to the same Wi‑Fi network. On both devices, open a browser and go to . The page automatically discovers other devices on the same network, showing them as circular icons. Tap the icon of the target device, select a file, and on the receiving device click "Save" to accept. Advantages: Nothing to install – just open a webpage. Files do not pass through any server; they are transferred directly between devices (peer‑to‑peer), so it is secure. Works on any device (Safari on iPhone, Chrome on Android, Edge on Windows – all fine). Disadvantages: Both devices must be on the same Wi‑Fi network (cannot work across different networks). Very large files may be slow – it is best for files under 100 MB. In one sentence: For quickly transferring a few photos or a small document, Snapdrop is the fastest. 19.3 KDE Connect: The Most Feature‑Rich Option KDE Connect is an open‑source, all‑purpose cross‑device communication tool. Originally developed for the KDE desktop environment on Linux, it now supports Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS. What it can do besides file transfer: Share clipboard between phone and computer (copy on your phone, paste on your computer with Ctrl+V). Sync phone notifications to your computer (read WeChat messages on your PC without picking up your phone). Use your phone as a remote control for your computer (control music playback, flip through PowerPoint slides). Find your phone (make it ring). Bidirectional file transfer. Installation: Windows: Search the Microsoft Store for "KDE Connect". Android: Search Google Play or F‑Droid for "KDE Connect". iOS: Search the App Store for "KDE Connect". No login required on the computer side. As long as the phone and computer are on the same Wi‑Fi, they can pair. Pairing steps: Connect both devices to the same Wi‑Fi network. Open KDE Connect on both devices. The phone should automatically discover the computer. Tap "Pair" and confirm on the computer. In one sentence: If you frequently switch between working on your phone and your computer, installing KDE Connect will make your life much smoother. 19.4 Shared Folder (SMB) Snapdrop and KDE Connect both require action on both ends (one sends, one receives). If you simply want to "browse files on my computer from my phone at any time", the best approach is to set up a shared folder on your computer and mount it as a network drive on your phone. Setting up on the computer (Windows) : Right‑click the folder you want to share → Properties → Sharing → Advanced Sharing. Check "Share this folder". In the permissions, add or and give "Read" permission. Note down your computer's local IP address: press , type , then type . Look for the "IPv4 Address" (e.g., ). Accessing from your phone: Android: Recommended app: CX File Explorer (from Google Play or the official website). Open CX File Explorer → Network → Remote Storage → SMB. Enter your computer's IP address (e.g., ) and your Windows username/password if required. Once connected, you can browse files on your computer just like local files. iOS: The built‑in "Files" app is sufficient. Open the "Files" app → tap the (three dots) at the top‑right → Connect to Server. Enter (note the prefix). Enter your Windows username and password (the same credentials you use to log into Windows). After connecting, the shared folder appears under "Shared". Advantages: Set it up once, and it is always available. You can directly watch videos or open documents from your computer on your phone – no need to download them first. Multiple devices can access the same shared folder simultaneously. Disadvantages: Only works on the local network (you cannot use it when away from your Wi‑Fi). 19.5 Temporary HTTP / FTP File Server If you only occasionally need to download files from your computer to your phone (and never upload), you can start a temporary HTTP or FTP server on your computer. Your phone can then access it through a browser. Quick HTTP server on Windows (no extra software) : Open the folder you want to share. In the address bar, type and press Enter. In the command prompt, type (requires Python to be installed). On your phone, open a browser and go to . You will see a file listing; tap any file to download it. Using FTP (better if you need to upload as well): Download a small FTP server application (e.g., Quick'n Easy FTP Server). It takes about 5 minutes to set up. On your phone, connect using CX File Explorer or a browser ( ). 19.6 Summary Simple choice: For a one‑off file transfer → use Snapdrop. If you want to deeply integrate your phone and computer → use KDE Connect. If you want to always have access to all files on your computer from your phone → set up a shared folder + CX File Explorer (Android) or the Files app (iOS). All of the methods above stay within your local network (same Wi‑Fi). They do not consume mobile data and do not raise privacy concerns. Once you leave your home or dorm, they will no longer work – but that is a NAT traversal problem, covered in Appendix 18.

title: LaptopBasics
content: Appendix 1: Laptop Basics This chapter covers only the most essential concepts and operations. If you have never used a computer before, start here. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section at the end. 1.1 Hardware Basics 1.1.1 What is a CPU The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the computing and control core of a computer. It interprets instructions, processes data, and coordinates all components. Think of it as the "brain" of the machine. 1.1.2 What is a GPU The GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) specializes in graphics and parallel computing. Laptop GPUs come in two forms: Integrated GPU (iGPU): packaged inside the same chip as the CPU, has no dedicated video memory – it borrows a portion of system RAM. Discrete GPU (dGPU): a separate chip with its own video memory. 1.1.3 What is RAM (Memory) RAM is the temporary warehouse where the CPU reads and writes data directly. It is fast, but loses all data when power is cut. When you open a program, the system copies its data from the storage drive to RAM. 1.1.4 What is a Storage Drive The storage drive holds data permanently – data survives after shutdown. Modern laptops almost exclusively use Solid‑State Drives (SSDs). 1.1.5 The Difference Between RAM and Storage Use a kitchen counter and a fridge as a metaphor: RAM is the countertop: the ingredients you are actively chopping and preparing are right in front of you for quick access. Counter space is limited, and when you finish cooking (power is cut), any leftover ingredients on the counter are thrown away. Storage is the refrigerator: all ingredients are kept there for the long term, and you take them out to the counter when needed. 1.2 Integrated vs. Discrete GPU (Basic Concepts) iGPU: low power, low heat – suitable for office work, web browsing, and light gaming. dGPU: high performance – suitable for demanding games, 3D modelling, video editing, etc. Real‑world gaming performance of iGPUs is limited by thermal and power constraints; see Extended Reading. 1.3 Touchpads (What You Need to Know) High‑end thin‑and‑light laptops in 2026 use mostly two types of touchpads: Haptic touchpad: cannot be pressed when the device is off. When powered, it detects pressure via sensors and provides vibration feedback through a haptic motor. The feel depends entirely on the manufacturer's tuning. Full‑area mechanical touchpad: the entire surface clicks down (unlike traditional touchpads where only the bottom half moves). However, on many Windows laptops, the required force differs between the top and bottom areas. Strongly recommended: go to an Apple store and try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark for haptic feedback) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (the benchmark for that type). Get a feel for their uniform, responsive clicks. Then come back and try Windows counterparts – you will immediately know what level of quality you can accept. 1.4 Laptop Classifications Thin and light: portable, long battery life, quiet. Uses low‑power CPU, no discrete GPU. Thickness around 15mm, weight under 1.3kg. Suitable for office work, study, light entertainment. Gaming laptop: high performance, with a high‑power CPU and mid‑range to high‑end discrete GPU. Heavy cooling, weight often exceeds 2kg. Suitable for demanding games, professional video editing, etc. All‑rounder / creator laptop: sits between the two – somewhat portable (around 1.8kg), with an entry‑level or mid‑range discrete GPU. Can handle office work and light gaming. 1.5 Buying Reference: 笔吧评测室 笔吧评测室 is one of the more authoritative laptop review sources in China. Follow their WeChat public account or Bilibili channel (also on Douyin and Xiaohongshu). Their WeChat account publishes weekly curated recommendations by price range, with detailed explanations. Read those to narrow down a few candidate models, then search for in‑depth reviews and user feedback. 1.6 Purchase Advice (2026) Prices are high: laptop prices are at historical highs in 2026. If you are not in urgent need (e.g., your current computer still works), you can wait – prices will likely drop. If you must buy: thin‑and‑light laptops offer better value in the current market. The iGPU performance of modern high‑end thin‑and‑light laptops is sufficient for many games and daily software. Government subsidies: many provinces offer 10‑20% consumer subsidies. If possible, consider travelling to a province with such subsidies to buy your laptop. Search for "province name + appliance subsidy" for details. 1.7 From Unboxing to Activation: Inspection Procedure (Core Steps) When you receive your laptop, follow these steps. Before activation, you have unconditional return rights. If you find any problem, return it immediately – do not attempt to fix it yourself. Check the packaging and exterior Confirm that the seals are intact. Inspect the lid (A‑cover) and bottom (D‑cover) for scratches or dents. Check the power adapter and charging port for signs of use. Gently open and close the lid a few times; listen for creaking. For a mechanical (traditional hinged) touchpad: gently wiggle the edges to see if it rocks, and press all four corners to feel for consistent resistance. For a haptic touchpad: test the feedback in different areas after booting into the OS. Lightly press different areas of the keyboard to feel for overall rigidity. If you find any anomaly that you couldn't accept, take photos at once and contact customer service for a return. Transport mode test Do not plug in the power adapter. Press the power button once. If it does not turn on → normal, proceed. If it turns on and boots into the OS immediately → the unit has been used. Return it immediately. First boot setup (skip internet) When you reach the login screen, do not connect to Wi‑Fi. To bypass Windows 11's forced internet requirement: At the region selection screen, press to open Command Prompt. Type and press Enter. The system will restart. After reboot, when you reach the "Let's connect you to a network" screen, click "I don't have internet" → "Continue with limited setup". Log in with a local account (use an English alphanumeric username). Screen inspection After entering the desktop, right‑click → Personalize → Background → Choose a solid color. Cycle through pure white, pure black, pure red, pure green, and pure blue. Carefully look for dead pixels (unexpected bright or dark dots). On a pure black background, check for backlight bleed. Minor IPS glow at the edges is normal, but if a corner glows like a small flashlight, consider a return. Verify the configuration Press Win + X → Task Manager → Performance to confirm CPU model and RAM capacity. Download a drive inspection tool (e.g., CrystalDiskInfo) to check the SSD's brand and model against reviews. CrystalDiskInfo's Offical Download Site: Or you may download with Usability test Lift the laptop with one hand – any unusual creaking? Plug in a USB drive and a mouse; confirm all ports work. After fully charging, use it on battery for an hour of light use to rule out abnormal battery drain. 7‑day no‑questions‑asked return If you find any of the following: dead pixels (especially in the centre), backlight bleed affecting normal viewing, abnormal touchpad click feel, unusual battery wear, or widespread reports of a defect in this batch – directly request a return (not an exchange) and either reorder or switch to another brand. Create a Microsoft account and activate Go to signup.live.com and create a free account. Log in to activate the pre‑installed Office suite (within 30 days, otherwise the license may expire). With an account, you can digitally reactivate Windows after a clean reinstall without entering a product key. Finally, connect to the internet After all checks are complete, connect to Wi‑Fi. Windows and Office will activate automatically. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: CPU Models and Performance Mainstream thin‑and‑light laptops in 2026 use CPUs such as the Intel Core Ultra 5 338H、Ultra X7 358H、Ultra X9 388H. Mainstream gaming laptops often pair an Intel Ultra 7 356H with an NVIDIA RTX 5060 or 5070. Laptop CPU naming can be confusing – the same architecture may spawn multiple model numbers. For example, AMD's 8845H is essentially a rebranded 7845H (identical specifications, only the name differs). Always search for performance reviews of the exact model before buying; do not judge by the numbers alone. Extended 2: iGPU Gaming – Expectations vs. Reality Some marketing claims "iGPU performance close to an RTX 3050 Ti". However, note that an iGPU has no dedicated video memory – it borrows system RAM – and the CPU and iGPU share the same thermal solution. Under sustained gaming loads, the CPU and iGPU compete for power and thermal headroom, so real‑world performance often falls short of benchmark numbers. If you plan to play AAA games on an iGPU laptop, watch game‑specific tests by reviewers like 笔吧评测室 before deciding. Extended 3: Sleep States (S0ix vs. S3) Windows defines several power sleep states. S3, known as "Suspend to RAM", powers down the CPU and most hardware while keeping RAM refreshed – wake‑up is very fast (about 1‑2 seconds). S0ix (Modern Standby, also called S2idle) is a low‑power idle state promoted by Microsoft since Windows 8, allowing the system to stay connected and update while the screen is off – similar to a smartphone. However, it can cause heat, battery drain, and unreliable wake‑up. Since Intel Meteor Lake (12th‑gen Core), Microsoft has required hardware vendors to drop full support for S3. Consequently, many new laptops support only S0ix. Even running Linux, the ACPI tables are stripped of S3 code, making reliable sleep impossible. If sleep reliability matters to you, check community feedback before buying – some business laptops (e.g., certain ThinkPad models) still retain S3 options. Extended 4: Touchpad Tuning Differences Even among haptic touchpads, the vibration feedback varies greatly by manufacturer – for example, Xiaomi and Honor feel completely different. Therefore, it is worth visiting a physical store to try them yourself. If you are unsure what you like, first try the MacBook Pro's haptic touchpad (the industry benchmark) and the MacBook Neo's full‑area mechanical touchpad (also a benchmark). Then compare with Windows laptops – you will clearly see what level of quality you can accept. Extended 5: Storage Drive Selection NAND Manufacturers vs. Assembly Houses The core of an SSD is the NAND flash chip. Companies that manufacture their own NAND are called NAND manufacturers or IDMs. Major active NAND manufacturers include Samsung, SK hynix (including the acquired Intel NAND business, now Solidigm), Micron, Kioxia, Western Digital, and China's YMTC. YMTC's Xtacking architecture (e.g., X4‑9040) is competitive in both performance and cost. The controller is the "small CPU" of an SSD, handling data management, wear leveling, garbage collection, etc. Notable retail controller vendors include Silicon Motion, Phison, Maxio, and InnoGrit. TLC vs. QLC TLC (Triple‑Level Cell): stores 3 bits per cell – good write endurance and speed. QLC (Quad‑Level Cell): stores 4 bits per cell – higher density, lower cost, but significantly worse write endurance and write speed. For a system drive or frequent large writes, QLC is generally not recommended. The Solidigm P41 Plus is a rare exception – its excellent firmware mitigates QLC's drawbacks. Original vs. Third‑party SSDs Original SSD: designed, packaged, and sold by the NAND manufacturer itself – e.g., Samsung, Western Digital, Kioxia, ZhiTai. Third‑party SSD: buys raw NAND wafers and then packages, tests, and assembles them – e.g., Kingston, ADATA. Quality depends on the vendor's packaging capability. Vendors with their own packaging and rigorous testing (e.g., UMIS's UnionMemory brand) are acceptable. Avoid any brand that only does sticker assembly – their NAND sources are unknown, and the drive may fail at any moment. OEM vs. Retail Drives OEM and retail drives are identical hardware. Retail drives come with official warranty and driver support; OEM drives are warrantied through the channel vendor at a lower price. OEM drives are typically sourced through secondary channels – always verify the seller's warranty terms before purchase. Personal Recommendations (for reference only) My first recommendation is original SSDs, e.g., ZhiTai TiPro 9000. Among OEM drives, the following three are worth considering: PVC10 (SK hynix) PCB01 (SK hynix) AM6C1 (UnionMemory, under UMIS) Avoid Samsung PM9A1 and any model known for "0e" errors (uncorrectable data corruption leading to permanent data loss). Also avoid any white‑label, gray‑label, or no‑name SSDs. Your storage drive holds all your important data – essays, photos, code, game saves. A low‑quality drive may die suddenly, and data recovery is expensive and not guaranteed. Saving a few dollars is not worth that risk. Considerations for Adding an SSD to a Laptop Before adding an SSD to your laptop, check the following: Empty M.2 slot: search for motherboard photos or disassembly videos of your model. The second slot on some laptops may only support short drives (2242 or 2230); installing a 2280 drive may not fit. M.2 form factors: common lengths are 2230 (30mm), 2242 (42mm), and 2280 (80mm). 2280 is the most common. For 2242, the PVC10 and PC411 are worthwhile choices. Power consumption and drop‑out risk: laptops have far less power delivery and cooling than desktops. Verify the drive's sustained power consumption – a high‑power drive can overheat and disconnect in a thin‑and‑light. Recommended reviewers: Bilibili creators "前进的四火" and "HOMOLAB" produce high‑quality SSD reviews – they use professional tools like fio for steady‑state testing, not just peak speeds. Current timing: SSD prices are high in 2026 – if not urgent, wait for prices to drop. Extended 6: Display Selection Display preference is subjective – I strongly recommend visiting a physical store to compare different panels with your own eyes. Personal preference Some users prefer high‑quality LCD panels (especially IPS or MiniLED backlit) because LCD has no OLED burn‑in risk, higher full‑screen brightness, and sharper text. Resolution vs. Refresh Rate Compared to high refresh rates (e.g., 120Hz), high resolution (e.g., 2560×1600 or 3840×2160) delivers crisper text and images, significantly improving productivity for office work, coding, and reading. 60Hz is sufficient for non‑competitive gaming. When budget is limited, prioritising resolution is a reasonable choice. Color Accuracy and Gamut Coverage Color accuracy (measured by Delta E) and gamut coverage are equally important. Color accuracy affects your judgement of colours – for example, you take a photo with your phone, edit it in Lightroom on your laptop; if the display is inaccurate, the colours you adjust may look completely wrong to others. Even for casual photo editing or watching movies, you want colours to be reasonably true. Gamut coverage determines how many colours the display can show – common standards include sRGB, DCI‑P3, etc. For most users, covering 100% sRGB is the baseline. Factory Calibration and Calibrators Modern thin‑and‑light laptops generally have decent out‑of‑box colour accuracy, but do not blindly trust "factory calibrated" claims. Factory calibration is often done on a few samples, and the reported Delta E is measured under specific brightness and mode – it does not guarantee your unit is the same. If you truly demand high colour accuracy (note: if you do not know what "colour accuracy" means, you probably do not need it for the foreseeable future), the most reliable method is to rent a colorimeter (e.g., Spyder or Calibrite) and calibrate your screen following a tutorial. Generate and load an ICC profile. Calibrate once a year. Extended 7: Buying Principles for Gaming and All‑rounder Laptops For gaming laptops, a common core principle is: given acceptable performance release and a decent display, choose the cheapest one. Different brands with the same CPU/GPU can have vastly different sustained power limits (i.e., performance release). Check real cooling and stress tests from reviewers like 笔吧评测室. Only after confirming that performance release is not crippled should you compare prices. For all‑rounder laptops, trying them in person is recommended – chassis thickness, cooling, and fan noise vary greatly between models.

title: Conclusion
content: Appendix 20: Conclusion The practical parts are mostly finished. The main book will cover lower‑level topics and code, and later appendices will include some personal sharing, placed in a separate folder. A Closing Poem I remember the first time I opened this machine. The keys were a field of unknown furrows. The screen, a blank ocean. My finger hovered — afraid that one wrong touch would send me wandering forever. Then someone told me a simple thing: Nothing inside is a tiger. No protocol is a net you cannot untie. No script is a spell — only a language waiting to be read. Press on. You'll find your way. So I did. I learned to carve my own folders from the wild disk, to name each branch so I could find it again. When the screen spat out gibberish, I learned it was just a missing map. When an error flashed red, I learned to ask the logs — and they answered, quietly, like old walls giving up a hidden door. I walked into the network. Seven layers of invisible silk. NAT, firewall, proxy — each a gate, not a wall. I learned to set my own path across the ocean, to let my packets choose their own currents. Clash in the background, a quiet compass. I learned how light becomes numbers. H.264, AV1, containers, codecs. OBS to catch the passing sky. FFmpeg in my palm — a knife that cuts any shape. And then I found the great invisible city — open source. Millions of hands passing fire. No one asks your name. They only ask: can you carry this forward? I learned the licenses, the forks that return to the same river. I found the mirrors where every stream gathers, so a student anywhere can drink. I learned Markdown — to write without heavy armour. Git — to track every heartbeat of my work, from one machine to every corner of the earth. SSH — a whisper that crosses mountains and opens a window on a distant desktop. And tunnelling — to slip through the back ways and sit down at the great table inside. Now I understand. When I first entered this box, I was standing in a dark room. Now I carry my own candle. What I feared, I use. What confused me has become my daily bread. I am not wiser than others. I only put one foot down, then another. And I am not alone — there is something else now, a quiet companion I can ask: AI, show me the way. Alas! So here is my short creed: I will build a house of gold for my data. I will walk through every cloud without a map. I will bend light and shadow until they please my eye. I will carve time itself into small, saved moments. This is not paradise. It is work. It is not a shortcut. It is long, and sometimes hard. But I have already begun. I will not look back — except to see you. Beyond this field, I see a new sun. And when you step onto the same path, I will already be there, hand outstretched. — A fellow traveller, who once stood where you stand, and now walks ahead — but never so far that I cannot turn back, take your hand, and say: you can do this too.

title: SystemTuningANDAntimalware
content: Appendix 2: System Tuning and Antimalware This chapter covers only the most essential maintenance principles and operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section that follows. 2.1 Core Principle: If You Don‘t Understand It, Don't Touch It The default configuration of Windows has been thoroughly tested and works well for the vast majority of use cases. Many online "optimisation" guides tell you to disable certain system services to free up memory, but this often breaks features you may need later (e.g., disabling the print spooler makes printers unusable), and you are unlikely to remember that you disabled it. The only safe rule: if you do not know exactly what a setting does, do not change it. Using your computer normally without blindly tweaking settings is the best optimisation. 2.2 Antimalware: The Built‑In One Is Good Enough Windows comes with Microsoft Defender Antimalware, which is more than sufficient for most personal users. Its signatures update frequently, it integrates deeply with the system, and it does not consume excessive resources. For the vast majority of people, no third‑party antimalware is needed. 2.3 Handling Third‑Party Security Software 2.3.1 Chinese Security Suites: Generally Not Needed Software such as 360, Tencent PC Manager, and Kingsoft Antivirus is usually not recommended. They often bring pop‑up ads, bundled promotions, consume background resources, and may even have security vulnerabilities of their own. 2.3.2 Pre‑installed McAfee: Recommended to Uninstall Many branded laptops (e.g., some Asus and Dell models) come with a pre‑installed McAfee trial, often including a two‑year license. Given that McAfee has had security vulnerabilities in the past and runs at the kernel driver level, issues can be serious. It is advisable to uninstall it. Search for "McAfee Consumer Product Removal tool" – run it to cleanly remove everything. 2.4 Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software: Keep Only the Control Centre Branded laptops come with various pre‑installed software. The only thing worth keeping is the hardware control centre, for example: Lenovo Vantage (Lenovo) Armoury Crate (Asus) Dell Power Manager (Dell) These tools let you adjust performance modes, fan speeds, battery charge thresholds, etc. All other pre‑installed software (e.g., AI assistants, music players, app store promotions, trial software) can be safely uninstalled. 2.5 Do Not Fill Up Your C: Drive (The Most Important Optimisation) Keep at least 20% free space on your C: drive (i.e., usage below 80%). If the C: drive runs out of space, your computer will become noticeably slow, because Windows uses the hard drive as temporary memory (swap). Once your C: drive gets close to full, immediately clean up unnecessary files or move your user folders (Documents, Downloads, Desktop, etc.) to another drive. Search online for "how to change the location of user folders in Windows" for instructions. 2.6 Good Habits Are the Best Security Measure Download software only from official websites or the Microsoft Store. Do not click random pop‑up ads, especially those claiming "Your computer is infected". Do not plug in unknown USB drives without caution. When installing any software, do not blindly click "Next" repeatedly. Slow down and check each step for options such as "install XX browser", "set as homepage", or "install to the C: drive" (you may prefer D:). Uncheck any options you do not need. Once you develop these habits, Microsoft Defender will handle the remaining security risks adequately. 2.7 First Steps After You First Boot into the System After connecting to the internet, go to Settings → Windows Update → "Check for updates". Install all available updates (may require several restarts). Go to Settings → Apps, and uninstall unnecessary pre‑installed software (including McAfee). Restart your PC. In the system tray, confirm that the Microsoft Defender shield icon is present and healthy. 2.8 Windows Update: Do Not Disable It Many old tutorials suggest "disabling Windows Update" because it consumes bandwidth or may restart your computer. That advice no longer applies today. Windows Update does far more than just fixing security holes. It also: Automatically updates many Microsoft applications, such as Office suites and runtimes. Updates hardware drivers (graphics, network, audio, etc.), preventing blue screens or performance issues caused by outdated drivers. Updates Windows Defender's virus definitions, keeping your computer protected against the latest threats. If you worry about sudden reboots interrupting your work, do this instead: Go to Settings → Windows Update → Advanced options → Active hours. Set the time period when you normally use your computer (e.g., 09:00 to 18:00). Windows will not automatically restart during those hours. Outside active hours, if a restart is required for an update, Windows will do it when idle, or you can manually choose a restart time. Not updating Windows does NOT make your system more stable. On the contrary, skipping updates for a long time accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities and driver bugs, which may lead to blue screens, sluggishness, or even malware attacks. Leave automatic updates on, configure active hours properly – that is the smarter approach. Extended Reading The following sections contain detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the must‑read part. Extended 1: Why You Should Not Mess with the Registry and Group Policy The Registry is Windows's configuration database, storing almost every setting for hardware, software, and users. Group Policy is a graphical interface for configuring the Registry in bulk. Incorrect modifications can render the system unbootable or break features permanently. For example, someone disabled the Print Spooler to "save memory", and months later could not print – it took them a long time to realise they had turned it off. If you do not know what these tools are, stay away from them entirely. Extended 2: Microsoft Defender vs. Common Chinese Security Suites Microsoft Defender has no ads, no pop‑ups, does not collect personal usage data, and uses few resources. By contrast, Chinese security suites (e.g., 360, Tencent PC Manager) offer extra gadgets (software updaters, network speed tests) but at the cost of frequent ad pop‑ups, bundled installs, and background data uploads. In major international security tests, Microsoft Defender consistently ranks in the top tier. For non‑high‑risk personal use, Defender is the safer choice. Extended 3: How to Uninstall McAfee Properly McAfee is recommended for removal not only because of past security vulnerabilities (e.g., remote code execution), but also because it is notoriously difficult to uninstall fully – normal "Add/Remove Programs" often leaves behind drivers and services. Use the official "McAfee Consumer Product Removal" from McAfee's website. Run it to automatically detect and clean everything. If your laptop is brand new and you haven't activated McAfee yet, uninstalling from Settings is cleaner and leaves fewer traces. Extended 4: Categorising Manufacturer Pre‑installed Software Must keep: Hardware control centre (performance modes, fans, battery thresholds). Without it, you may lose the ability to adjust screen brightness, keyboard backlight, or set charge limits. Safe to remove: "AI assistants", "PC manager", app store promotions, music/video trials, cloud storage promotions – most are third‑party customisations with mediocre experience and resource usage. Optional: Driver update utilities from the manufacturer (e.g., Lenovo Driver Manager). If you can download drivers from the official website yourself, you can remove these as well. Extended 5: Swap (Virtual Memory) Explained Operating systems use a mechanism called swap (or page file). When physical RAM is insufficient, the system moves some temporarily unused data from RAM to a file on the hard drive (pagefile.sys), freeing RAM for active programs. Even when physical RAM is abundant, Windows may pre‑swap some data to optimise memory layout. This page file resides on the C: drive by default. If the C: drive has very little free space, the page file cannot expand properly, or the free space is fragmented. The system then constantly reads and writes to the hard drive for swapping, making the computer extremely slow. This is why a full C: drive is disastrous. Extended 6: SLC Cache and Write Principles on SSDs Most consumer SSDs use TLC (3 bits per cell) or QLC (4 bits per cell) NAND. To boost write speed, the SSD internally reserves a portion as SLC cache (1 bit per cell, fast writing). When the amount of data written exceeds the cache size, the drive switches to TLC/QLC direct write mode, and speed drops dramatically. When SSD usage exceeds roughly 60%, the controller gradually reduces or even disables the SLC cache, forcing TLC direct write. Worse, the remaining free space is often not a single contiguous area – it is scattered with logical traces of deleted files. Writing new data then requires the SSD to read the existing block, modify it in memory, and write it back (read‑modify‑write). This further reduces performance and increases write amplification, shortening the drive's lifespan. Therefore, keeping your C: drive sufficiently free is not only for virtual memory but also to maintain the SSD's high‑speed writing capability. Extended 7: Malware‑Patch and Similar Tools Malware‑Patch is a small open‑source tool (project page: https://github.com/the1812/Malware-Patch). It does not actively scan for malware; instead, it uses UAC (User Account Control – the pop‑up that asks for permission when installing software) to intercept installation attempts by common unwanted software. When you double‑click on certain "family bucket" installers, it shows a warning. For beginners, this is a mild aid, but it is not essential. If you already have the habit of downloading software only from official sources, you do not need it. Extended 8: On "Make Your PC Fly" Optimisation Videos Many online videos claim that a few registry tweaks can dramatically boost performance. Most such "optimisations" are either placebo, trade stability for a tiny gain, or even disable important security mechanisms. The only real ways to keep a computer running smoothly are: Keep enough free space on your C: drive. Ensure proper cooling (clean dust, elevate the laptop). Do not install software that noticeably slows down the system (e.g., certain antimalware suites). For everything else, Windows manages memory and background processes on its own. Trust the default configuration and spend your time on real work and entertainment – that is the best optimisation. Extended 9: The Myth of "Disabling Windows Update" There was once a popular belief that disabling Windows Update improves performance and avoids forced restarts. This stemmed from the poor update experience and lack of restart control in early Windows versions (like Windows 7/8). Since Windows 10, Microsoft has significantly improved the update mechanism: Most updates download silently in the background, consuming little to no foreground resources. The "Active hours" feature gives users reasonable control. Driver updates are delivered through Windows Update, saving users the trouble of hunting for drivers themselves. In fact, many issues on long‑unupdated computers (random blue screens, inability to install new software, peripheral incompatibility, etc.) often disappear automatically after installing all Windows and driver updates. Therefore, keeping Windows Update enabled and checking it regularly is one of the simplest and most effective ways to maintain a healthy system.

title: FileManagement
content: Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker Turn Off BitLocker The very first thing you do after getting a new laptop: turn off BitLocker. BitLocker is Windows's full‑disk encryption feature. It encrypts your drive, and only a recovery key can unlock it. That sounds secure, but for individual users, the downsides heavily outweigh any benefit: You will almost never need it. BitLocker is designed for corporate or government scenarios where a lost device might leak sensitive data. The chance of losing your personal laptop is tiny, and your data is not that valuable to an attacker. If your system crashes, the motherboard fails, or you lose the recovery key, all your data is gone forever. Microsoft will not help you decrypt it. It slightly reduces drive performance, especially for small file reads and writes. Your data is priceless. I strongly suggest you turn BitLocker off to avoid the risk of permanent data loss. How to check and disable it: Open Settings → Privacy & security → Device encryption (or search for "BitLocker"). If it says "Off", you are fine. If it says "On", open PowerShell or Command Prompt as Administrator and run: Wait for decryption to complete. You can check progress with in the same terminal. Decryption may take from a few tens of minutes to hours. You can use your computer normally during this time, but keep it plugged in and powered on until done. Ignore anyone who tells you to "keep BitLocker". For you, turning it off is the smarter choice. Appendix 3: File Management and Storage Philosophy This chapter covers only the most essential file management and storage operations. More in‑depth discussions are in the "Extended Reading" section. 3.1 Partition Your Drive: Separate C: and D: New computers usually come with a single C: drive. Putting everything (system, documents, downloads) on C: means that if the system crashes and you need to reinstall Windows, all your data is lost. So it is wise to split the drive into two partitions. Example: Your laptop has a 1TB SSD. You can leave 300GB for C: and use the remaining ~650GB for D:. C: drive (system): Only Windows, drivers, and a few programs that must be on C: (e.g., certain development tools). Nothing else. D: drive (data): Your documents, photos, videos, downloaded installers, Steam library, project code, etc. Why do this? If Windows breaks and you have to reinstall, you only need to format C:. Everything on D: remains untouched. After reinstalling Steam, you can add the D: Steam library folder in settings – no need to redownload games. How to do it: Use the built‑in Disk Management (right‑click "This PC" → Manage → Disk Management). Right‑click C: and choose "Shrink Volume" to free up space, then create a new simple volume with the free space and assign it drive letter D:. If unsure, search for "how to partition laptop drive" on YouTube and follow a recent tutorial. 3.2 Organise Files with Numbered Prefixes Do not just pile folders directly on D:. It is much better to use a category + number scheme. For example: 01Work: Internships, part‑time jobs, student club documents. 02Study: Course materials, papers, eBooks. 03Media: Personal photos, music, movies. 04Downloads: Browser cache. Clean it once a week or month – move useful files to other folders, delete the rest. 05_Archive: Things you no longer use but cannot bear to delete (e.g., old versions of your graduation project). Why the number prefix? Windows sorts by character order. appears before , so your most important folders are always the first you see when you open D:. 3.3 Game Storage: Delete When Done, Keep Cloud Saves Games on Steam and Epic are now huge (50–100GB). You usually play only two or three at a time. Games you have finished and will never touch again just waste space. My approach: Keep only the games you are actively playing. When you finish a game (or know you will not touch it for a while), first make sure your cloud saves are synchronised (Steam does this by default), then uninstall it from Steam. When you want to replay it, just download it again. 3.4 Backup Strategy: The 3‑2‑1 Rule (Simplified) The 3‑2‑1 rule is a basic consensus in data protection: 3 copies of your data (original + two backups) 2 different storage media (e.g., internal SSD + external hard drive) 1 off‑site copy (e.g., cloud storage) For students, you can simplify: Original data: On your laptop D: drive. Local backup: Every two weeks or every month, copy your most important folders (documents, photos, code projects) to an external hard drive. Off‑site backup: Use a cloud service like Baidu Netdisk, OneDrive, or Aliyun Drive to sync a copy of your important files. Never use a no‑name USB flash drive as your only backup! Cheap drives can die after just a few uses. If you need a flash drive, buy a reputable brand (e.g., SanDisk CZ74). For more details on hard drive selection and backup, see the Extended Reading section. 3.5 Simple Cloud Storage Choices If possible, prefer international services: OneDrive (the 1TB that comes with Office 365), Google Drive, Dropbox. Their clients are stable and they treat privacy somewhat better. Chinese alternatives: Baidu Netdisk (speed limited but usable for incremental backup), Aliyun Drive (currently less throttling). Highly sensitive data (e.g., ID card scans, password backups): Never upload them directly to any cloud. Use an open‑source encryption tool like VeraCrypt or a password‑protected AES‑256 7‑Zip archive, then upload the encrypted file. 3.6 Keep Your Computer Clock Accurate: Change the NTP Server If your computer clock is often wrong (e.g., a few minutes slow after boot), it is because Windows's default time server is overseas and has high latency. Manual sync steps: Right‑click the clock on the taskbar → "Adjust date/time". Under "Synchronise your clock", click "Sync now". If it fails, click "Add clocks for different time zones" → switch to the "Internet Time" tab → "Change settings". In the "Server" box, enter one of these: (Tencent Cloud) (Alibaba Cloud) Click "Update now". Wait a few seconds for success. If you are a university student, search for "your university name + ntp server" to get an on‑campus server (e.g., Tsinghua has ), which has even lower latency. After this, your clock will automatically stay accurate. Extended Reading The following sections contain more detailed technical discussions and advanced knowledge. Each is independent – you can read any of them without relying on the main text. Extended 1: When BitLocker Actually Makes Sense (You Don't Need It) BitLocker is only useful for the very few people who need extremely high security – handling trade secrets, legally sensitive information. If that is not you, ignore it. Just turn it off. Extended 2: A Closer Look at Partitioning When using Disk Management to partition: The C: drive on a new computer has lots of free space. The "Shrink Volume" option shows the maximum you can shrink. After shrinking, you see unallocated space. Right‑click it → "New Simple Volume", follow the wizard, assign D: as the drive letter, and choose NTFS file system. If you accidentally delete the system partition, do not panic. Search for "Windows installation media repair boot". Recommended video tutorial: Search for "how to partition laptop drive" on Bilibili or YouTube, pick a recent one with high views. Extended 3: Manually Backing Up Game Saves Although platforms like Steam offer cloud saves, some older games or pirated copies do not sync. Saves are usually located at: or (AppData is hidden; you can type the path directly into File Explorer's address bar) After finishing a game, consider manually copying its save folder to . Extended 4: Buying and Using Hard Disk Drives for Backup (In‑Depth) If you plan to buy a mechanical hard drive for cold backups (rarely powered on), here are some practical points. HDDs are sensitive to vibration while running. Do not move or bump them when powered on. CMR vs. SMR – My personal preference CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) offers stable random write performance and easier data recovery – even if a small part is damaged, the rest is usually still accessible. SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) overlaps tracks to increase density (about 25% more capacity than CMR at the same platter count), which lowers cost per gigabyte (typically 10‑20% cheaper). For purely sequential writes of cold data, SMR is technically fine. But personally, I simply dislike SMR. Its random write IOPS can drop by more than 50%, and localised damage may affect related tracks, making recovery trickier. So I only recommend CMR drives. Among consumer drives, Western Digital Red Pro and Seagate IronWolf Pro are typically CMR – search for "model number + CMR" before buying. Can SSDs be used for cold backups? Not recommended. SSDs store data as electrical charge, and over long periods without power (2‑3 years) the charge gradually leaks, causing data corruption. At higher temperatures, retention time drops further (about one year at 30°C, only half a year at 55°C). For important cold data, a mechanical hard drive is safer – but of course, always keep multiple copies everywhere. Using spare SSDs with an M.2 enclosure If you have a spare M.2 SSD, you can buy an M.2 enclosure to turn it into a fast portable drive. A brand I know with decent value is ITGZ (also called IGTZ). They offer an all‑metal enclosure with a 9210B controller, supporting 2230/2242/2280 drives, priced around 6‑10 USD. Note that the enclosure itself is cheap, but since SSD prices are currently high, buying a brand new SSD just for this purpose may not be cost‑effective. B Key vs. M Key – for those who happen to need it M.2 slots come in three key types: M Key: Supports PCIe x4 (high‑performance NVMe SSDs), notch on the right, bandwidth up to 32Gbps. B Key: Mainly supports SATA and PCIe x2, notch on the left, lower bandwidth. B+M Key: Both notches present, compatible with both slot types, but actual protocol depends on the slot. Regular power‑on – for all electronics Whether mechanical or solid‑state, leaving a drive without power for too long can cause issues. Mechanical drives need the spindle motor to spin occasionally for lubrication. For SSDs, JEDEC specifications state that data retention is measured under specific temperature conditions beyond which data may be lost. It is advisable to power on your backup drives every 3‑6 months, let them run for a few minutes, and check their health status. USB‑to‑SATA adapters and safe removal If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter (often called an "easy cable") with a 3.5‑inch mechanical drive, make sure it comes with a separate 12V power supply. USB power alone is often insufficient and may cause recognition failures or damage. When unplugging, always click the "Safely Remove Hardware" icon in the Windows system tray and wait for confirmation before unplugging. The safest method is simply shutting down the computer – on shutdown, the system will automatically park the heads. Never pull the USB cable while the drive activity light is still blinking; that can easily cause the heads to crash onto the platters, creating physical bad sectors. SATA connector insertion limit SATA connectors have a limited insertion cycle (typically around 50‑100 times). Do not plug and unplug just for fun. If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter board, you can leave the drive attached to the board and only unplug the USB cable – this spares the SATA connector. The same applies to USB‑to‑SATA cables: keep the whole assembly connected and avoid repeatedly disconnecting the SATA end. Cable recommendation When buying Type‑C cables for external drives or laptop charging, consider looking for Luxshare OEM cables. Luxshare is a key Apple supply chain manufacturer and a leader in high‑speed cables. On second‑hand markets (e.g., Xianyu), you can sometimes find Luxshare 240W PD 3.1 USB‑C cables for less than 3 USD. Their build quality and electrical performance far exceed no‑name cables at the same price, making them great for drive enclosures or laptop charging. Another channel called "Scientific Picking" may also offer good deals on factory‑surplus cables. Extended 5: Practical Cloud Encryption For sensitive files (ID scans, financial records, password backups), you must encrypt them before uploading. Method 1 – VeraCrypt Download VeraCrypt and create an encrypted volume (a virtual hard drive). Drag your sensitive files into it. After closing, you get a file. Upload that file to the cloud. To decrypt, you need VeraCrypt and the password. The cloud provider cannot read the contents. Method 2 – 7‑Zip encryption Right‑click the files/folder → 7‑Zip → Add to archive. Set a password, choose AES‑256 as the encryption method. Upload the resulting or file. Remember to also check "Encrypt file names" so that the contents are truly hidden. Extended 6: How NTP Time Synchronisation Works NTP (Network Time Protocol) is used to calibrate your computer's clock over the internet. The motherboard has a CMOS battery that keeps time when the PC is off, but the battery eventually dies (usually after 3‑5 years). If your computer resets to 1970 every time you boot, the CMOS battery is dead – replace it with a CR2032. Changing to a domestic NTP server greatly improves sync success rates. Besides Tencent and Alibaba, you can also try: (for Chinese educational networks)

title: Ports
content: Appendix 4: Quick Reference for Common Ports This chapter helps you identify the shape, purpose, speed, and power delivery of various ports on your laptop – so you don‘t buy the wrong cables or docking stations. The Must-Read part covers only what you need day‑to‑day (does it fit? can it do the job?). Detailed version tables are in Extended Reading – consult them when you need specifics. First, understand the unit conversion Port speeds are often quoted in Mbps (megabits per second) or Gbps (gigabits per second), but file copy dialogs show MB/s (megabytes per second). The conversion is: 8 Mbps = 1 MB/s Examples: USB 2.0 theoretical speed: 480 Mbps → about 60 MB/s (slower in practice) Gigabit Ethernet: 1000 Mbps → 125 MB/s Just divide by 8 to get the theoretical MB/s (real‑world will be lower). 4.1 The Minimum You Need to Know For most ports, if the shape matches, it will work. Only a few cases require checking versions. USB: Black or white plastic inside means slow (USB 2.0, about 30‑40 MB/s actual). Blue plastic or "SS" logo means fast (USB 3.x, several hundred MB/s actual). Charging: Only Type‑C ports, with both your laptop and charger supporting PD (Power Delivery), can fast‑charge the laptop. Regular Type‑A ports cannot charge a laptop. External display: Both HDMI and Type‑C work. For 4K 60Hz or higher, prefer Type‑C or DisplayPort (DP). Ethernet and headphone jack: If the shape fits, plug it in. 4.2 USB Ports (Practical Guide) Shapes Type‑A (flat rectangle): Common on flash drives, mice. Blue plastic or "SS" logo means high speed. Type‑C (oval, reversible): The main port on new laptops. You cannot tell speed by shape alone – it could be slow USB 2.0 or very fast USB4. Check your laptop's specs. Type‑B (square / trapezoidal): Used on printers, scanners, some drive adapters. Insertion cycles are limited – keep it plugged in and only unplug the other end. Mini / Micro USB: Old devices, now obsolete. Power delivery (laptop charging) Only Type‑C with PD can charge your laptop. The port usually has a PD or lightning bolt logo next to it. Charger, cable, and laptop must all support the same or higher PD power level. Detailed USB version table (2.0 / 3.x / USB4) is in Extended Reading at the end of this appendix. 4.3 Display Ports HDMI (trapezoidal, flat): Connect to TVs, monitors, projectors. If your 4K monitor shows only 30Hz (choppy motion), the cable or port may be an old version. Use a cable labelled "HDMI 2.0" or higher. DP / Mini‑DP (rectangular or small rectangle): High bandwidth, good for high resolution and high refresh rates. Common on desktop monitors and some laptops. VGA (blue trapezoid, 15 pins): For old projectors. New laptops don't have it – you'll need an active HDMI‑to‑VGA adapter. Simple rule: For 4K 60Hz or higher, prefer Type‑C to DP or DP directly. HDMI can also do it, but check your hardware. 4.4 Network Port RJ45 (square with a clip): Wired Ethernet – stable and low latency. Thin‑and‑light laptops often omit it; use a Type‑C to RJ45 adapter. 4.5 Audio Port 3.5mm headphone jack (round): Almost all laptops keep this. Plug in headphones, mic, or headset. 4.6 Thunderbolt vs. USB4 Thunderbolt port: Type‑C shape with a ⚡ lightning bolt logo next to it. Without that logo, it‘s just regular USB. Do you need Thunderbolt? Only if you need to connect an external GPU or two 4K displays simultaneously. For daily office work, one monitor, or ordinary storage, regular USB 3.x or USB4 is enough. Detailed Thunderbolt vs. USB4 comparison table (bandwidth, power, daisy‑chaining) is in Extended Reading. 4.7 One‑Cable Display with Reverse Charging "One‑cable connection": a single Type‑C cable between laptop and monitor that carries video, charges the laptop, and extends USB ports. Requirements: Monitor supports PD output (at least 65W) Laptop supports PD charging Cable supports 5A current (100W or higher) No side effects – your laptop‘s power management handles it safely. 4.8 TGX Port (Specific Laptop Models) Looks like a slim Type‑C, labelled TGX. Only found on a few Lenovo ThinkBook models (14+/16+). Used to connect an external desktop graphics card. Regular users can completely ignore this. 4.9 Cable Advice A poor‑quality cable will cripple your expensive devices. Common problems: slow charging, 4K display blackout or flickering, device not recognised. Recommendation: Luxshare's 240W USB4 universal cable – supports PD 3.1 240W charging, USB4 40Gbps data, and 8K video. 4.10 Memory Cards (SD / microSD) Laptop card slots come in two shapes: SD card (full‑size, about the size of a postage stamp) microSD / TF card (tiny, used in phones and drones) Speed rating simplified Photos or normal video: buy a card labelled C10 (10 inside a circle) or U1. 4K video recording: buy a card labelled U3 or V30. Ignore other letters (A1/A2, V60/V90) unless you know you need them. Physical interface type Most thin‑and‑light laptops have UHS‑I slots (one row of gold contacts) – theoretical maximum about 100 MB/s. A few high‑end models have UHS‑II (two rows of contacts) – can do >300 MB/s. To tell: flip the card over and count the contact rows. Check your laptop‘s manual for what it supports. CFexpress (for professional cameras) Regular users can ignore this completely. If you own a high‑end camera and need very fast continuous shooting or high‑bitrate video, check your camera's manual for the correct CFexpress type (A, B, or C) before buying a card. 4.11 SATA Port SATA (Serial Advanced Technology Attachment) is an older interface standard for connecting hard drives. New laptops no longer include SATA ports, but you may encounter external drive enclosures, desktop hard drives, or drives pulled from old laptops. Shape and versions A SATA connection has two parts: Data connector (L‑shaped, 7 pins): short flat connector, carries data. Power connector (longer, 15 pins): supplies power. Common SATA versions: SATA 3.0: mainstream, speed 6 Gbps (about 550‑560 MB/s actual). SATA 2.0: 3 Gbps, older devices. All versions have identical physical connectors and are backwards compatible. Usage 2.5‑inch drives (laptop HDDs, older SSDs): use SATA data + power. 3.5‑inch desktop drives: also SATA, but require 12V power (2.5‑inch drives need only 5V). Therefore, external 3.5‑inch drives need a separate power supply. Optical drives (obsolete): also use SATA. Using an external SATA drive (USB‑to‑SATA adapter / enclosure) If you have a spare SATA drive and want to use it as an external drive: Buy a USB‑to‑SATA adapter cable (often called "easy cable") or a drive enclosure. Watch the power: 2.5‑inch drives can run on USB power (5V). 3.5‑inch drives must use an adapter with a separate 12V power supply; otherwise they won‘t spin up. Safe removal: Always use "Safely Remove Hardware" in the Windows system tray, or shut down the computer before unplugging. Never unplug while the drive is reading or writing – this can damage the heads or create bad sectors. Insertion cycle limit SATA connectors have a limited mating life (about 50‑100 cycles). If you frequently connect an external SATA drive, leave the SATA side of the adapter or enclosure permanently attached to the drive, and only unplug the USB side. This preserves the SATA connector. Extended Reading (Technical Details) The following sections contain detailed tables and advanced knowledge. Read them when you need specifics.
