Extended 1: USB Version Full Table | USB Version | Alias | Max Speed | Theoretical Bandwidth (approx) | Common Use | |-------------|-------|-----------|-------------------------------|-------------| | USB 2.0 | Hi‑Speed | 480 Mbps | 60 MB/s | Keyboards, mice, old flash drives | | USB 3.0 / 3.1 Gen1 | USB 3.0 | 5 Gbps | 500 MB/s | Normal flash drives, external HDDs | | USB 3.1 Gen2 | USB 3.1 | 10 Gbps | 1.2 GB/s | Fast external SSDs | | USB 3.2 Gen2x2 | USB 3.2 | 20 Gbps | 2.4 GB/s | High‑end external SSDs | | USB4 | USB4 | 40 Gbps | 4 GB/s | Laptops, docks, displays | Identification: USB 2.0 ports usually have black or white plastic inside. USB 3.x ports typically have blue plastic or logos like "SS" (SuperSpeed) or "10" (10Gbps). Type‑C ports cannot be identified by appearance alone. Extended 2: HDMI Version Quick Table | HDMI Version | Max Resolution / Refresh | Bandwidth | Notes | |--------------|--------------------------|-----------|-------| | 1.4 | 4K 30Hz | 10.2 Gbps | Legacy | | 2.0 | 4K 60Hz | 18 Gbps | Mainstream | | 2.1 TMDS | 4K 60Hz | 18 Gbps | Essentially renamed 2.0 | | 2.1 FRL | 4K 120Hz / 8K 60Hz | 48 Gbps | True 2.1 | When buying an HDMI cable, look for "HDMI 2.1 certified" and explicit support for 4K 120Hz or 8K. Extended 3: Thunderbolt vs. USB4 Comparison | Feature | Thunderbolt 3 | Thunderbolt 4 | Thunderbolt 5 | USB4 (baseline) | |---------|---------------|---------------|---------------|------------------| | Theoretical bandwidth | 40 Gbps | 40 Gbps | 80 Gbps (120/40 symmetric mode) | 40 Gbps (optional) | | Minimum PCIe bandwidth | 16 Gbps | mandatory 32 Gbps | 64 Gbps | not guaranteed | | Minimum video output | 1x 4K | mandatory 2x 4K | 2x 6K / 3x 4K | not guaranteed | | Minimum port power | 9W | mandatory 15W | 15W+ | only 7.5W | | Daisy‑chaining | supported | supported | supported | not guaranteed | | Certification | Intel | Intel | Intel | none | Conclusion: USB4 baseline is loose – vendors can make cut‑down versions (20Gbps, low power). Thunderbolt 4/5 enforce higher minimums. A Type‑C port without a lightning bolt logo is just regular USB. Extended 4: Memory Card Speed Class Full Table | Logo | Name | Minimum Write Speed | |------|------|---------------------| | C2/C4/C6/C10 | Speed Class | 2/4/6/10 MB/s | | U1 / U3 | UHS Speed Class | 10 / 30 MB/s | | V10–V90 | Video Speed Class | 10–90 MB/s | | A1 / A2 | Application Performance Class | random IOPS | A card may show C10, U3, V30, A2 together – it meets all those minimums. Extended 5: SD Express and CFexpress SD Express: Brings PCIe bus to SD cards. Theoretical speed up to 985 MB/s (PCIe 3.0 x1) or 4 GB/s (PCIe 4.0 x2). However, as of 2026, very few laptops support it – ordinary users do not need it. CFexpress: For professional cameras, based on PCIe/NVMe. Three physically incompatible types: Type A (~2 GB/s), Type B (~4 GB/s), Type C (~8 GB/s). Always check your camera's manual before buying. Extended 6: SATA Versions and AHCI SATA 3.0 has a theoretical speed of 6 Gbps, but due to 8b/10b encoding (each 10 bits transmitted contain 8 bits of real data), the effective bandwidth is about 4.8 Gbps, or roughly 560 MB/s. This is the ceiling for SATA – even the fastest SSD cannot exceed this speed when connected via SATA. AHCI (Advanced Host Controller Interface) is the driver protocol for SATA drives. It was designed for mechanical hard drives and is not well optimised for the high queue depth and parallelism of SSDs. In contrast, NVMe (used by M.2 drives) fully unlocks SSD performance. This is why M.2 NVMe drives are much faster than SATA SSDs. If you use a USB‑to‑SATA adapter, Windows will handle AHCI automatically – you don‘t need to worry about it.

title: Browsers
content: Appendix 5: Web Browsers This appendix covers basic browser usage, search techniques, how to ask questions effectively, and commonly used extensions. 5.1 Which Browser to Choose Windows comes with Microsoft Edge, which is built on Chromium and offers good compatibility. You can use it as is. Firefox is also a solid choice. Please avoid any Chinese-branded browsers such as 360 Extreme Browser or 2345 Browser. 5.2 Multi‑Threaded Downloading: FDM The built‑in downloader in browsers is single‑threaded. Large files download slowly, and if the connection drops, you may have to restart from scratch. Multi‑threaded tools split a file into chunks and download them simultaneously, which is faster and supports resuming interrupted downloads. FDM (Free Download Manager) is recommended. It is free, open‑source, and ad‑free. During installation, enable the browser integration plugin. No manual configuration is needed. When you download a large file (several hundred MB or more), FDM will be invoked automatically. FDM Download Link 5.3 Search Engines Bing is recommended. It is accessible from within China and shows fewer ads than Baidu. If you have access to Google, its English search results are more accurate. 5.4 Effective Search Tips Do not type full sentences. Extract and use only the core keywords. Examples: Bad: Better: Useful search operators: | Operator | Purpose | Example | |----------|---------|---------| | | Restrict to a specific website | | | | Restrict to a file format | | | | Exact phrase match | | | minus sign | Exclude a word | | When searching for an error message, copy the complete error code (e.g., ) rather than describing what happened – it works much better. 5.5 Judging Whether Information Is True or False Check the source: Prioritize official sources and reputable media. Be cautious with unknown self‑media accounts. Check the date: Outdated information may no longer be valid. Cross‑validate: Compare different sources. Look at comments: If many commenters disagree or point out factual errors, the content is likely unreliable. Watch for clickbait headlines: Words like “shocking,” “urgent,” “watch before deletion” often signal hype or misinformation. For academic purposes, use Google Scholar or your university library’s databases. The references in English Wikipedia articles can serve as a starting point. 5.6 How to Ask Questions and Netiquette When asking for help, include as much of the following as possible: The full error message (text or screenshot) Your environment: OS version, software version, hardware model, etc. Log files: Many programs and games generate files in their installation folder or under . Copy the last few dozen lines. Example (game crashing to desktop): Problem: Game goes black and crashes on startup Environment: Windows 11 22H2, graphics driver 610.47, game version 1.2.3 Error message: Last lines of the log: [paste here] Already tried: Updated drivers, verified game file integrity Basic netiquette: Try to find the answer yourself first. If you can’t, then ask. Describe the problem clearly and mention what you have already tried. After receiving help, report back the outcome so others can learn. Do not send private messages for public questions – ask in public forums/channels. 5.7 Useful Browser Extensions Extensions should be installed from the official stores (Edge Add‑ons, Chrome Web Store, Firefox Add‑ons). 5.7.1 Ad Blocking: uBlock Origin Open‑source, lightweight, and blocks most ads and trackers. For small websites or personal blogs that you visit often, if the ads are not intrusive, you can disable uBlock (click the extension icon → the power icon turns gray) or add the site to the allowlist. Those sites rely on ad revenue to stay running. 5.7.2 Cat Catch Sniffs out the real addresses of audio and video on a page and lets you download them. When a page has media playing, the extension icon shows a number; click it and choose what to download. Useful for recording online lectures, background music, etc. 5.7.3 LeechBlock NG Limits the time you can spend on certain websites. You can set a maximum daily allowance or specific allowed time windows. Once the limit is reached, access is automatically blocked. Helps control time spent on social media or video sites. 5.7.4 Tampermonkey A user‑script manager. You can install scripts from GreasyFork (greasyfork.org) to auto‑fill forms, remove ads, and add custom functionality. Security reminders: Do not install scripts from unknown sources, especially those promising “free VIP” or “shopping bot”. Before installing, look at the script code. If it requests many external permissions (e.g., ), do not install it. Do not install extensions from outside the official stores, especially “free VPN” or “web accelerator” tools. Extended Reading The following sections go into browser internals and technical details. They are more advanced. It is recommended to skim them first – just be aware these concepts exist. When you run into a specific problem later, you can search again using the keywords you learned here. If something puzzles you or you want to dive deeper, I suggest looking up MDN and W3Schools. Extended 1: Browser Engine The browser engine (rendering engine) turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code into a visible page. Blink: Used by Chrome, Edge, Opera, Brave, and others. Currently the highest market share. Gecko: Used by Firefox, completely open‑source. WebKit: Used by Safari. Blink originally forked from WebKit. Ordinary users do not need to worry about these differences. Very rarely, an old website may say “Please use Chrome” – but Edge will actually work fine too. If a site looks broken, try switching browsers. Extended 2: Web Page Structure (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) A web page is built from three languages: HTML: Defines content and structure. The browser parses it into a DOM tree. CSS: Defines style and layout – colors, fonts, positioning, etc. JavaScript: Defines interactive behavior – button clicks, carousels, form validation, etc. TypeScript: A superset of JavaScript that adds type annotations. It needs to be compiled into JavaScript to run. ES6: The 2015 version of JavaScript, introducing arrow functions, classes, modules, etc. All modern browsers support it. Responsive design: Uses CSS media queries ( ) to automatically adapt to different screen widths. Press F12 → click the device simulation icon (a small phone) to see how a site looks on mobile. Progressive enhancement: Start with basic content (plain HTML) accessible on all devices, then add styles and interactions on top. This works better for older devices and users with disabilities. Extended 3: Response Headers and Status Codes When a browser requests a page, the server returns response headers. Press F12 → Network tab → click any request to see them. Common status codes: 200: Success 301: Permanent redirect 302 (or 307): Temporary redirect 403: Forbidden 404: Page not found 500: Internal server error Extended 4: User‑Agent (UA) A string the browser sends to the server, containing browser name, version, and operating system. The server can use the UA to return different versions (e.g., mobile site vs. desktop site). Press F12 → device simulation (choose a phone model), then refresh the page – you are now pretending to be a mobile device. You can also install a UA switcher extension. Do not use UA spoofing to scrape website data; always follow the rules. Extended 5: Cookie, localStorage, IndexedDB Three ways browsers store data locally: | Name | Capacity | Lifetime | Sent with requests | Main use | |------|----------|----------|--------------------|-----------| | Cookie | 4KB | Can set expiration | Yes | Login state, user tracking | | localStorage | 5–10MB | Permanent (unless manually cleared) | No | User preferences, theme settings | | IndexedDB | Hundreds of MB | Permanent | No | Offline cache for large structured data | Cookie: Stores a session ID. If you clear cookies, you will be logged out. localStorage: Simple API, good for small settings. IndexedDB: Supports indexes and transactions, but the API is more complex. Many PWAs use it to cache data. View and manage: F12 → Application → Storage section. Extended 6: Chrome/Edge Flags and Firefox about:config Entry points for experimental browser features: Chrome/Edge: Type or in the address bar. Firefox: Type in the address bar, then click “Accept the Risk”. If changes cause problems, click “Reset all” to restore defaults. Extended 7: Main Panels of Developer Tools (F12) Elements: View and edit HTML/CSS (temporary, local only). Console: Shows JavaScript errors and warnings; you can also execute JS code. Sources: View source files and set breakpoints to debug JS. Network: Records all network requests – status codes, timings, request/response data. Application: Manage cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB, and Service Workers. Performance: Record performance data to analyze lag or jank. Lighthouse: Provides a comprehensive score for performance, accessibility, SEO, etc. Extended 8: Service Worker and PWA Service Worker: A script that runs in the background of the browser. It can intercept network requests, manage caches, and send push notifications – even when the page is not open. PWA (Progressive Web App): Uses Service Workers and other technologies to give a web app a native‑like experience – it can be installed on the desktop, work offline, and receive push notifications. When you see an install icon (a computer screen with a down arrow) in the Chrome or Edge address bar, you can click it to install the site as a desktop app. Extended 9: CORS (Cross‑Origin Resource Sharing) The browser’s security policy, the “same‑origin policy”, prevents a web page from making requests to a different domain. If a page legitimately needs to request data from another domain, that target server must include the header in its response. When developing local web pages, you often run into CORS errors. To fix them, either configure the backend to send the proper headers or use a proxy. Understanding CORS helps you understand why certain API calls from a web page might fail. Extended 10: WebFonts, Browser Cache, and WebAssembly (Wasm) WebFonts Fonts used on websites (e.g., Noto Sans, Source Han Sans) are often not installed on the operating system, so they must be downloaded from the server. These font files ( , , ) are called WebFonts. A website declares which font files to download using the rule in CSS. The browser downloads them and caches them locally, so they don’t need to be downloaded again on subsequent visits. Common formats: WOFF2 (high compression, used by modern browsers), WOFF (for older browser compatibility), TTF (uncompressed, rarely used). If text on a site flickers or appears as squares (gibberish), WebFonts might have failed to load. Press F12 → Network tab → filter by “Font” to see if font requests return 404. Browser Cache The HTTP cache stores downloaded resources (images, CSS, JS, fonts, etc.) on the local disk. When you revisit the same page, resources are read from the local disk instead of being requested from the server again, which speeds up loading significantly. Cache mechanism in a nutshell: When a server returns a resource, it includes headers like or that tell the browser how long it may cache the resource. For example, means the resource is valid for 24 hours; the browser will use the cached copy without even asking the server during that time. After the cache expires, the browser sends a “conditional request” using or to ask the server whether the resource has changed. If it hasn’t, the server returns and the browser continues using the cached copy. Manually controlling the cache: Press to force a refresh that re‑downloads everything from the server. Press F12 → Network tab → check “Disable cache” to force fresh downloads during debugging. Clear the browser cache: Settings → Privacy and security → Clear browsing data → choose “Cached images and files”. WebAssembly (Wasm) WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that runs in the browser. Its goal is near‑native execution speed while maintaining safety. Languages like C, C++, Rust, and Go can be compiled into Wasm and then called from JavaScript inside a web page. Why do we need Wasm? Traditional JavaScript is interpreted (though modern JS engines use JIT compilation), but for computationally intensive tasks (video encoding/decoding, image processing, game physics, cryptography) it may still not be fast enough. Wasm offers a lower‑level, pre‑compiled format that executes significantly faster. A simple Wasm example Here’s how to write a C function that adds two numbers, compile it to Wasm, and call it from HTML. Step 1: Write C code ( ) Step 2: Compile to Wasm After installing the Emscripten toolchain, run: This generates an file. Step 3: Load and call it from HTML Real‑world use cases: Figma: The graphics rendering engine is implemented in Wasm. AutoCAD Web: The browser version of the CAD software. Video / image processing: For example, ffmpeg compiled to Wasm enables online transcoding. Game engines: Unity and Unreal Engine can export to Wasm for web deployment. Ordinary users do not need to interact with Wasm directly. But knowing about it helps you understand why certain web apps run so fast and why your CPU usage might suddenly spike – the page could be running a heavy Wasm computation task.

title: Proxy
content: Appendix 6: Proxy This appendix explains the differences between proxy, VPN, and related concepts, as well as how to use common proxy tools. No specific service providers are recommended. 6.1 Relationship Between Concepts Proxy: An intermediary network service. Your device sends requests to a proxy server, which accesses the target website on your behalf and returns the result. Proxies can bypass network restrictions, but they usually only work for specific applications (e.g., browsers). VPN (Virtual Private Network) : Creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and the target server. All network traffic (including system background traffic, UDP, etc.) goes through the tunnel. VPNs operate at the network layer and affect the entire system. Ladder: A colloquial term for circumvention tools, including both proxies and VPN services. Airport: Slang for a commercial proxy service provider – literally “the place where you get a ladder”. Users purchase a plan and receive a subscription link, which they import into a client. To put it simply: proxy and VPN are technical implementations, while “ladder” and “airport” are community slang. 6.2 Clash and Its Variants Clash is a rule‑based proxy core that supports multiple protocols (HTTP, SOCKS5, Shadowsocks, VMess, etc.). It has no graphical interface on its own and needs a GUI front‑end. Main variants: | Name | Description | |------|-------------| | Clash (original) | The earliest core, now unmaintained. | | Clash Premium | A closed‑source version by the original author, added features like TUN mode, also discontinued. | | Clash Meta (mihomo) | An active fork maintained by the open‑source community, with more features and the most commonly used today. It is described separately later. | | Clash Verge Rev | A cross‑platform GUI front‑end (Windows/macOS/Linux) based on the Clash Meta core. Clean interface, suitable for daily use. | | Clash for Windows (CFW) | Once the most popular Windows GUI, now discontinued and no longer recommended. | | ClashX / ClashX Pro | GUI front‑ends for macOS. | | ClashMetaForAndroid (CMFA) | Android GUI based on the mihomo core. | For ordinary users, simply use Clash Verge (desktop) and ClashMetaForAndroid (Android). 6.3 YAML Configuration Files The core of Clash is a configuration file (usually ) written in YAML format. The subscription link you get from an airport is essentially this file. Basic structure of a configuration file: How to use: Obtain a subscription link (usually ) or download a file directly from your airport. In Clash Verge, click “Import” → “Import from URL” and paste the link; or manually place the config file into the config directory. Select a proxy group (e.g., choose a node in “PROXY”), then enable “System Proxy” or “TUN Mode”. Key fields: : List of nodes, each with type, address, port, encryption, etc. : Policy groups. means manual selection; automatically picks the fastest; switches in order. : Matching rules. They are evaluated from top to bottom; the first match applies. matches domain suffixes, matches IP ranges, matches geographic location, and is the catch‑all rule. 6.4 Shadowrocket Shadowrocket is a proxy client for iOS, supporting protocols such as SSR, VMess, Trojan, and also subscriptions. How to use: Purchase from the App Store (requires a US region account), about $2.99. Open the app, tap the “+” in the top‑right corner → choose “Subscribe”. Paste the subscription link provided by your airport and save. Go back to the home screen and tap the switch to connect. The first time you do this, you will be prompted to add a VPN configuration – allow it. You can adjust routing rules via “Configuration” → “Rules”. 6.5 Mihomo Mihomo (formerly Clash Meta) is the core maintained by the Clash open‑source community and is the foundation of all active Clash clients today. It fixes many issues from the original Clash and adds new protocols (such as WireGuard, Hysteria) and new features. Mihomo itself is a command‑line program; you do not need to run it separately. GUIs like Clash Verge and ClashMetaForAndroid all bundle the mihomo core. If you need to run it manually, download the binary for your platform from GitHub and start it with: 6.6 System Proxy Mode vs. TUN Mode Clash provides two ways to route traffic through the proxy. System Proxy Mode: Configures an HTTP/SOCKS5 proxy address in your system network settings (usually ). Only programs that “respect the system proxy” will go through the proxy. Most browsers and some applications do; but games, command‑line tools, and UDP traffic (e.g., DNS, voice chat) usually do not. Pros: Lightweight, good compatibility. Cons: Many types of traffic bypass the proxy. TUN Mode: Creates a virtual network interface. The operating system routes all traffic (TCP, UDP, ICMP) to this interface, where Clash processes it and forwards accordingly. Essentially a global proxy that works without any program having to cooperate. Games, Spotify clients, and system DNS will all go through the proxy. How to enable: In Clash Verge, go to “Settings” → install the TUN service (requires administrator privileges) → turn on the TUN Mode switch. Cons: Slightly higher resource usage than system proxy; may affect local network access (you may need to configure rules to allow LAN traffic). In general, use system proxy if you only browse the web. If you play games or use software that does not respect the system proxy, enable TUN Mode. 6.7 Shizuku Mode on Android Shizuku is an Android tool that allows ordinary apps to execute system‑level commands via ADB or root privileges, granting high permissions without root. In ClashMetaForAndroid (CMFA) , enabling TUN Mode normally requires root or Shizuku. Shizuku mode lets CMFA use TUN on non‑rooted phones. How to use: Install the Shizuku app (from GitHub or CoolAPK). Activate Shizuku as instructed (needs ADB or root): Connect to a computer and run Or activate via wireless debugging (Android 11+). Open CMFA → Settings → TUN Settings → choose “Shizuku Mode”. After granting permissions, TUN Mode will work normally. If your phone is already rooted, you can directly select “Root Mode” and skip Shizuku. Extended Reading The following sections cover proxy protocols and underlying mechanisms. They are more advanced. It is recommended to skim them first – just be aware these concepts exist. When you run into a specific problem later, you can search again using the keywords you learned here. Extended 1: Common Proxy Protocols HTTP Proxy: Only proxies HTTP traffic, transmits in plain text without encryption. Rarely used alone today. SOCKS5 Proxy: Proxies TCP and UDP traffic, does not inspect content, can be used with other encryption protocols. Clash’s mixed port offers both HTTP and SOCKS5. Shadowsocks (SS) : Encrypted SOCKS5 proxy, lightweight, weak obfuscation; already recognized by some ISPs. ShadowsocksR (SSR) : A derivative of SS with added obfuscation plugins, now gradually obsolete. VMess: The core protocol of V2Ray, strong encryption, supports dynamic ports. Trojan: Mimics HTTPS traffic, good camouflage. Hysteria: A QUIC (UDP)‑based protocol designed for aggressive speed boosting, works well on high‑packet‑loss networks. WireGuard: A next‑generation VPN protocol with kernel‑level implementation, now also supported by Mihomo. Extended 2: Detailed Clash Rule Types : Exact full domain name match. : Matches domain suffix, e.g., matches and . : Matches a keyword appearing in the domain name. : Matches IPv4 address ranges. : Matches IPv6 address ranges. : Uses the MaxMind database to determine the country of an IP address. (TUN mode only): Matches by process name. : Matches by source IP address (used for sharing proxy on a LAN). : Catch‑all rule; must be placed last. Extended 3: Virtual Network Interface Principle of TUN Mode TUN mode creates a virtual layer‑3 network interface (e.g., ) inside the operating system. The Clash core reads raw IP packets from this interface, parses the destination address, and decides – based on rules – whether to forward the request through a proxy or directly. For requests that need to go through a proxy, Clash encapsulates the original packet into a proxy protocol (e.g., Shadowsocks) and sends it to the remote server. The remote server decapsulates it, accesses the target, and sends back the response, which is then re‑encapsulated and returned. Because TUN mode requires full decapsulation and re‑encapsulation of packets, its CPU consumption is slightly higher than system proxy mode. Extended 4: IPv6 and Proxies Many airport nodes do not support IPv6. If your device has a public IPv6 address and you visit an IPv6 website, improper rule configuration may either cause the traffic to go direct (accessible) or go through a proxy (which might fail if the node doesn’t support IPv6). It is recommended to set in your configuration file, or explicitly handle IPv6 ranges with rules. Extended 5: DNS Split Routing Clash supports split DNS routing, meaning it uses different DNS servers depending on the domain name. A typical configuration: Domestic domains go to a domestic DNS (e.g., 114.114.114.114), returning domestic CDN addresses. Blocked domains go to the proxy node’s own DNS (or a trusted DNS such as 1.1.1.1) to avoid DNS poisoning. can detect whether a DNS result points to a foreign IP, providing further protection against poisoning. title: Softwares
content: Appendix 7: Useful Software This appendix introduces several pieces of software that are frequently used in daily work, covering compression, playback, downloading, editing, and system enhancement. 7.1 Compression Software: NanaZip / WinRAR The built‑in extraction tool in Windows only supports files. When you encounter or archives, you need a third‑party compression tool. NanaZip: Open‑source, based on 7‑Zip, with a modern interface that fits Windows 11 and supports dark mode. You can install it from the Microsoft Store or download the directly. It is fully featured for both extracting and creating archives. WinRAR: A classic compression tool that supports creating archives (using a proprietary algorithm). After installation it shows a 40‑day trial reminder, but you can continue using it afterward. If you need to send encrypted or split archives to others, either WinRAR or 7‑Zip will work. Both are fine for everyday use – just pick one and install it. 7.2 Video Player: PotPlayer The built‑in “Movies & TV” player on Windows has limited codec support and cannot open many formats (such as , , ). PotPlayer launches quickly, supports almost all codecs out of the box, and can play the vast majority of video files without tweaking. Note: PotPlayer is not the absolute best choice from a technical standpoint. More advanced users might prefer MPV with custom‑compiled codecs, or a specific version that supports Dolby Vision and HDR mapping. But for ordinary users, PotPlayer is stable and easy to use. If you already know how to set up a complex playback environment, this recommendation is not for you – your skill level is beyond the target audience of this appendix. 7.3 BitTorrent Client: qBittorrent For downloading torrents or magnet links, qBittorrent is recommended. It is open‑source, ad‑free, and feature‑complete. It supports search plugins, sequential downloading, speed limits, IP filtering, and more. Common link types: Torrent file ( ): A small file (typically tens to hundreds of KB) containing metadata about the resource – file names, piece hashes, tracker addresses, etc. The download client opens the torrent and uses the information inside to connect to other peers and download the data. Magnet link ( ): An “upgraded” version of a torrent. You do not need to download a file first. The client uses the hash inside the link to locate the resource via the DHT network. Copy the whole link and add it to qBittorrent. ed2k link ( ): A link for the eMule protocol, used on older P2P networks. Few resources use it now, though some old archives still do. qBittorrent does not support ed2k; you would need eMule or another client that supports that protocol. A few settings suggestions: Add public tracker lists (see ) to improve connection success rates. Limit your upload speed (e.g., to 1 MB/s) to avoid hogging bandwidth and slowing down your network. Seed after downloading completes (e.g., to a 1:1 ratio or for 24 hours) – this is part of the BitTorrent sharing spirit. 7.4 Code and Plain‑Text Editor: VS Code Even if you do not write code, VS Code is a plain‑text editor worth installing. Compared to Notepad, it offers: syntax highlighting (automatically colors , , files), tabs, regex search, and extensions (Markdown preview, spell checking, etc.). Two simple things to do after installation: Set the font: In settings, search for and enter ; also enable to support ligatures. Install the Chinese language pack: Search the extension marketplace for “Chinese (Simplified)”. From then on, use VS Code to view and edit any configuration file, log file, script, or note. 7.5 Image Extensions for Apple Devices: HEIF / HEVC Photos taken on iPhones may be in format (HEIF), and videos in format (HEVC / H.265). Windows cannot open them or show thumbnails by default. You need to install two official extensions from the Microsoft Store: HEIF Image Extensions (free) HEVC Video Extensions (from the device manufacturer, free) After installation, you can view photos and videos from Apple devices directly in File Explorer. 7.6 Terminal Enhancement: Windows Terminal The default windows for CMD and PowerShell are rather basic – no tabs, mediocre font rendering, awkward copy‑and‑paste. Windows Terminal is a modern terminal from Microsoft that supports: Multiple tabs and split panes GPU‑accelerated rendering, crisp fonts Custom themes, background images, transparency Simultaneously running PowerShell, CMD, and WSL in any combination Pin it to your taskbar after installation, and use it for all command‑line operations from then on. Extended Reading The following sections cover technical details and alternatives for the software mentioned above. They are of medium difficulty. Read selectively depending on your interest. Extended 1: 7‑Zip Command Line Usage The core of 7‑Zip is the command‑line version . Many automation scripts (e.g., batch extraction, compressed backups) rely on it. Common commands: Extract: Compress: Test integrity: NanaZip does not provide the command‑line version by default. If you need it, download the standalone command‑line program from the 7‑Zip website. Extended 2: PotPlayer and Hardware Decoding PotPlayer uses its built‑in decoders by default, which may cause high CPU usage when playing 4K HDR content. You can switch to hardware decoding via your graphics card: Right‑click the video → Options → Filters → Video Decoder → Built‑in Decoder → Hardware Decoding (DXVA2 / D3D11) → set to “Automatic”. If your GPU supports it, you can also enable “HDR Passthrough” (requires a compatible display) or “Pixel Shader HDR Conversion”. Extended 3: qBittorrent Search Plugins qBittorrent has a built‑in search feature, but you need to install Python and download search plugins (from the official GitHub repository). Once installed, you can search various resource sites directly from within the program (plugins must be added manually; none are provided by default). This feature involves copyright issues; use it in compliance with local laws. Extended 4: Recommended VS Code Extensions PDF Viewer: Browse PDF files inside VS Code. Remote - SSH: Connect to remote servers via SSH and edit files. Extended 5: Windows Terminal Configuration File Location Windows Terminal settings are stored in (accessible via the drop‑down menu → Settings → “Open JSON file” in the lower‑left corner). You can edit this file directly to add custom color schemes, background images, etc. There are many ready‑made themes from the community (e.g., , ). Extended 6: Two Versions of the HEVC Video Extension There are two HEVC extensions in the Microsoft Store: HEVC Video Extensions (paid) : Costs 7 RMB, officially published. HEVC Video Extensions from Device Manufacturer: Free, but may require specific hardware conditions (such as a driver provided by the manufacturer). Most laptops come with Intel graphics drivers that include this extension; you can search for and install it directly. If the free version tells you that you do not meet the installation requirements, try searching for the direct Store link for “HEVC Video Extensions from Device Manufacturer” via a search engine – often you can install it anyway.

title: Gaming
content: Appendix 8: Gaming After all that talk, we finally get to the most exciting part – gaming. This appendix covers how to use major gaming platforms, account security, and a few useful features. I will cover macOS gaming in a separate appendix. I haven't used macOS myself yet, but I will have a chance to try it soon. 8.1 Steam Steam is the world’s largest digital game distribution platform. Most PC games can be bought here. 8.1.1 Finding the Official Website The official Steam website is . When you search for “Steam” in China, you might see a site called “Steam China” ( ), which is the domestic version operated by Tencent. Its game library and account system are separate from the global Steam – it is not recommended. Always look for the domain. If you cannot open this website, you can use the Watt Toolkit (introduced below) to accelerate access. 8.1.2 Creating an Account When registering, it is advisable to use a more secure email address, such as Outlook, Gmail, or ProtonMail. QQ email has a relatively higher risk of being stolen, and losing your Steam account can be a big loss. You can also download the Steam mobile app for 2FA authentication. During registration you may encounter Google’s reCAPTCHA. If it doesn’t load, the Watt Toolkit mentioned below can also help. 8.1.3 Watt Toolkit (formerly Steam++) This is a free, open‑source, multi‑function Steam toolbox. You can download it from GitHub or its official website. Main features: Network acceleration: speeds up access to Steam Community, GitHub, Google CAPTCHA, Ubisoft Connect, etc. Account switching: quickly switch between multiple logged‑in Steam accounts. Inventory management: directly manage your game inventory, edit game information (name, cover, background, etc.). Idle card farming: automatically farm Steam trading cards. It is completely free and ad‑free, much more practical than many paid boosters. 8.1.4 Steam Account Contents Steam Points: You earn points when you buy games (roughly 100+ points for every 10 RMB spent). Points can be used to decorate your profile (avatar frames, backgrounds, animated stickers), buy chat emoticons, post “funny” awards on reviews, etc. Steam Level: Raised by crafting badges or spending money. Higher levels increase your friend list limit and give more profile showcases. Not very meaningful for the average player. 8.1.5 On Changing Regions Changing your Steam account to another region (e.g., Argentina, Turkey, low‑price regions) is not recommended. Steam officially cracks down on cross‑region purchases. At best, you will be forced back to your home region; at worst, your account may be banned. The China region is already one of the low‑price regions globally, and most games are reasonably priced – no need to go through the hassle. 8.1.6 Family Sharing Steam Family Sharing allows you to share your game library with up to 5 family members. After enabling it, your friends can play games from your library and vice versa, provided that you are not playing the same game at the same time (playing different games at the same time is fine). How to enable: Steam Settings → Family → check “Authorise Library Sharing on this computer”, then check the accounts you want to share with. Note: Some games (especially those that require an additional third‑party account) do not support sharing. Saves are separate and do not affect each other’s progress. 8.1.7 Remote Play Together For local multiplayer games like It Takes Two or Overcooked, Remote Play Together lets you invite a friend to play online – your friend does not need to own the game. How to use: The person who owns the game launches it. In the Steam friends list, right‑click on your friend → select “Remote Play Together”. After your friend accepts, the screen is streamed to them, and you play together in split‑screen. Your friend only needs a stable internet connection and a Steam account – no purchase necessary. 8.2 Epic Games Store Epic is Steam’s main competitor, operated by the makers of Fortnite and Unreal Engine. Its biggest draw is the weekly free games. Official website: . You can log in with a Steam account or register separately. Free games: Every Thursday, one or more free games are updated. Once claimed, they stay in your library permanently. Past free games have included GTA5, Civilization VI, Batman, and other big titles. It’s a good idea to install the Epic client and log in weekly to claim them – they add up over time. Extended Reading The following sections cover more advanced tips for Steam and Epic. Extended 1: Steam Refund Policy If you have played a game for less than 2 hours and bought it within the last 14 days, you can request a no‑questions‑asked refund. The refund is returned to your original payment method (or to your Steam Wallet). This is useful for games you try and do not like. Refund path: Steam Support → select the game → “I would like a refund”. Extended 2: Steam Wishlist and Discount Notifications When you add a game to your wishlist, Steam will send you an email when it goes on sale. During major sales (Summer Sale, Winter Sale, Lunar New Year Sale), many games are 50–80% off. It is best to wait for these sales before buying. Extended 3: Steam Cloud Saves Steam enables cloud saves by default. Your game saves are automatically synced to the server. When you log in on another computer, your saves are downloaded automatically. Some older games may not support this. You can view and manage cloud saves in the game’s properties. Extended 4: Epic and Steam Interoperability Some games support cross‑platform play (e.g., Rocket League, Fall Guys). However, Epic and Steam are two separate platforms; their game libraries are not shared. Buying the same game on both platforms does not let you share progress, unless the game itself supports cross‑platform saves. Extended 5: Epic Coupons and Cashback Epic sometimes distributes $10 coupons (for games priced at $14.99 or more), which can let you get games at very low prices when combined with discounts. Additionally, Epic has an “Epic Rewards” cashback program – 5% of each purchase is returned as Epic Rewards (usable for future purchases). Extended 6: Game Activation Keys Steam activation keys purchased from third‑party sites (e.g., Satoru, Humble Bundle) can be redeemed in the Steam client via “Add a Game” → “Activate a Product on Steam”. Be careful about the source – do not buy from unknown sellers or black‑market key resellers (keys may be revoked or your account banned). Extended 7: Steam Big Picture Mode Steam has a built‑in Big Picture Mode (the controller icon), with an interface optimised for controllers and TVs. It is great for playing in the living room with a controller. It can also be used to stream games to a tablet via the Steam Link app.

title: TipsANDGlossary
content: Appendix 9: Shortcuts, Tips, and Glossary This appendix collects some small tips you might find useful, along with a bunch of technical terms that may sound intimidating. No need to memorize everything at once – just get a rough idea. When you run into a problem later, or come across a term that looks familiar, you can come back and look it up. Shortcut Keys Most of these shortcuts work across Windows. Pick a few that seem useful – once you get used to them, they will be much faster than reaching for the mouse. | Shortcut | What it does | |----------|---------------| | | Copy | | | Paste | | | Cut | | | Undo the last action | | | Redo (bring back what you undid) | | | Select all | | | Save | | | Find (search for text in a webpage or document) | | | Switch windows (hold Alt and press Tab to choose) | | | Open Task View; you can create new desktops here | | | Open “This PC” (File Explorer) | | | Show the desktop; press again to restore | | | Lock the screen | | | Open the “Run” dialog | | | Open Settings | | | Open Search | | | Open the Quick Link menu (more on this in the next section) | | | Take a screenshot | | | Open Task Manager directly | | | Open clipboard history (must be enabled in Settings first) | | or | Open the emoji panel | | | Open the nth program on the taskbar | | | Snap windows (left half, right half, maximize, minimize) | | | Create a new folder in File Explorer | | | Close the current window; when on the desktop, brings up shutdown options | | | Rename the selected file | | | Refresh | | | Delete a file (goes to Recycle Bin) | | | Permanently delete (does not go to Recycle Bin – use with care) | Tips 2.1 Right‑click the Windows Logo (Win + X) Right‑click the Start button at the bottom‑left corner of your screen, or press . A menu pops up. Everything in it is a built‑in system management tool – much faster than digging through the Control Panel. | Menu option | What it is for | |-------------|----------------| | Apps and Features | Uninstall unwanted programs | | Mobility Center | Adjust brightness, volume, screen projection | | Power Options | Change sleep settings, power plan | | Event Viewer | View system logs; crash reasons (blue screen) are often here | | System | Check computer specs (CPU, RAM, Windows version) | | Device Manager | View and update drivers | | Network Connections | See network adapters, manually set IP addresses | | Disk Management | Partition your hard drive | | Computer Management | A bundle of several management tools | | Windows PowerShell / Terminal | Open the command line | | Task Manager | View processes, performance, close frozen programs | Most items in this menu require administrator privileges. When you are troubleshooting, this is the fastest entry point. 2.2 File Selection Tricks in File Explorer In File Explorer (the window that opens when you go to “This PC”), there are two very common ways to select files: Hold while clicking files: Selects them one by one. For example, click one file, then hold Ctrl and click another – both are selected. Click one of them again to deselect it. This is great for “I want these few, but not that one”. Click one file, then hold and click another file: Selects that file, the other file, and everything in between – all at once. Perfect for “I want everything from A to B”. You can combine these. For example, use Shift to select a continuous range, then Ctrl to add a few scattered files. 2.3 You Can See the PID in Task Manager Open Task Manager ( ), click “Details”, and you will see a table. Right‑click on the header row (where it says “Name”, “CPU”, “Memory”) and you can add more columns. One of them is called PID. What is PID: Process Identifier. A unique number the system assigns to each running program (process). Why it’s useful: Sometimes a program freezes, but Task Manager shows several entries with the same name, and you cannot tell which one to kill. Looking at the PID solves that. Also, some command‑line tools (like ) need the PID to know which process to terminate. How to add it: Task Manager → Details → right‑click the header → Select columns → check “PID”. 2.4 Windows Terminal and PowerShell 7 Windows Terminal: A modern command‑line window program. Compared to the traditional CMD black box, it supports tabs, split panes, crisper font rendering, and custom themes. It was mentioned in Appendix 7 – after installing it, pin it to your taskbar and use it for all command‑line operations. Windows Terminal is just a “shell” – inside it you can run CMD, PowerShell, or any other command‑line tool. PowerShell 7: A command‑line tool (more details appear in the Extended Reading of Appendix 7). It is a different version from the Windows PowerShell that comes with Windows – both can coexist. PowerShell 7 has more consistent commands, more features, and is cross‑platform (Windows, Mac, Linux). The average user may not need to install it, but if you later follow tutorials or write scripts, you might. Their relationship: Windows Terminal is the “window”, PowerShell 7 is the “person sitting inside the window”. You open Windows Terminal, and inside you can create a new tab running PowerShell 7. 2.5 Environment Variables What are environment variables: Think of them as “global sticky notes” in the system. Each sticky note has a name and a value. Any program can read them to know where to find things. Common examples: PATH: A list of folder paths. When you type in the command line, the system looks through these folders to find . When you install Python or FFmpeg and want to run them from the command line, you are essentially adding their installation folders to the PATH. TEMP: Where temporary files are stored. USERNAME: The currently logged‑in user’s name. How to change them: Right‑click “This PC” → Properties → Advanced system settings → Environment Variables. There are “User variables” (affect only your account) and “System variables” (affect everyone). You do not need to know how to edit them yet. But if later you type a command and get “is not recognized as an internal or external command”, you will know it might be a PATH issue – and you can search in that direction. 2.6 Registry What is the Registry: Windows’ giant configuration database. Almost everything you change in Settings – wallpaper, startup items, folder options – ends up written in the Registry. How to open it: , type , press Enter. What it looks like: On the left are “keys” (like folders), on the right are “values” (like files). The top‑level keys are called root keys: : Settings for the current user : Global settings for the whole computer : File associations (e.g., opens with Notepad by default) An important warning: Changing the Registry incorrectly can break software, and in severe cases even prevent your system from booting. Before you make any changes, always make a backup: right‑click the key you are about to modify → Export → save as a file. If something goes wrong, double‑click that file to restore it. You do not need to change anything now. But later, when you see an online tutorial that says “edit the Registry to fix X”, you will know what the Registry is, and you will know to back it up first. That is enough. 2.7 Group Policy What is Group Policy: Think of it as “Registry with graphical switches”. Group Policy packages a bunch of related Registry changes into individual options; you just select “Enabled” or “Disabled”, and the system handles the Registry edits for you. No need to hunt through the Registry yourself. How to open it: , type , press Enter. (Note: Windows Home editions do not have Group Policy by default.) Example: You want to disable USB storage so others cannot copy files from your PC using a USB drive. In Group Policy, find “Removable Storage Access”, select “Deny all access”, and enable it. Trying to find that setting in the Registry directly would take much longer. If you have Windows Home and want Group Policy, you can search for tools like “gpedit‑enabler” – but they are not guaranteed to be stable, and you do not have to go through that trouble. 2.8 Memory Management (Page File and Commit) You can see these three concepts in the “Performance” tab of Task Manager. They are often misunderstood, so here is a simple explanation. Page File The page file is a hidden file on your hard drive (usually named ). As mentioned in the Extended Reading of Appendix 2 (System Tuning), it is also called SWAP. When your physical RAM is full, the system moves data that is not currently needed from RAM into this file, freeing up RAM for applications that need it right now. Think of it as: your desk (RAM) is too small, so you temporarily put documents you are not using right now into a drawer (hard drive), and take them back out when you need them. The hard drive is much slower than RAM, so if the system is constantly using the page file, your computer will become noticeably slower. When drive C: runs low on space, the page file cannot expand properly, and your computer may stutter. This is why Appendix 2 stressed not to fill up drive C:. Commit The “Committed” number in Task Manager represents the total amount of memory that the system has promised to all running programs. This number can be larger than your physical RAM – because part of that promise is fulfilled using the page file. Think of it like this: you only have 100 RMB in cash (physical RAM), but your credit card gives you 200 RMB of credit (page file space). You can “commit” to spending more than 100 RMB, as long as you make up the difference with the credit card. When the total “Committed” amount exceeds physical RAM + page file size, the system will warn you that “Your computer is low on memory” and may even force‑close some programs. Paged Pool vs. Nonpaged Pool The Windows kernel (the core of the operating system) reserves some memory for its own critical data. This memory is split into two types: Nonpaged Pool: Always stays in physical RAM and never gets moved to the page file. Some critical data (e.g., for handling hardware interrupts) must always be instantly accessible – you cannot wait for it to be read back from the hard drive. Paged Pool: Can be moved to the page file. This holds kernel data that can tolerate a short delay if it is needed. Ordinary users do not need to track the exact values of these pools. But when you see them on Task Manager’s Performance page, just know: “paged” can be moved to disk, “nonpaged” must stay in RAM. 2.9 Hardware Codecs When we introduced PotPlayer in Appendix 7, hardware decoding was mentioned. Here is a bit more detail. Hardware codec: A dedicated circuit inside your GPU (graphics card) that handles video encoding or decoding. This circuit is separate from the streaming processors that run games. Hardware decoding: When playing a video, the GPU uses that dedicated circuit to decode it. The CPU barely works, power consumption is low, heat is minimal, and even high‑bitrate 4K video plays smoothly. Hardware encoding: When recording your screen, streaming, or exporting a video, that same circuit compresses the video. It is fast and has little impact on game performance. Software codec: The CPU does all the work. The CPU can do it, but it is much less efficient than dedicated hardware. Playing 4K video or exporting video this way can max out your CPU, making your computer sluggish and hot. Scenarios you will actually encounter: When recording games with OBS, choose NVENC (for Nvidia GPUs) or QSV (for Intel integrated graphics) – that uses hardware encoding. It has little impact on game frame rates. When you play a high‑bitrate 4K video and see very high CPU usage, the player is not using hardware decoding. Go into the player’s settings and look for “Hardware Decoding” or “DXVA”, then turn it on. In the “Performance” tab of Task Manager, the GPU section often has two small graphs – “Video Encode” and “Video Decode” – showing hardware codec usage. Keep an eye on them. 2.10 Disk Performance (IOPS, MB/s, Mbps) IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second) Measures how well a drive handles “many small, random files”. For example, opening a folder full of small images, loading a game level, or running a virtual machine – in these scenarios, IOPS matters much more than sequential speed. Mechanical hard drive (HDD): several dozen to ~100 IOPS Typical SATA SSD: several thousand to tens of thousands of IOPS A good NVMe SSD: hundreds of thousands or even millions of IOPS This is why installing your operating system on an SSD makes booting and launching software so much faster – not because of sequential read/write speeds, but because IOPS are hundreds or thousands of times higher than on a mechanical drive. MB/s vs. Mbps These two units are often confused, especially when measuring internet speed. MB/s (megabytes per second): The speed you see when copying files. 1 MB/s means transferring 1 megabyte of data per second. Mbps (megabits per second): The speed advertised in broadband plans. For example, a “100 Mbps” plan. The conversion: 1 MB/s = 8 Mbps. So a 100 Mbps connection has a theoretical maximum download speed of 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB/s. Remember: lowercase ‘b’ stands for bit, uppercase ‘B’ stands for byte, and 1 byte = 8 bits. To get the download speed you actually see, divide the advertised Mbps by 8. MB/s vs. IOPS: These are not the same thing. MB/s is “how much data per second”, IOPS is “how many requests per second”. Copying a large movie file stresses MB/s; opening a thousand small images at once stresses IOPS. A good drive should be good at both – but it will also cost more. 2.11 Just Get a Rough Impression Environment variables, the Registry, Group Policy, and the page file – you do not need to change any of them now, and definitely should not mess with them randomly. But “getting a rough impression” matters: Later, if you install something and the command line says “not recognized as an internal or external command” – you will know it might be a PATH problem. Later, if an online tutorial says “edit the Registry” – you will know what that is, and that you should back it up before changing anything. Later, if the system complains that it is “low on memory” – you will know it might be because physical RAM or page file space is running out. Later, if your computer suddenly becomes sluggish and drive C: is full – you will know the page file might be affected. Later, if video playback is choppy or CPU usage is very high – you will know hardware decoding might not be enabled. Later, if a speed test shows a number that does not match the download speed you see – you will remember to divide Mbps by 8. Just knowing roughly what these things are, and which direction to search when something goes wrong, already puts you ahead of most users. Glossary 3.1 Process A process is simply a running program. When you open a browser, a game, or Notepad, the system creates a process for it. Each process has its own memory space, separate from others. When you end a frozen program in Task Manager, you are essentially killing its process. Be careful not to end things that look like system processes (e.g., ), as that might cause problems. 3.2 Thread A process can have multiple threads. Threads are the ones that actually do the work. Think of it this way: a process is a factory, and threads are the workers inside it. A factory can have just one worker (single‑threaded) or many workers working at the same time (multi‑threaded). The advantage of multi‑threading is being able to do several things at once – your browser downloading a file while still rendering a webpage is the work of multiple threads. The CPU usage percentage you see in Task Manager is actually the sum of usage across all threads. A heavy application often runs dozens or even hundreds of threads. 3.3 Handle A handle is an integer number that Windows uses to refer to some resource (an open file, a window, a thread, etc.). When you open a file, the system gives you a handle; every operation on that file (read, write, close) uses that handle. Handle leak: A program forgets to close a handle when it is done with the resource, so the resource remains occupied. The most common symptom: you try to delete a file, and Windows says “The file is in use”, even though you have closed every program that might have opened it. Very likely, some process has a handle that it never closed. You can use tools like Process Explorer or LockHunter to see which process is holding onto the file. 3.4 Quick Reference for More Terms | Term | Simple explanation | |------|---------------------| | API | Application Programming Interface – a contract that lets programs call each other | | BIOS / UEFI | The low‑level system on the motherboard, responsible for booting and initialising hardware | | DLL | Dynamic Link Library – a piece of code that can be shared by multiple programs | | Driver | The “translator” that lets the operating system recognise and control hardware | | GUI | Graphical User Interface – the windows, buttons, and things you click | | CLI | Command‑Line Interface – the black box where you type commands | | Kernel | The core of the operating system – manages hardware, processes, and memory | | RAM | Random Access Memory – loses its data when power is off | | ROM | Read‑Only Memory – usually stores firmware; the user cannot change it | | SDK | Software Development Kit – a collection of tools needed to develop for a specific platform | | Shell | A command‑line interpreter – both CMD and PowerShell are shells | | UUID / GUID | A very long, almost‑guaranteed‑unique identifier, used to label something uniquely |

title: Introduction
content: Chapter Zero: Introduction 0.1 The Appendix and the Main Book Are Different Kinds of Things This book is split into two major parts: the Appendix and the Main Book. Their goals, writing styles, and examples are not the same. 0.1.1 What the Appendix Looks Like The Appendix is everything you just finished reading. Here's what defines it: It teaches you how to do things: how to partition a drive, disable BitLocker, change NTP servers, pick browser extensions. This is hands‑on guidance. It focuses on daily usage: it addresses problems you might actually run into while using your computer – things like "it's frozen" or "I don't know where to change that setting". It uses Windows 11 for examples: all screenshots, commands, and path formats assume you're on Windows 11. Anyone can read it: you don't need to know how to program, or even be sure you want to study CS. As long as you use a computer, some part of the Appendix will be useful to you. The Appendix is meant to be a reference manual you keep within arm's reach. 0.1.2 What the Main Book Looks Like The Main Book is what you're about to read. Here's what defines it: It explains why things work: why can a compiler turn source code into an executable? Why does memory have the stack and the heap? The Appendix doesn't go deep on questions like these; the Main Book does. It walks you through writing code: the Main Book contains a lot of code. You'll need to type it yourself, compile it, modify it, and run it. Just reading along won't help. It uses WSL2 Ubuntu for examples: all commands, compilation instructions, and path formats assume you're working inside Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL2. It's aimed primarily at CS/EE students: if you've already decided on (or are seriously considering) a CS or EE major, the Main Book is written for you. If you choose a different path, the Main Book can still deepen your understanding of how computers work – but you should be aware that it won't always hold your hand. The Main Book's goal is to help you move from "knowing how" to "understanding why". Once you understand the principles, many of the "how‑to" questions answer themselves. 0.2 How I Write the Main Book The Appendix and the Main Book are written differently. I want to make those differences clear upfront so you can read more smoothly. 0.2.1 Very Few Analogies The Appendix uses some analogies – for example, comparing memory vs. disk to a cutting board vs. a refrigerator, or explaining swap space using a kitchen counter. Those analogies work well in the Appendix because its goal is to give you a quick mental picture. The Main Book avoids analogies as much as possible. The reason is simple: An analogy tries to explain something unfamiliar using something you already know. But many concepts in computing don't have real‑world equivalents. A pointer is a pointer – it holds a memory address. A file descriptor is just an integer that points to an entry inside the kernel's table. Forcing an analogy often leads to more confusion than clarity. Eventually, you'll need to get comfortable with these concepts on their own terms. Analogies are training wheels – if you keep using them, you won't move very fast. So the Main Book gets more direct. That doesn't mean deliberately difficult – it just means fewer detours. 0.2.2 There Will Be a Lot of Terminology Every section introduces new terms. There's no way around it – learning any craft requires learning its jargon. The Quick Reference Table at the beginning of each section is designed to help you handle this: Glance at it before you start reading, so you know what the section will cover. When you forget what a term means while reading, flip back to the table. After finishing the section, use it as a review checklist to see whether you've actually remembered the terms. If you run into a term you don't understand, copy it straight into a search engine or an AI assistant – those terms are already the best keywords to search for. Don't expect to remember every term on the first pass. Learning programming and low‑level concepts is a spiral process – you'll encounter these words again and again, and each time you'll remember them a little better. 0.2.3 You Have to Run Things Yourself Every claim in the Main Book can be verified with code or commands. If you only read and never type, you'll end up with a vague impression. That vague impression won't help you one bit when you run into compilation errors, segmentation faults, or link failures. What will help is the muscle memory you build by typing, running, modifying, and debugging examples yourself. So all code examples in the Main Book assume you'll execute them inside your own WSL2 environment. Some examples are deliberately broken – you'll need to read the error messages, understand why they fail, and then fix them. 0.3 How to Read This Book 0.3.1 If You're a New CS/EE Student Read in order. You must complete the validation checklist at the end of each section. If a validation step fails, don't skip it – stop and figure out why. The process of troubleshooting is itself a learning experience. If you encounter a concept that was mentioned in the Appendix (like environment variables, PATH, or swap space), feel free to flip back to the Appendix for a refresher. However, the Appendix's explanations tend toward "rough idea", while the Main Book is more precise – when in doubt, trust the Main Book. 0.3.2 If You're Not Planning to Study CS You can skip some of the very low‑level chapters (like the ones on process scheduling or memory paging later on). But I strongly recommend reading the chapters on compilers, build systems, Git, and debuggers. Those topics aren't tied to any particular major – anyone who does creative work on a computer will benefit from them. 0.3.3 About AI Of course, you're welcome to use AI as a learning aid – but AI cannot replace your own brain. Claude Code can produce beautiful code in ten minutes. You get an application out of it, but that's all. Genuine learning requires your own gradual trial and error. Even if you use agents like Claude Code, I hope you'll read the code they generate and actually understand it. You can ask an AI what a certain term means, how to interpret a piece of syntax, or what might be causing a particular error message. AIs make mistakes. The final judge is what you see when you actually run your code. 0.4 Moving On to Chapter One Ready? Let's begin.

title: WSL2
content: Section 1: WSL2 Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Linux | An operating system kernel – a completely different foundation from Windows | | Distribution | A full system built on top of the Linux kernel, bundled with various software tools – Ubuntu is one example | | Ubuntu | One of the most widely used Linux distributions; all commands in this book are tested on Ubuntu 24.04 | | WSL2 | Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 – a way to run Linux inside Windows | | Virtual Machine | Software that emulates an entire computer, allowing another operating system to run inside it | | Hyper-V | Windows' built-in virtualization technology – both WSL2 and traditional VMs rely on it | | Mirrored Networking | A WSL2 networking mode that gives WSL the same IP address as Windows | | DNS Tunneling | Allows WSL to resolve domain names through Windows, fixing DNS issues in certain network environments | 1.1 Why You Need Linux If you're fortunate enough to attend a decent university – one that doesn't force you to use a fossil like VC6.0 as your IDE – then the lab code for your CS courses (operating systems, computer networks, compilers, parallel computing) will almost always assume a Linux environment. Here's why: The vast majority of servers run Linux. The code you write will eventually be deployed to servers. Developing locally on Linux helps avoid the classic "but it works on my machine" embarrassment. Supercomputing centers run Linux. If you eventually do research, run simulations, or fine‑tune models, you'll SSH into those machines and work from the command line. Open‑source toolchains are built for Linux first. They work most smoothly on Linux, have the richest documentation, and yield the most searchable solutions when you hit a problem. Yes, you could run Linux in a VM on Windows, or go through the extra steps on macOS. But WSL2 provides the lowest barrier to getting a Linux environment on Windows, with the smoothest experience. No separate partitions, no lag inside a VM, no waiting for Linux to boot every time you turn on your machine. WSL2 isn't a traditional VM, yet it still relies on virtualization technology. Let's break down how they relate. 1.2 Installing WSL2 These steps assume you're on Windows 11. Step 1: Turn on the necessary Windows features Open PowerShell or Windows Terminal as Administrator and run: The first command enables WSL. The second enables the Virtual Machine Platform. WSL2 needs virtualization support to run a full Linux kernel. Restart your computer after this step. Step 2: Set WSL2 as the default version After rebooting, run this as Administrator: From now on, any Linux distribution you install will use WSL2 by default. To switch between WSL1 and WSL2 for a specific distribution, use or . Step 3: Install Ubuntu 24.04 In your terminal: Once the installation finishes, launch Ubuntu 24.04 from the Start Menu, or type in your terminal. First launch: You'll be prompted to create a username and password. A few things to keep in mind: Don't use as your username. is the system administrator account – your daily work should be done under your own username. When you type your password, nothing will show on screen (not even asterisks). That's normal. Just type it and hit Enter. Verify the installation: You should see something like: The asterisk marks the default distribution. When you type without any arguments, this is the one you'll enter. 1.3 How WSL2 Differs from a Virtual Machine A common question: "Isn't WSL2 just a virtual machine?" The answer: It uses VM technology (Hyper‑V) under the hood, but it doesn't feel like one. What a traditional VM (like VirtualBox or VMware) does: It emulates a complete set of hardware – CPU, memory, disk, network adapter, graphics card, sound card, USB controller – and then installs a full OS on top of that emulated hardware. That guest OS never touches your real hardware directly; it only sees what the VM software simulates. The result: slow startup, heavy memory consumption, poor graphical performance, and clumsy file sharing. Yes, isolation is strong, but for everyday development, the trade‑off is often too costly. What WSL2 does: WSL2 also runs inside a lightweight virtual machine (based on Hyper‑V), but this VM is special: No full hardware emulation. It only virtualizes the hardware required to run the Linux kernel. Everything else (graphics, audio, USB) goes straight through Windows' drivers. A custom‑built kernel. Microsoft maintains its own Linux kernel, heavily tuned for WSL scenarios – especially file system and network performance. Seamless integration with Windows. You can access WSL's file system directly via . Windows processes and WSL processes can talk to each other. When should you use a traditional VM? You need a full graphical Linux desktop (not just a terminal), direct USB device access, or several completely isolated environments. When should you use WSL2? You need a Linux command line and/or you need to compile code in a Linux environment. 1.4 Configuration File: .wslconfig WSL2's default network settings can be problematic in certain scenarios. The most common pain points: WSL gets an IP address on a different subnet than Windows, so accessing services running inside WSL (like Jupyter or an HTTP server) from other devices on your LAN requires extra port‑forwarding setup. DNS resolution occasionally fails – you can ping an IP address from WSL, but not a domain name. After running for a long time, WSL2 consumes a large amount of memory (Linux likes to use spare RAM for disk caching and doesn't give it back aggressively). A single configuration file can address all of these. In your directory (that's ), create a new file named . Pay attention: the name starts with a dot and has no file extension. Paste the following content: What each setting does: Mirrored network mode. When enabled, WSL gets the exact same IP address as Windows, and all network interfaces are "mirrored" inside WSL. The big win: other devices on your LAN can directly access services running inside WSL without any port‑forwarding tricks. Any port your WSL app binds to will automatically be listened to on the same port by Windows. DNS tunneling. DNS requests from inside WSL are forwarded to Windows, which handles the actual domain resolution. This bypasses all sorts of network quirks that can occur when WSL sends DNS packets directly (for example, DNS hijacking on certain campus networks). With this turned on, operations like , , and become much more reliable. Makes the Windows Firewall apply to WSL traffic. By default, WSL traffic bypasses the Windows Firewall, which can cause network policies (in corporate or campus environments) to block it. Turning this on subjects all WSL inbound and outbound traffic to Windows Firewall rules. Automatically inherits Windows system proxy settings. If you're running a proxy tool on Windows (like Clash or v2ray), command‑line tools inside WSL (curl, apt, git, etc.) will automatically use that proxy – no separate configuration needed inside WSL. Automatic memory reclamation in gradual mode. When WSL2 is idle, the background system will slowly return memory from the Linux kernel back to Windows. The default is . Enabling this prevents WSL from hogging more and more memory over time until you're forced to run to free it. means gentle reclamation that avoids performance hits on running programs. There's also , which is more aggressive but can make file accesses slower the first time after reclamation. How to apply the changes: After editing , you need to fully shut down WSL for the new settings to take effect. Run this in PowerShell: Then restart WSL (open your Ubuntu terminal or just type ). The configuration will be loaded. Verification: After restarting, run inside WSL. You'll see that the network interface configuration has changed. The exact differences depend on your network environment – don't worry too much about the details. 1.5 Section Validation Checklist Go through these checks to confirm your WSL2 environment is ready: Verify the version: should show Ubuntu 24.04 with VERSION set to 2. Confirm network connectivity: Inside your WSL terminal, run . You should see replies. Confirm file system basics: Run . You should see directories like , , . Then run – you should see the contents of your Windows C: drive. If step 2 fails (no ping response), first double‑check that contains and correctly, then run and try again. 1.6 Common Issues Installation tells you "need to update the WSL kernel" Search Microsoft's official site for "WSL2 kernel update package", download and install it, then retry. Ubuntu gets stuck on "Installing..." for a very long time when launching Network issues. Try turning off any proxy tools, or wait for a different time of day. Ubuntu starts slowly after running The first launch rebuilds certain caches – this is normal. The next launch will be faster. Configuration file changes don't take effect Make sure the file is named exactly (not ). Double‑check that it's placed in ( ), not inside WSL. After editing, don't forget to run .
