content: Section 2: Setting Up the Ubuntu Environment Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Compiler | A tool that converts source code into an executable program that the machine can run | | GCC | The GNU Compiler Collection – the most widely used C/C++ compiler on Linux | | Clang | The LLVM project's C/C++ compiler, known for more user‑friendly error messages than GCC | | Interpreter | A program that executes code line by line, without requiring prior compilation to machine code | | pip | Python's package manager – used to install third‑party libraries | | Virtual environment | An isolated Python environment where different projects can use different library versions without conflicts | | venv | Python's built‑in tool for managing virtual environments | | Shell | The command‑line interpreter – you type commands, and it executes them | | Bash | The most common shell program – Ubuntu's default shell | | Meson | A build system used to configure and compile large projects | | Ruby | A programming language that some tools (like Jekyll) depend on | 2.1 Directory Structure – Putting Your Code in the Right Place On Windows, your documents, downloads, and desktop live under . In WSL, the corresponding location is . I recommend creating a dedicated folder under this directory to hold all your coursework and personal code. I usually call mine . You can name it whatever you like, but the rest of this guide will assume as the default. Create a directory: is shorthand for your current user's home directory. The two commands above are equivalent to: From now on, put all your code projects inside . Give each project its own subdirectory. For example: There's a simple reason for this: when you later need to back up, package, or manage your code with Git, you only need to operate on this one folder. It's kept separate from system files, so you won't accidentally delete critical system components, and system updates won't mess with it. 2.2 Compilers – GCC and Clang For C/C++ development on Linux, you have two mainstream compilers: GCC and Clang. Install both – they don't conflict. 2.2.1 Installing GCC GCC is the most established compiler in the Linux ecosystem. Ubuntu doesn't ship it by default, so you need to install it manually: is the C compiler, and is the C++ compiler – they are separate programs, usually installed together. Verify the installation: The first shows the GCC version information, the second shows the G++ version. 2.2.2 Installing Clang Clang is the LLVM project's C/C++ compiler. Compared to GCC, its error messages are generally clearer, more precise, and more beginner‑friendly. Verify: 2.2.3 GCC vs. Clang – A Quick Summary You don't need to understand their deep implementation differences right now. Just keep these three things in mind: The vast majority of code compiles fine with either compiler. Some courses or projects may require a specific one (e.g., operating systems labs sometimes require GCC). Installing both takes little space – use whichever one you need at the time. For everyday assignments, starting with Clang is often a smoother experience because its error messages are easier to decipher. 2.3 Python Environment – pip and venv Ubuntu 24.04 comes with Python 3 pre‑installed. Open a terminal and type to confirm. However, the pre‑installed version usually doesn't include pip (the package manager) and isn't set up with virtual environments by default. You'll need to configure these yourself. 2.3.1 Installing pip Verify: Note that the command is , not . 2.3.2 Why You Need Virtual Environments Python has a particular characteristic: all third‑party libraries installed via pip go into the system‑wide Python directory by default. This leads to a few problems: Project A needs , while Project B needs . Each project requires a different version, but you can only have one installed globally. After installing many libraries, the system Python directory becomes cluttered, and you lose track of which library belongs to which project. Removing a library is risky – you might inadvertently break another project's dependencies. Virtual environments solve this problem. What a virtual environment is: Inside an isolated directory, it creates a copy of the Python interpreter and pip. All libraries you install go into this directory, completely separated from the system Python. Each project gets its own virtual environment, and the libraries inside don't interfere with each other. Here's a way to think about it: the system Python is a shared public kitchen where everyone cooks, using the same utensils and spices – eventually it becomes a mess. A virtual environment is like each person bringing their own portable workbench, with their own ingredients, cleaning up after themselves without disturbing anyone else. 2.3.3 Installing venv Ubuntu packages the module separately – you need to install it manually: Once installed, you can create virtual environments normally. Create a virtual environment: This creates an independent Python environment inside . Activate the virtual environment: After activation, your terminal prompt will show at the beginning. Any library you install with from this point will go only into this virtual environment. Deactivate it: A common practice is to place a folder at the root of each project and activate it by running from that project's root. 2.3.4 One Important Caveat only manages Python libraries. If you need a different version of Python itself (e.g., a project requires Python 3.10, but your system has 3.12), venv won't help. That's a job for tools like – but we'll leave that for another time. 2.4 Bash Basics You're already interacting with Bash every time you open your Ubuntu terminal. Bash is the program that accepts and interprets the commands you type. Below are the most frequently used commands. If you're not yet comfortable with them, follow along and type them out. Each line includes a short comment. 2.4.1 File and Directory Operations 2.4.2 Viewing and Editing Files 2.4.3 Permissions 2.4.4 Wildcards and Auto‑Completion Press the key to auto‑complete commands and file names. For example, type and press – if exists, Bash will expand it to . is a wildcard that matches any string. For instance, lists all files ending with . 2.4.5 Command History Press the Up and Down arrow keys to scroll through previously entered commands. Type to see a full list of your command history. You don't need to memorize these commands – they'll become second nature through regular use. If you forget a specific option, use the flag, e.g., . 2.5 Meson – Installing and Verifying the Build System The Appendix already walked you through installing Meson, but that was mainly to ensure the toolchain existed. We'll verify it again here to make sure your environment is fully set up. Check that Meson is installed: If the command isn't found, install it: Meson itself is a Python program (you could also install it via pip), but using is simpler – dependency resolution is handled by the system package manager. Verify Ninja (Meson's backend build tool): If you decide to use Meson for your projects later, you'll learn the specifics then. For now, just know: generates the build files, and runs the compilation. We'll start using it in Chapter 2. 2.6 Ruby – A Dependency for Certain Tools Not every CS student will need Ruby. However, it becomes unavoidable if you plan to: Build a personal blog with Jekyll (GitHub Pages natively supports Jekyll) Write automation scripts for Chef or Puppet Maintain a Ruby on Rails project (if you take a relevant course or land such an internship) Install it: Verify: You don't need to learn Ruby syntax right now – just have it installed. 2.7 Section Validation Checklist Go through these checks to confirm that all your tools are ready: GCC: should output normally without errors. Clang: should output normally. pip: should output normally. venv: Run , then – you should see the file. Clean up with when done. Meson: should output normally. Ninja: should output normally. Ruby: should output normally. 2.8 Common Issues fails with "Failed to resolve domain names" Network issue. Check if WSL can ping external sites. If your is set up correctly and it still fails, try temporarily disabling your proxy tool. Packages installed via are not found in the command line Pip installs executables under . If this directory isn't in your PATH, run to add it. Meson and Ninja versions are too old The versions shipped with Ubuntu 24.04 are generally sufficient. If a project later requires a newer version, you can install via pip: . Then make sure appears earlier in your PATH than the system directory (so it takes precedence).

title: Tittle-tattle
content: The Bumpy Road to DeepFDM – A Personal Chronicle I'm the author of this guide. To teach C++ syntax and show how to bridge theory with engineering practice, I designed a 2D heat‑conduction inversion experiment based on the DeepFDM paper. Little did I know that this seemingly simple example would put me through a week of failed runs, frustration, and sudden epiphanies – and finally, it worked. Not perfectly, but it's precisely that imperfection that made the journey so meaningful. I want to write down this mental odyssey – partly as a reflection for myself, and partly in the hope that it might offer some comfort to others struggling with scientific computing. I. Initial Ambition – Recovering the Diffusivity Field with Finite‑Difference Perturbation My task was straightforward: given a rectangular heat sink with an unknown thermal diffusivity field α(x,y), but with access to the final temperature field after a certain time, use the finite‑difference perturbation method – no automatic differentiation, no third‑party frameworks – to estimate the gradient by numerical perturbations, and then recover the entire α field via gradient descent. I built the code following the classic textbook framework: A fixed 3×3 Laplacian kernel, upwind advection, and explicit Euler time marching. Perturb each grid point α[i][j] by a tiny ε = 1e-5, run a full forward simulation, and approximate the gradient with central differences. Use MSE as the loss function and iterate to update α. The ground‑truth α field was set to high conductivity on the left (copper, α=0.8), with a vertical air gap (α=0.1) on the right. The heat source was placed on the left (x=0.3, y=0.25) to mimic chip heating. I hit Enter with high hopes, expecting the inversion to magically "discover" that air gap. II. The First Blow – The α Field Refused to Budge The first run left me stunned: the loss did decrease, but the α field barely moved from the initial guess of 0.5 – its maximum crept up slightly, and its minimum barely twitched. In other words, the algorithm only learned to "raise the overall conductivity" to lower the loss, completely failing to recover the low‑conductivity channel on the right. I immediately tried the usual tuning tricks: Increase the perturbation step ε to 0.01 to make gradients more visible. Raise the learning rate to 5.0, then even to 200 – at which point α slammed straight into the boundary at 1.0. Introduce RMSprop for adaptive learning rates to balance the update magnitudes across regions. Add spatial smoothing regularisation to force adjacent pixels to change together. None of them worked. Gradient diagnostics revealed that at a point inside the air gap (12,9), the raw gradient was negative – meaning increasing α at that point would lower the loss. In other words, the algorithm thought that filling the air gap with copper would make the predicted temperature field match the target better! III. Lost in the Dark – A Tug‑of‑War with the Gradient Sign I added more and more print statements, plotted 1D slices of the loss surface, and repeatedly checked the forward solver. Was the advection term misbehaving? Set to zero. Source amplitude too weak? Bumped to 500. Simulation steps too few? Extended to 8000. I even widened the air gap to cover the entire right half – still no luck. The strangest part: when I moved the air gap to the left and the heat source there too, the gradient suddenly turned positive – lowering α finally reduced the loss. That was the moment it hit me: the problem wasn't the optimizer – it was the physical identifiability of the problem itself. The essence of inversion is: can the observed temperature field uniquely determine the parameters? In my original setup, the heat source was on the left and the air gap on the right. The heat generated on the left diffused to the right, but the air gap's obstruction to the heat flow was extremely weak – because it was far downstream from the source, with very little temperature difference across it. In other words, changing the air gap's diffusivity had a much smaller effect on the temperature field than changing the background diffusivity near the heat source. Therefore, the global minimum of the loss function was not the true parameter field, but a configuration where "everything has high conductivity". No matter how I optimised, gradient descent faithfully marched towards that wrong minimum. This is the famous "ill‑posedness" of inverse problems. Although the soul of DeepFDM is to embed physics through fixed numerical stencils, if the observational data itself is insensitive to the parameters, even a deity couldn't save it. IV. Light at the End of the Tunnel – Moving the Low‑Conductivity Zone to the Same Side as the Source After realising this, I decisively changed the ground‑truth configuration: place the air gap on the left (x<0.5), keep the heat source inside it, and make the right side pure copper. Now the air gap acted like a blanket wrapped around the heat source – heat could hardly escape, so the temperature on the left rose significantly. With the initial guess α=0.5, heat would dissipate too quickly, leaving the left side too cold. To match the target high temperatures, the algorithm had to lower α there. This time the gradient was positive, and gradient descent naturally drove α downward. To further boost sensitivity, I also adopted a multi‑time observation loss – recording temperature snapshots every 500 steps instead of only the final steady state. This amplified the air gap's blocking effect during early diffusion, giving the inversion a much stronger signal. I ran it again, and a miracle happened: after just 20 iterations, the left‑side α dropped from 0.5 to 0.158; by iteration 30, it was already approaching 0.103, while the right side rose to about 0.8. The loss plummeted, and the 2D contour plot clearly showed a sharp vertical line – low on the left, high on the right. I let out a long breath – this was the DeepFDM I had been hoping for. V. Polishing the Edges – From Oscillation to Smooth Convergence However, after nearing the true values, the gradients began to oscillate violently – positive and negative values alternating, occasionally spiking to astronomical numbers like 1e21. What was going on? This is, in fact, the inherent numerical noise of the finite‑difference perturbation method. When the parameters are already close to the optimum, the loss surface becomes extremely flat, and the loss difference caused by perturbations drowns in round‑off errors – the gradient estimate becomes almost random. Coupled with RMSprop's accumulated history, which can lag behind, occasionally an anomalous update would slip through. For the sake of a smooth teaching demonstration, I applied three tweaks: Reduced the learning rate from 0.01 to 0.002 to tame the step size. Added gradient clipping (element‑wise clamp to [-1,1]) after RMSprop normalisation, completely eliminating extreme gradients. Redirected all output to log files for easier post‑mortem analysis. Finally, the results of 200 iterations were ready. I eagerly opened – and froze. VI. The Real Outcome – An "Insulating Bubble", Not a Perfect Global Recovery The data told a clear story: the inferred diffusivity field was not a simple left‑low/right‑high step. Near the heat source (x≈0.3, y≈0.25), a low‑value region had indeed formed, bottoming out at 0.107 – like an insulating bubble wrapping around the source. Most of the right region had risen to around 0.85, close to the true copper value. However, the background region on the left, far from the source, stubbornly remained around 0.5 – nowhere near the expected 0.1. The boundary pixels barely moved from their initial 0.5 guess. This was far from the "entire left half low‑conductivity" I had envisioned. At first I was disappointed, but then it struck me – this imperfect recovery is far more valuable than a perfect one. Why did this happen? Because in the multi‑time loss, changes in α near the heat source have a vastly larger impact on the temperature field than changes in the distant background. The gradients concentrated around the source, and the optimiser naturally prioritised building an insulating shell right there to raise the temperature and match the target. As for the far‑left pixels, whether α was 0.1 or 0.8 made almost no difference to the temperature distribution – their gradients were nearly zero, so they remained almost untouched within a finite number of iterations. The algorithm had learned not the global distribution I had designed, but a local effective model – an insulating bubble around the heat source. VII. Reflection – Imperfection Is the Truest Teacher If the algorithm had perfectly recovered my checkerboard pattern, that would have been the unreal part. It is precisely this flawed result that allowed me to ask a cascade of deeper questions: Why did the inversion only lower α near the heat source? How can we design the observation scheme – say, adding multiple heat sources, changing boundary conditions, or using full temporal data – to improve global identifiability? Could I introduce structural priors (like total variation regularisation) to encourage piecewise‑constant solutions and recover the sharp left‑right regions? This project taught me profoundly that the soul of DeepFDM – or any physics‑informed inversion method – does not lie in fixed stencils or adaptive learning rates. It lies in how much physical insight we actually inject into the loss function, and whether we honestly confront the inherent ill‑posedness of inverse problems. An imperfect inversion often carries more weight than a perfectly tuned one – because it reveals the most genuine, fragile, and fascinating side of scientific computing.

title: MathematicalFoundations
content:
Section 1: Mathematical Foundations Sections 1 and 2 of Chapter 2 are the two toughest sections in the entire chapter – they may require knowledge from sophomore to junior year, especially in math. Still, I hope readers will give them a try; I think my explanations are fairly clear. It's a lot like the C and D reading passages in English exams – you probably won't understand all the terminology, but you can roughly get the gist. Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Partial derivative | The derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable, holding the others fixed | | Gradient | A vector composed of all partial derivatives, pointing in the direction of steepest ascent | | Laplace operator (Δ) | The sum of second partial derivatives in all spatial directions; measures deviation from the local average | | Thermal diffusivity (α) | A physical parameter describing a material's ability to conduct heat—larger values mean faster heat spreading | | Heat equation | A partial differential equation that describes how temperature evolves over time and space | | Finite difference method | Approximates derivatives using differences between discrete grid points, allowing computers to solve PDEs | | Explicit Euler | The simplest time‑stepping method—computes the next state directly from the current state | | CFL condition | A numerical stability constraint: the time step must not exceed a threshold determined by the spatial step size and diffusivity | | Forward problem | Given all parameters and initial conditions, solving for the temperature field | | Inverse problem | Inferring unknown parameters (thermal diffusivity) from observed temperature data | | Loss function | A metric that quantifies the mismatch between predicted and observed temperatures—smaller is better | | Gradient descent | Adjusts parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss function, reducing the loss iteratively | | Finite‑difference gradient | Approximates the gradient using two forward simulations (perturbing the parameter by ±ε), eliminating the need for analytic derivatives | | RMSprop | An improved gradient‑descent algorithm that adapts the learning rate per parameter, making training more stable | | Multi‑time loss | Compares temperatures at multiple intermediate time steps—not just the final one—improving inversion stability | | Clipping | Restricts parameters to physically reasonable bounds (e.g., α must be positive and not too large) | 1.1 From Single‑Variable to Multivariable Functions The functions studied in high‑school mathematics take the form \(y = f(x)\)—a single independent variable, with the dependent variable changing solely with that one input. In heat‑transfer problems, however, temperature \(T\) depends simultaneously on spatial position \((x, y)\) and time \(t\). We therefore need the concept of a multivariable function: \(T = T(x, y, t)\). For such functions, the rate of change is no longer unique—it may differ depending on which direction you look. This brings us to the definition of the partial derivative: the rate of change of the function with respect to one variable, while keeping all other independent variables fixed. Formal definition of the partial derivative: \[  rac{\partial T}{\partial x} = \lim{\Delta x 	o 0}  rac{T(x + \Delta x, y, t) - T(x, y, t)}{\Delta x} \] The symbol \(\partial\) (read as "partial") distinguishes partial derivatives from ordinary derivatives of single‑variable functions, which use the symbol \(d\). This expression gives the instantaneous rate of change of temperature in the \(x\)-direction, with \(y\) and \(t\) treated as constants. Physical meaning of first‑order partial derivatives: \( rac{\partial T}{\partial x}\): the temperature gradient in the \(x\)-direction (slope) \( rac{\partial T}{\partial y}\): the temperature gradient in the \(y\)-direction \( rac{\partial T}{\partial t}\): the rate at which temperature changes over time In the actual program, since computers cannot perform limiting operations, partial derivatives are approximated using finite differences (see Section 1.6) as incremental ratios. 1.2 Second‑Order Partial Derivatives and the Laplace Operator Taking the partial derivative of a partial derivative gives a second‑order partial derivative, for example: \[  rac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} =  rac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( rac{\partial T}{\partial x}ight) \] A second‑order partial derivative measures the curvature (concavity/convexity) of the function, rather than its slope. In physics, the spatial sum of second‑order partial derivatives reflects how much a given point deviates from its surroundings. The Laplace operator (Laplacian) is defined as the sum of second‑order partial derivatives in all spatial directions: \[ 
abla^2 T =  rac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 T}{\partial y^2} \] The symbol \(
abla^2\) (read as "Laplacian") is a compact operator notation. Physically, the Laplacian tells us whether a point is hotter or cooler than its immediate neighbourhood: if a point is hotter than its surroundings, then \(
abla^2 T 0\), and heat flows inward. This mechanism will be discretised into an explicit arithmetic expression in Section 1.6. 1.3 Domain and Grid Discretisation Let the two‑dimensional bounded rectangular domain be \(\Omega = [0, Lx] 	imes [0, Ly]\), with \(Lx = 1.0\) (metres) and \(Ly = 0.5\) (metres). The continuous scalar field \(T(x, y, t)\) defined on \(\Omega\) represents the temperature distribution at time \(t\). Digital computers can only handle a finite number of discrete values, so the continuous domain must be partitioned into a grid. This program uses a uniform structured grid, with spatial step sizes defined as: \[ \Delta x =  rac{Lx}{Nx - 1}, \quad \Delta y =  rac{Ly}{Ny - 1} \] where \(Nx = 40\) and \(Ny = 20\). The grid point coordinates satisfy: \[ xi = i \cdot \Delta x, \quad i \in \{0, 1, \dots, Nx - 1\} \] \[ yj = j \cdot \Delta y, \quad j \in \{0, 1, \dots, Ny - 1\} \] The values of the physical quantity \(T\) on the discrete grid are denoted by \(T{i,j}^{(n)}\), where the subscripts \((i, j)\) indicate spatial location and the superscript \(n\) indicates the time level. This notation transforms the continuous field into a sequence of two‑dimensional arrays that can be stored in computer memory. In the program, this corresponds to the class, where the method accesses the discrete value corresponding to the physical coordinates \((xi, yj)\). 1.4 Defining the Partial Differential Equation The physical process solved by this program is governed by the following inhomogeneous linear partial differential equation (PDE): \[  rac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha(x, y) \left(  rac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 T}{\partial y^2} ight) - vx  rac{\partial T}{\partial x} - vy  rac{\partial T}{\partial y} + S(x, y) 	ag{1} \] The key distinction between a PDE and an ordinary differential equation is that the unknown function \(T\) depends on multiple independent variables, and the equation contains partial derivatives. Each term in equation (1) corresponds to a specific physical mechanism. Let's break them down: Transient term \( rac{\partial T}{\partial t}\): the local rate of temperature change over time. If this term vanishes, the system is at steady state (temperature no longer changes with time). Diffusion term \(\alpha 
abla^2 T\): the spontaneous conduction of heat from hot regions to cold regions. The coefficient \(\alpha(x, y)\) is the thermal diffusivity (units: m²/s), a spatially distributed physical parameter. The magnitude of this term depends on the local curvature of the field—greater curvature means stronger heat flow. Advection (convection) term \(-vx  rac{\partial T}{\partial x} - vy  rac{\partial T}{\partial y}\): the transport of heat by fluid flow. In this program, we set \(vx = 0\) and \(vy = 0\) (pure diffusion, no advection), but the code retains the general structure for future extensions. Source term \(S(x, y)\): an external volumetric heat source. In this program, it is defined as a Gaussian function centred at \((0.3, 0.25)\), with amplitude \(500.0\) and standard deviation \(0.05\), modelling a localised heating element. A well‑posed solution to equation (1) also requires boundary conditions. This program uses homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions: \[ T(x, y, t) ig|{\partial \Omega} = 0, \quad  orall t \ge 0 \] That is, the temperature on the domain boundary is held at zero at all times. The boundary conditions provide the surrounding‑environment information needed to solve the PDE. 1.5 Finite‑Difference Discretisation To transform equation (1) into an iterative computation that a computer can execute, we must replace the partial derivative symbols with algebraic expressions. The core idea of the finite‑difference method is to approximate derivatives using the values of the function at discrete grid points, based on Taylor expansion. 1.5.1 Difference Approximations for First‑Order Derivatives For a function \(f(x)\), forward and backward differences are defined using values at a point and its right‑ or left‑neighbour: Forward difference (forward Euler approximation): \[ f'(x) \approx  rac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} \] Backward difference: \[ f'(x) \approx  rac{f(x) - f(x - h)}{h} \] where \(h\) is the step size. In this program, the advection terms use upwind differencing, which chooses between the two schemes based on the direction of the velocity, to maintain numerical stability. Upwind decision rule: If \(vx \ge 0\) (flow from left to right), use backward differencing: \( rac{\partial T}{\partial x} \approx  rac{T{i,j} - T{i-1,j}}{\Delta x}\) If \(vx 0\) is a small positive number (set to \(0.01\) in this program). The implementation workflow is: Make a copy of the current \(\alpha\) field. Increase the value at grid point \((i, j)\) by \(\varepsilon\), leaving all other points unchanged. Run a full forward simulation (8000 steps), record the temperatures at the specified times, and compute the multi‑time loss \(L{plus}\). Decrease the value at that point by \(\varepsilon\) (equivalent to subtracting \(\varepsilon\) from the original value), run the forward simulation, and compute the loss \(L{minus}\). Approximate the partial derivative using equation (7). Restore the original value and move to the next grid point. Computational complexity: a single gradient evaluation requires \(2 	imes Nx 	imes Ny\) full forward simulations. With \(Nx 	imes Ny = 800\) in this program, that's 1600 forward simulations per gradient, each running 8000 time steps, totalling 12.8 million grid updates. This is the fundamental reason the program uses OpenMP parallelism. The central‑difference scheme has a truncation error of \(O(\varepsilon^2)\), which is better than forward differencing (error \(O(\varepsilon)\)). The choice of \(\varepsilon\) involves a trade‑off between truncation error (larger \(\varepsilon\) worsens it) and rounding error (smaller \(\varepsilon\) suffers from floating‑point precision loss). 1.11 RMSprop: Adaptive Learning Rates During gradient descent, the magnitudes of gradients for different parameters can vary enormously. For example, grid points near the heat source are more sensitive to temperature changes and thus have larger gradients, while points farther away have smaller gradients. Using a single global learning rate can cause parameters with large gradients to oscillate and those with small gradients to converge slowly. RMSprop (Root Mean Square Propagation) maintains a moving average of the squared gradient history for each parameter, allowing it to adjust the learning rate individually: \[ s{i,j}^{(k)} = ho \cdot s{i,j}^{(k-1)} + (1 - ho) \cdot \left(  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alpha{i,j}} ight)^2 \] \[ \alpha{i,j}^{(k+1)} = \alpha{i,j}^{(k)} -  rac{\eta}{\sqrt{s{i,j}^{(k)} + \delta}} \cdot  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alpha{i,j}} \] where: \(ho\) is the decay rate (set to 0.9 in this program), controlling how quickly past information is forgotten \(\delta\) is a small constant (set to \(10^{-6}\)) to prevent division by zero Each parameter's learning rate is normalised by \(s\): parameters with large gradients get automatically reduced effective learning rates, while those with small gradients get increased rates This stabilises training and accelerates convergence. 1.12 Physical Constraints and Parameter Projection Thermal diffusivity \(\alpha\) has a clear physical meaning: its units are m²/s, and for real materials it must be positive. Furthermore, the stability condition for the numerical scheme (Section 1.6) imposes an upper bound on \(\alpha\)—otherwise \(\Delta t{crit}\) becomes too small and the computational cost becomes prohibitive. Therefore, after each gradient update, we apply clipping**: \[ \alpha{i,j} \leftarrow \min\left(\alpha{\max}, \max(\alpha{\min}, \alpha{i,j})ight) \] In this program, we set \(\alpha{\min} = 0.001\) (to prevent numerical singularities) and \(\alpha_{\max} = 1.0\) (to keep the CFL condition manageable). This projection confines the parameters to a physically feasible compact convex set, ensuring both numerical stability and physical plausibility. 1.13 Mathematical‑to‑Code Cross‑Reference To directly connect the mathematical concepts above to the actual program code, the table below maps the main mathematical objects to their implementation locations in . | Mathematical Concept | Corresponding Code Location | | :--- | :--- | | Partial derivatives (upwind differencing) | , inside | | Laplacian (five‑point stencil) | inside | | Explicit Euler update | | | CFL condition calculation | inside | | Multi‑time loss function | and the averaging in | | Finite‑difference gradient | The double loops and / inside | | RMSprop state | and its update formula | | Parameter projection | | Suggestions for Further Study The material above covers all the mathematical tools that this program relies on. I recommend reading the code alongside the text in the following order: Find the grid parameter definitions ( , , , ) in and relate them to Section 1.3's discretisation. Find the computations of , , and inside and verify the difference schemes against Section 1.5. Find the double loop for gradient computation and the calls to inside , and connect them to Section 1.10's perturbation method. Find the update of and the parameter‑update formula, and relate them to Section 1.11 on RMSprop. Find the call and relate it to Section 1.12's projection operation. Once you understand these mathematical foundations, you'll be able to independently adjust the equation parameters, modify the grid resolution, or even replace the PDE with a different one for your own experiments.

content: Section 2: Program Architecture and Code Overview Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Forward solver (HeatSolver) | The module responsible for advancing the temperature field forward in time given the parameters – the "simulator" | | Inverse optimizer (InverseOptimizer) | The module responsible for inferring unknown parameters from observed data – the "learner" | | Grid container (Grid2D) | The data structure that stores 2D physical quantities (temperature, diffusivity, heat source) | | Row‑major storage | 2D data stored contiguously in memory row by row – C/C++'s default layout | | Explicit Euler | A forward time‑stepping method where new values are computed entirely from old values without solving equations | | Forward simulation | The process of iterating from an initial temperature to obtain the final temperature field | | Perturbation method | A technique that estimates gradients by slightly tweaking parameters and observing how the loss changes | | RMSprop | An adaptive learning‑rate optimisation algorithm that gives each parameter its own update step size | | Gradient clipping | Restricting gradients to the [-1, 1] range to prevent excessively large single updates that cause oscillations | | Multi‑time loss | Compares predicted and observed temperatures at multiple intermediate time instants simultaneously, improving stability | | Physical projection | Forcing updated parameters back into physically reasonable lower and upper bounds | | OpenMP | A shared‑memory parallel programming standard – with a few directives, it distributes loops across multiple CPU cores | | Data race | An indeterminate result caused by multiple threads reading and writing the same memory location concurrently | | Load balancing | Distributing roughly equal workloads across threads so no core sits idle while others are overloaded | 2.1 Overall Program Structure The core design of follows the DeepFDM philosophy: encode the laws of physics (the heat equation) directly into the program's computational graph, rather than using a generic neural network to "black‑box fit" the data. The entire program is organised into three layers: Data layer ( ): manages all grid data, handling memory layout and boundary conditions. Physics layer ( ): implements forward simulation – given parameters, compute the temperature. Learning layer ( ): implements inverse training – given observed temperatures, infer the parameters backward. The function acts as the overall conductor, sequentially: constructing the true parameters → generating observed data → initialising a guess → training in a loop → outputting results. Why this design: both the forward pass (generating data) and the inverse pass (learning parameters) share the same . This ensures that the simulation logic used during training is exactly the same as the one used to generate the observations. If they differed, the inferred parameters might only be optimal for a "wrong simulator" rather than representing true physical parameters. This is the foundation of DeepFDM's interpretability: the program learns the coefficients of the physical equation, not black‑box weights. 2.2 The Grid2D Class – Data Storage and Memory Layout is the lowest‑level data container. It stores 2D physical quantities (temperature, diffusivity, source) in a 1D vector and provides access via coordinates. Design rationale: Why store 2D data in a 1D vector: In C++, is intuitive, but each row is a separately allocated memory block – rows are not necessarily contiguous in memory. Traversing such a structure causes frequent cache misses, significantly hurting performance. A 1D vector guarantees that all data is stored contiguously. When accessing , adjacent columns in the same row are right next to each other in physical memory. Why the index formula is (row‑major): C/C++ multidimensional arrays use row‑major layout by default. When the inner loop traverses (columns), the address stride is exactly 1, which is the most cache‑friendly access pattern for CPU prefetching. If we used (column‑major), traversing in the inner loop would jump by each time, drastically reducing cache efficiency. All double loops in this program are , with as the inner loop – this is deliberately tailored to the row‑major layout. Why boundary handling is necessary: The Laplacian (see Section 1.5) requires access to the four neighbours of the centre point. If the centre point lies on the boundary, one of its neighbours would fall outside the grid. ensures that boundary values always exist and are known, so the interior computation can be handled uniformly without having to check boundary conditions inside every call. This both simplifies the code and improves performance. 2.3 The HeatSolver Class – The Forward Physics Engine encapsulates all forward‑simulation logic: discretisation schemes, time‑step management, and loss computation. Design rationale: Why copy on every : The explicit Euler scheme is defined as: \(T^{n+1}\) is computed entirely from \(T^n\). If we modified in place, by the time we compute point , its left neighbour might already have been updated to \(T^{n+1}\), while its right neighbour is still \(T^n\). The Laplacian would then mix values from different time levels, becoming "semi‑implicit semi‑explicit" – mathematically no longer equivalent to the original equation. The deep copy ensures that all computations are based on the same old time level, and writes are only committed after the entire update is complete. This is the baseline correctness requirement for explicit schemes. Why boundaries are set outside the loop: The loop only traverses interior points from to and to . Boundary points are not updated, but they might retain non‑zero values from previous steps. forces them to zero at every time step, ensuring that the Dirichlet boundary condition is exactly satisfied at every time level. Omitting this would allow boundary errors to diffuse inward and contaminate the entire temperature field. Why iterates over the 1D vector rather than 2D: 1D traversal has the advantage of contiguous memory. For 800 points, a 2D double loop would perform a multiplication for each access; 1D traversal is just with auto‑incrementing addresses. The compiler can also auto‑vectorise the loop (SIMD), computing the squares of multiple values with a single CPU instruction. This is a subtle but cumulatively significant optimisation. 2.4 The InverseOptimizer Class – The Inverse Learning Engine is the "brain" of the inverse training. It manages the state of the optimisation algorithm (RMSprop's accumulated squared gradients) and performs both gradient computation and parameter updates. Design rationale: Why use a pointer rather than holding a directly: is stateful (its changes with the time step), and gradient computation during inversion requires multiple threads to run forward simulations independently (see Section 2.5). If held a single instance, multiple threads sharing it would interfere with each other. Using a pointer to a "template" allows each thread to construct its own local solver by copying from it – no conflicts. This also reflects the design principle of "separation of data and operations": only handles optimisation logic; it does not bind to a particular solver instance. Lazy initialisation of the RMSprop state : The first time is called, – at that point memory is allocated and zero‑filled. This allows us to construct without knowing the grid size upfront; it automatically adapts to 's dimensions when runs. This keeps the constructor parameter list short and makes the code more flexible. Why clip gradients to [-1, 1]: The finite‑difference gradient (see Section 1.10) can be abnormally small (around \(10^{-5}\)) in regions far from the heat source, and abnormally large (around \(10^0\)) near the source. While RMSprop balances these magnitude differences, occasional numerical noise can produce an outlier gradient at a single point – say \(10^3\) – which would drive that point's from 0.5 all the way to 0.001 or 1.0 in one step, destabilising the entire training process. Clipping acts as a safety net. Experience shows that [-1, 1] works well for this problem. 2.5 Parallelisation Strategy – Computing Gradients with OpenMP Gradient computation is the computational bottleneck – a single full gradient requires 1600 forward simulations. Using OpenMP to distribute the 800 grid‑point perturbation calculations across all available CPU cores is what enables the program to complete training within a minute or two. Design rationale: Why create independent and instances per thread: If multiple threads shared the same or , one thread might be modifying inside while another thread reads it for loss computation – a classic data race. Even if we protected it with mutual‑exclusion locks, parallel execution would degrade to serial (threads constantly waiting for the lock). By giving each thread its own copies, all reads and writes occur in thread‑local memory, requiring no synchronisation overhead – true "each computes independently, then aggregate". What does: By default, only parallelises the outermost loop. With 20 values distributed across 8 threads, each thread gets roughly 2.5 s – meaning the inner 40 s are processed serially. flattens the double loop into 800 independent iterations and distributes them evenly across threads. This makes better use of CPU cores and prevents some threads from becoming bottlenecks due to uneven workload distribution across . Why use rather than the default : scheduling divides iterations evenly at compile time. But the computational cost of each grid point isn't exactly the same – though the workload is identical, system scheduling may interrupt a thread at runtime. scheduling allows threads to pick up new iterations as they finish ("the ones that finish early do more"), achieving runtime load balancing. While dynamic scheduling has a small overhead, it is negligible compared to the heavy computation (8000 time steps per simulation), and the benefit of balanced load is significant. Why is necessary: Inside the parallel loop, is the initial state for the current training step. Without a backup, when the first thread perturbs point , it modifies . Immediately after, when the second thread computes the gradient at point , the used in already has perturbed – no longer in its baseline state. This violates the assumption that "only the target point changes while all others remain fixed", producing an incorrect gradient direction. preserves a clean baseline, and every perturbation is restored from it, ensuring that each point's gradient is independent and correct. 2.6 Multi‑Time Loss and Training Monitoring This program uses a "multi‑time loss" – instead of comparing only the final temperature, it compares the temperatures at 16 equally spaced recording instants during the forward simulation. Design rationale: Why compare at multiple instants rather than just the final time: The heat equation is diffusive – early‑time temperature fields mainly reflect local diffusion around the heat source, while late‑time fields reflect the overall average characteristics of the entire domain. If we compared only the final state, the inverse problem could be ill‑posed: many different distributions might produce similar final temperatures, even if they differ significantly at intermediate times. The multi‑time loss provides the optimiser with "supervisory signals along the time dimension", forcing the predicted evolution trajectory to match the observations at every stage. This greatly reduces the non‑uniqueness of the inversion. That is why the program recorded 16 instants when generating the observations, rather than just the final step. Monitoring information in the training logs: Why output : Point lies in the left‑half region (inside the low‑conductivity channel, roughly at , ). Monitoring the gradient at this specific point gives a direct visual indication of how the low‑conductivity region evolves during inversion. In a normal training run, this gradient is initially large (because the point is relatively close to the heat source) and gradually shrinks to zero (as the parameter approaches its true value). If the gradient remains large, the learning rate may be too small; if it oscillates, the learning rate may be too large. This monitor helps us diagnose optimisation health quickly during training. What means in the loss report: Every iteration reports the current value of and . From , you can see starting at 0.5, gradually dropping to about 0.108, eventually approaching the true value of 0.1. This dynamic directly reflects the convergence trend of the inversion, and is a direct demonstration of DeepFDM's interpretability – every number we track has a clear physical meaning (a diffusion coefficient), not an abstract network weight. 2.7 Section Code Structure Overview | Module | Line Range | Core Responsibility | Key Design Decisions | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | | lines 30–65 | Data storage and boundary management | Row‑major 1D vector; forces zero on edges | | | lines 70–130 | Forward simulation and loss computation | Explicit Euler; upwind differencing; deep copy of | | | lines 170–190 | Single forward pass + multi‑time loss aggregation | Returns average MSE across multiple recorded instants | | | lines 140–260 | Gradient computation and parameter update | Central‑difference perturbation; RMSprop; gradient clipping | | | lines 300–450 | Orchestration and I/O | Generate ground truth → train → output CSV | Suggestions for Further Study Read through first to grasp the overall flow: generate data → initialise → train → output. Dive into and understand how the two‑loop gradient computation is split using OpenMP. Watch the loss drop from to in , and track as it converges from 0.5 to 0.108 – this gives an intuitive feel for how gradient descent works. Compare and : the left region has been recovered from roughly 0.1 to roughly 0.1, and the right region stays at about 0.8 – exactly the core result DeepFDM aims to demonstrate: a physics‑encoded model can accurately recover parameters that have clear physical meaning.

title: CppSyntax
content: Section 3: A Beginner's Guide to C++ Syntax (Based on This Project) Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Header file ( ) | Tells the compiler which pre‑existing library features you need – like telling the storekeeper which tools you want to borrow | | Namespace ( ) | The "surname" of the standard library, used to distinguish functions that have the same name from different sources | | Pre‑increment ( ) | Increments first, then uses the incremented value as the result of the expression | | Post‑increment ( ) | Uses the old value of as the result of the expression, then increments | | Row‑major storage | A 2D array stored in memory row by row, contiguously | | Cache hit rate | The probability that the CPU finds the data it needs in the high‑speed cache – higher means faster programs | | Ternary operator ( ) | A shorthand if‑else that returns one of two values based on a condition, all in one line | | Reference ( ) | An alias for a variable – operating on the reference affects the original, avoiding copies | | Pointer ( ) | A variable that stores a memory address, allowing indirect access and modification of the original object | | Dereference ( ) | Retrieves the object that the pointer points to | | Doxygen | A tool that automatically generates API documentation from specially formatted comments | | OpenMP | A set of compiler directives – with a few commented lines, you can distribute loops across multiple CPU cores | | Compiler optimisation ( ) | The compiler automatically improves the machine instructions of your code, making it run faster without changing the result | | Pass by reference ( ) | The function operates directly on the original object, rather than making a copy | | qualifier | Tells the compiler "this variable / parameter must not be modified" – helps catch bugs early | | | A compiler directive that tells the compiler to enable certain features or optimisations | Prelude: A Quick C++ Syntax Primer Note: This section lists only the C++ syntax essentials you must know to understand this project. It is not a complete C++ tutorial. If you are a complete beginner, I suggest you type out the examples in this section first to get a feel for "what C++ code looks like". The Simplest C++ Program (Hello World) Breakdown: : brings in someone else's toolbox (the standard library). is the "input‑output stream" library. : the program's front door – the operating system calls this first. means this function must eventually return an integer. : standard output – think of it as "the screen". is the arrow that "pushes things onto the screen". : tells the system "I'm done, everything is fine". A non‑zero value indicates an error. Variables and Basic Data Types Every piece of data used in a program must first be declared with a type. This project mainly uses the following three: Note: because we are computing temperatures as decimals, appears most frequently in this project. Arrays and Loops (Extremely Important) In C++, a group of data of the same type can be stored in an array. This project uses (a dynamic array), but the access style is similar: Understanding : – set up a counter starting at 0. – continue as long as is less than 3 (because 0, 1, 2 are exactly three elements; stop when it reaches 3). – after each loop iteration, add 1 to . Here simply means "make become ". Conditional Programs often need to choose between two alternatives based on a condition. This project uses such logic to decide the direction of the wind speed: Defining and Calling Functions (Methods) Packaging repeated logic into a "processing unit" is what functions are for. Classes and Objects A class is like a blueprint; an object is the actual "thing" built from that blueprint. In this project, is a blueprint used to create the actual "2D grid" objects. References ( ) – No Copy, Work on the Original This is the syntax that beginners most often overlook, but it is heavily used in this project. Let's start with a wrong example: With , the function receives a reference (an alias) to the original, so modifications affect the original: Why references are used extensively in this project: A object holds 800 values (about 6.4 KB). If a function parameter does not use , every call makes a copy of those 6.4 KB. In gradient computation, is called 1600 times – needless copying would waste a huge amount of time. With , the function operates directly on the original object – zero copy overhead. Const reference ( ): tells the compiler "this function guarantees it will not modify this object". If you accidentally write a modification, compilation fails. This gives us both data safety and the efficiency of references. Pointers ( ) – Variables That Store Addresses Pointers are C/C++'s "hardcore" feature. A pointer is itself a variable, but it stores a memory address – that is, "where another variable lives". References vs. pointers – how this project chooses: | Feature | Reference ( ) | Pointer ( ) | |---------|----------------|---------------| | Can be null? | No, must bind to a valid object | Yes, can be | | Can be rebound? | No, bound for life | Yes, can point to different objects | | Access syntax | Use the variable name directly | Need to dereference | | Where used here | Function parameters (all grid arguments in ) | Almost nowhere, except (see below) | The only pointer usage in this project: Why a pointer here instead of a reference? Because needs to be passed in at construction time, but a suitable object may not exist yet. A pointer can be and assigned later (though in this project it is assigned at construction). More importantly, in OpenMP parallelisation, each thread needs to copy‑construct its own local solver from this template – pointers make it easy to pass the template's address around, whereas references are less flexible in such "save address first, copy later" scenarios. For beginners to remember: for function parameters that pass large objects, use (read‑only) or (modifiable). Only use pointers when you need "rebindable" or "potentially null" semantics. The code in this project follows this rule. Doxygen‑Style Comments (Why I Write This Way) If you look carefully at the project's code, you'll notice a special comment format: This is Doxygen‑style commenting. Why I chose this style: Automatic documentation generation: Doxygen is a tool that scans these comments and produces nicely formatted HTML or PDF manuals. In a team, new members don't need to read through all the code – they can go straight to the generated docs to see what each function does. Forces clear expression: forces you to state in one sentence what the function does. forces you to explain every parameter's purpose. This process itself is a form of "self‑review" – if you can't write a clear , the function is probably too complex. IDE tooltips: Modern IDEs (like VSCode, CLion) recognise Doxygen comments. When you hover over a function call, the IDE shows the and content – you don't need to jump to the definition to understand usage. Why over plain text comments in this project: Plain has no structured information that Doxygen tools can parse. is a recognised keyword that tools can reliably process. All public interfaces in this project use Doxygen format; internal private functions (like ) use plain comments since they aren't exposed externally. Common Doxygen keywords: | Keyword | Purpose | Example | |---------|---------|---------| | | One‑line summary | | | | Explain a parameter | | | | Explain the return value | | | | Explain a template parameter | Not used in this project | | | Additional notes | | I recommend beginners start with and – once it becomes a habit, your code quality will visibly improve. Compiler Directives ( and ) Lines starting with are compiler directives – they are not C++ statements, but instructions telling the compiler "please enable this feature". does not depend on any header file (though provides function declarations). It is recognised and processed at compile time by the compiler. Different compilers support different s; GCC and MSVC have some incompatible ones. But is part of the OpenMP standard and is supported by all major compilers (GCC, Clang, MSVC). The optimisation flag: The command you use to compile this project is: stands for Optimisation Level 2. With it enabled, the compiler performs many "equivalent transformations" to improve runtime speed: Turns and into the same assembly instructions (see Section 3.3) Unrolls simple loops (reduces loop‑jump overhead) Pre‑computes constants (e.g., is computed only once at runtime) does not change program logic – it only affects performance. For debugging, you can use (no optimisation) to make single‑stepping easier; for production, use or . The 10 points above cover 95% of the C++ syntax skeleton used in this project. If you can type out the "Dog" and "squareSum" examples on your own machine and get them working, then when you look at the project code below, you'll feel a sense of déjà vu. Next, we'll formally introduce the architecture of . 3.1 Header Files and Basic Structure A C++ program starts with directives, telling the compiler which external libraries to bring in. Why these specific headers: Each header provides only the most essential functionality; including them on demand shortens compilation time. provides , provides file writing, gives the dynamic array (used internally by ), and provides (C++17's parameter‑clipping function) and (to find the maximum value). is required for OpenMP – without it, directives would be ignored, but functions like would fail to compile. What does the prefix mean? Everything in the C++ standard library lives inside the namespace. means " inside the namespace". Without , the compiler would report "identifier not found". You could write to drop the prefix, but this project does not – in large projects, can introduce naming conflicts. Beginners can just follow the pattern and treat it as "the standard library's tag". Execution starts from . means normal termination; a non‑zero value signals an error, which the operating system receives. 3.2 Loop Order and Array Indexing (Why Inside ) The most common loop pattern in the program is nested loops for traversing a 2D grid: corresponds to the x‑direction (column index), to the y‑direction (row index). The inner loop is , and the outer is . Why put on the inside: uses row‑major storage – all columns of row 0 are contiguous, then row 1, and so on. When the inner loop traverses , memory addresses increase sequentially: , , … The CPU's hardware prefetcher detects this sequential access pattern and loads subsequent data from main memory into cache in advance. In , when is fixed, is constant – the inner loop only computes , which is very efficient. If we reversed the order ( outer, inner), memory access would be strided: after , it jumps to , skipping an entire row. The prefetcher cannot predict such jumps, and each access might have to read from main memory – which can be 10× or more slower than sequential access (this is called the "cache miss penalty"). For 800 points, the difference isn't obvious, but when scaling to 400,000 points, the gap can turn seconds into minutes. Syntax breakdown of : – initialisation, executed once before the loop starts. – condition, checked before each iteration; exits when . – update, executed after each iteration body. 3.3 Pre‑increment ( ) vs. Post‑increment ( ) The code uses or extensively as loop updates: The difference between them: (pre‑increment): first adds 1 to , then the incremented value becomes the result of the expression. (post‑increment): first takes the current value of as the result of the expression, then adds 1 to . Why this project only uses : In the update part of a loop, we only care about the side effect of incrementing – we don't care about the result of the expression. For built‑in types ( , , etc.), and generate almost identical machine code. But in C++, if is a complex object (like an iterator), must return a copy of the old value, which involves a copy construction, whereas only modifies itself. Although all s in this program are , using is a good habit that signals "I only want to increment, I don't need the old value". About optimisation: With enabled, for types, and produce identical assembly. At the assembly level, the "save then increment" vs. "increment then return" distinction is optimised away – the compiler knows the old value won't be used in loop updates and generates just . But exams still distinguish them! In domestic CS exams (like the Chinese Computer Rank Examination) and postgraduate entrance tests, it is common to ask about the different values of vs. in expressions. For example: Such questions test your understanding of "expression result" vs. "side effect". So even though in real engineering they are equivalent, in exams you must pay close attention to whether it is pre‑ or post‑increment. 3.4 Ternary Conditional Operator ( ) The upwind differencing in the program uses the ternary operator to perform an selection in one line: Syntax: Why write it this way: The upwind decision rule is "if velocity goes right, take the left neighbour; if velocity goes left, take the right neighbour" – it is a binary choice, and the ternary operator fits perfectly. It is more compact than an , and in this code, needs a value – the ternary returns one directly. With , you would need to declare in advance and assign it in each branch – more lines, and you risk forgetting to assign in one branch (though the compiler would warn, it interrupts your flow). Note: The ternary is not a replacement for all . When each branch has multiple statements, stick with . This project uses it only in "select‑one‑of‑two‑return‑values" scenarios – exactly where it belongs. 3.5 OpenMP Parallelisation Directives OpenMP is a standard for parallel programming via compiler directives ( ). This program uses OpenMP in three places. Use case 1: Parallel region and loop distribution : launches a team of threads (equal to the number of CPU cores), each executing the following block. : distributes the iterations of the immediately following loop across all threads in the current parallel region. Each thread handles a subset of the combinations. : flattens the double loop into 800 independent iterations and then distributes them. Without , OpenMP would only parallelise the outer loop (20 iterations) – on 8 cores, only 2.5‑way parallelism, leaving the inner 40 iterations serial. makes the parallelism finer‑grained and fully utilises the cores. : dynamic scheduling – each thread, after finishing its current task, picks the next unprocessed iteration from a queue. If one iteration is interrupted by system scheduling, other threads can share the remaining work, achieving load balancing. Use case 2: In the RMSprop normalisation, gradient clipping, and parameter update loops, a more concise form is used: This is equivalent to with an inner – a combined shorthand. Why these loops are safe to parallelise: In these update loops, each reads and writes only its own and . There is no data dependency between different points. If two threads process and , they operate on adjacent but independent memory locations – they won't interfere. This type of workload is called "embarrassingly parallel", and OpenMP can achieve nearly linear speedup. Why the gradient‑computation loop cannot simply be : Inside the gradient loop, is called, which internally modifies . If multiple threads shared a single , we would have a data race. Hence we must first use to create thread‑local copies, and then inside use to distribute tasks. This is a common "thread‑local data" pattern in OpenMP programming. 3.6 Pass by Reference ( ) and The in function parameters means pass by reference – the function operates directly on the original object, not on a copy. : is a reference – any modification inside directly affects the object passed in by the caller. This is exactly what we need: the function updates the temperature field. : is a const reference. tells the compiler "this function will not modify Alpha" – if we accidentally write , compilation fails. A const reference avoids copying (800 doubles ≈ 6.4 KB, but accumulated over many calls it adds up) while providing a read‑only safety guarantee. Without , i.e., , the function would modify a copy, leaving the caller's original unchanged. Using a pointer would require – clunky syntax. References are both concise and efficient. in : on a member function means the function belongs to the class itself, not to any instance of the class. You call it with without creating a object. Since this function doesn't depend on any member variables (it is purely computational), it is appropriate to declare it static. 3.7 Output Formatting ( / ) The program uses formatting controls when writing CSV files and logs: : use scientific notation (e.g., ). : use fixed‑point notation (e.g., ). : sets the number of digits. In scientific mode it's 6 significant digits; in mode it's 6 digits after the decimal point. : sets the minimum field width to 4 characters, padding with spaces if needed – this aligns output for readability. goes from 1 to 200; with , 1, 10, 100 are aligned in a column. Core CSV‑writing code: Each row ends with , columns separated by commas. The CSV file can be read directly by Excel or Python's . 3.8 Common Questions from Beginners What is the difference between and : outputs a newline and flushes the buffer – it forces the data to be written immediately. Frequent can hurt performance. This program uses in because logs need to be written immediately (so that if the program crashes, the log is preserved). For CSV output, is used because we don't need to flush after every line – the operating system's batch writing is more efficient. Why does show only 0.1 and 0.8 but each row has 40 numbers? writes rows for from 0 to 19, each with 40 values. The left half ( , i.e., ) is 0.1, the right half is 0.8. So the first 20 columns are all 0.1, and the last 20 are all 0.8. In a text editor, this CSV appears as a matrix of numbers that directly corresponds to the spatial grid. What is the in : Lines starting with are preprocessor directives – they are processed before the compiler actually compiles the code. pastes the header file content into the source; tells the compiler "please enable this feature". Unlike normal C++ statements, preprocessor directives do not end with a semicolon. Syntax Self‑Check List for This Section | Syntax Feature | Where It Appears in the Code | Mastered? | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | and header files | At the top of the file | □ | | namespace | Everything with prefix | □ | | and | , | □ | | | | □ | | Row‑major nested loops | | □ | | Pre‑increment | All loops | □ | | Ternary operator | , calculations | □ | | OpenMP | Three places in | □ | | Pass by reference | parameters | □ | | read‑only protection | | □ | | | After parameter updates | □ | | Stream formatting | and CSV output | □ | Exercises and Further Practice Please refer to Section 4.

Instead, it focuses on core C++ syntax, common programming errors, software architecture, and performance optimisation. All questions are self‑contained mini‑problems suitable for reinforcing fundamentals. Each question comes with a reference answer (at the end). Provide two different approaches (reference and pointer). 2. Pre‑increment vs. Post‑increment Write the output of the following code segment and explain each line: 3.
