title: FromPapertoProduction
content: Section 5: From Paper to Production – How DeepFDM Was Brought to Life Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Discretisation | Turning continuous mathematical equations (PDEs) into algebraic equations that a computer can solve | | Five‑point stencil | A discrete Laplacian that involves the centre point and its four orthogonal neighbours (up, down, left, right) | | Upwind differencing | Choosing forward or backward differencing based on the flow direction to maintain numerical stability | | Explicit scheme | New time‑level values are computed directly from old values – no system of equations to solve | | CFL condition | The time step must not exceed a critical value, otherwise the numerical solution explodes | | Dirichlet boundary | Fixed temperature on the boundary (zero in this program) – the simplest and most common boundary condition | | Forward simulation | Computing the temperature evolution from known parameters | | Inverse problem | Inferring unknown parameter distributions from observed temperature data | | Loss function | A metric that measures the mismatch between predictions and observations – the "judge" of the inversion | | Finite‑difference perturbation | Using two forward simulations (perturbing the parameter by +ε and −ε) to approximate the gradient | | RMSprop | An adaptive learning‑rate algorithm that gives each parameter its own step size | | Gradient clipping | Limiting single‑step updates to [-1, 1] to prevent training from going out of control | | Multi‑time loss | Comparing temperatures at multiple intermediate instants simultaneously, adding more supervisory signals | | Physical projection | Forcing parameters to stay within physically reasonable bounds (α cannot be negative or too large) | | Parallelisation | Using multiple CPU cores simultaneously – distributing 800 forward simulations across 8 cores | | Thread‑local data | Each thread has its own copy of data to avoid cross‑thread interference | | Cache locality | When data is stored contiguously in memory, the CPU can access it much faster | | Hyperparameters | Parameters that must be set before running the algorithm – e.g., learning rate, perturbation step size | | Convergence | The property that the loss function gradually decreases and stabilises over iterations | | Ill‑posed problem | A problem where the solution is not unique or is highly sensitive to noise – a common challenge in inversion | 5.1 From Mathematical Formulas to Executable Code – The Abstraction Process The partial differential equations in a paper are written in mathematical language, which computers do not understand. The programmer's first job is to translate those few lines of formulas into data structures and algorithmic steps. The core equation from the paper (heat equation): \[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha(x,y)\left(\frac{\partial^2T}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2T}{\partial y^2}\right) + S(x,y) \] This equation describes how temperature evolves over time. To make a computer execute it, we must perform the following abstractions: Step 1: Discretisation – from continuous to discrete | Continuous concept | Discrete implementation | | :--- | :--- | | Continuous space \((x,y)\) | Grid points \((i,j)\), \(xi=i\cdot\Delta x,\ yj=j\cdot\Delta y\) | | Continuous time \(t\) | Time step \(n\), \(tn=n\cdot\Delta t\) | | Temperature field \(T(x,y,t)\) | Array \(T{i,j}^{(n)}\), stored in a | | Thermal diffusivity \(\alpha(x,y)\) | Array \(\alpha{i,j}\), stored in another | | Heat source \(S(x,y)\) | Array \(S{i,j}\), pre‑computed and stored | | Laplacian \(\Delta T\) | Five‑point finite‑difference stencil (see Section 5.3) | | Time derivative \(\partial T/\partial t\) | Forward Euler difference \(T^{n+1} = T^n + \Delta t \cdot (\cdots)\) | Step 2: Forward simulation – forward iteration This process is the forward simulation – given the parameters, compute the temperature. Step 3: Inversion – backward optimisation The "inverse problem" mentioned in the paper is transformed into an optimisation problem in engineering: \[ \alpha^ = \arg\min\alpha \sumt \|T\text{pred}(\alpha, t) - T\text{obs}(t)\|^2 \] Translated into code: This "three‑step sequence" is the core logic of the entire project: discretisation → forward simulation → inversion. The paper provides the mathematical description; the project provides the executable code. 5.2 Constructing the Coefficient Field – Why the Ground Truth Was Designed This Way The way to validate an inversion algorithm is to first construct a known ground truth, simulate synthetic observations from it, and then see whether the algorithm can recover that ground truth from the data. If it cannot recover a known answer, it will certainly fail on real data. The ground‑truth design in this project: Why this particular "left‑right" distribution: A sharp interface exists: at \(x=0.5\), there is a clear discontinuity – left side conducts slowly, right side conducts quickly. This type of discontinuity is the hardest feature for inversion to recover: neural networks tend to produce smooth solutions, whereas DeepFDM stores α directly on the grid, so it can naturally capture jumps. Physically interpretable: the low‑diffusivity region can be thought of as insulation, an air gap, or a damaged area, while the high‑diffusivity region represents a metal matrix. This is a realistic scenario in engineering non‑destructive testing – finding internal defects (voids, cracks, inclusions) inside materials. The initial guess \(\alpha=0.5\) is not arbitrary: it lies halfway between 0.1 and 0.8, giving the algorithm freedom to "decide whether to go left or right". If the initial guess were 0.1, the left half might converge quickly but the right half would have to climb up; if 0.8, the opposite. 0.5 minimises the initial bias. 5.3 The Explicit Euler Scheme – Why Choose the Simplest Option The paper mentions the Forward Euler method, and the project directly adopts it. The trade‑offs are as follows: Explicit Euler is extremely simple to implement: One line of code is the entire update formula for one time step – no linear system to solve, the code directly mirrors the math, and it is almost impossible to get wrong. Why not choose a more sophisticated time‑stepping scheme (like Crank‑Nicolson or Runge‑Kutta): | Scheme | Advantages | Disadvantages | Decision for this project | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Explicit Euler | Very simple, O(N) per step | Time step limited by CFL condition | ✅ Selected – code clarity wins | | Crank‑Nicolson | Unconditionally stable, larger steps | Requires solving linear systems, code 10× more complex | ❌ Not selected | | RK4 | High accuracy (O(Δt⁴)) | Four right‑hand‑side evaluations per step, gradient cost quadruples | ❌ Not selected | | Adaptive stepping | Automatically adjusts for efficiency | Non‑fixed steps complicate gradient comparisons | ❌ Not selected | The inversion context amplifies the advantage of explicit schemes: gradient computation requires 1600 forward simulations. If each forward simulation involved solving a linear system (implicit) or four extra RHS evaluations (RK4), the total cost would multiply from 1600×8000 steps to 1600×8000×(tens of times) – turning "2 minutes" into "2 hours". Although explicit Euler uses smaller time steps, each step is extremely lightweight. For an inversion scenario that runs "ten thousand forward simulations", the explicit scheme is globally optimal. 5.4 Discretising the Laplacian and Implementing Boundary Conditions in Code The five‑point stencil in code: This stencil only uses the four orthogonal neighbours – not the diagonal ones like . Why? Second‑order accuracy is sufficient: the truncation error is \(O(\Delta x^2)\). If we refine the grid from 40×20 to 80×40, the error drops to one‑quarter – more than enough to resolve the left‑right contrast in α. Low computational cost: the five‑point stencil requires only 5 memory accesses. A nine‑point stencil (including diagonals) would need 9 accesses – almost double the work, with only marginal accuracy gains. Isotropy: on a square grid, this stencil is perfectly symmetric in the x and y directions, so it introduces no directional bias. Engineering boundary‑condition handling: Why handle boundaries separately instead of adding checks inside the loop: If we added inside the interior loop, we would perform a conditional check every iteration. Over 800 points × 8000 steps × 1600 forward simulations ≈ 10.2 billion checks – a huge cumulative overhead. The boundary consists of only 2×40+2×20-4=116 points (14.5% of the grid). Handling those 116 points in a separate loop leaves the main loop (684 points) branch‑free, maximising CPU pipeline efficiency. 5.5 Turning the Inverse Problem into an Optimisation Problem The paper says "the inverse problem is ill‑posed". Engineering needs to turn it into a "computable" problem. This project uses mean squared error + gradient descent to solve it. Loss function design: This looks simple, but why use squared error instead of absolute error? Squared error penalises large deviations more heavily (a difference of 2 gives a penalty of 4, while 0.5 gives 0.25), pushing the optimiser to eliminate large errors first. The derivative of squared error is continuous: \(\partial(\text{MSE})/\partial T = 2(T{pred} - T{target})/N\). Absolute error is non‑differentiable at zero, which causes numerical trouble for gradient computation. Squared error corresponds statistically to a Gaussian noise assumption – if the observation errors are normally distributed, MSE is the maximum‑likelihood estimator. The actual loss in the code is "multi‑time averaged": If we compared only the final time, the "solution space" of the inverse problem would be huge – many different α distributions might produce similar final temperatures because the diffusion process has already smoothed out early details. Adding intermediate instants forces the optimiser to match temperatures at all times simultaneously, yielding a stronger constraint and a more unique solution. 5.6 Why 8000 Forward Simulation Steps From the code, and , giving 16 recorded instants. How 8000 steps were determined: Why run up to 0.8 seconds? The characteristic time for heat to diffuse from the source (at x=0.3) across the whole domain (Lx=1.0) is roughly \(Lx^2 / \alpha \approx 1.0^2 / 0.8 = 1.25\) seconds. 0.8 seconds covers the process from the source spreading out to most of the domain. If we used too few steps (e.g., 2000, physical time 0.2 s), the heat would not have reached the right boundary yet, and the observations would contain only information near the source – making it difficult to infer α on the right side. If we used too many steps (e.g., 20000), the system would be near steady state (temperature no longer changing), and extra time steps would add computational cost without providing new information. Important: the time step during inversion may differ from the one used to generate the ground truth! If the current guess of αmax is larger than the true value (say 0.6), then becomes smaller than the used in the forward truth simulation. That means the same 8000 steps now cover a shorter physical time. The predicted temperature evolution will lag behind the observations, increasing the loss. This very deviation provides the gradient direction – the optimiser will tend to reduce αmax to make the time step longer, bringing the evolution speed back in line with the observations. 5.7 Engineering Implementation of Gradient Computation The paper does not specify how to compute the gradient – that is an engineering choice. This project uses central finite‑difference perturbation. Engineering trade‑off: why not use Automatic Differentiation (AD)? If we used a framework like TensorFlow/PyTorch, AD would be built‑in. But this project is pure C++ (no third‑party dependencies). Implementing AD manually would require a computational graph, back‑propagation infrastructure, etc. – ballooning the code from ~500 lines to ~5000 lines. The finite‑difference perturbation method, though computationally heavier (1600× more forward runs), is extremely simple to implement, logically clear, and has no dependencies. Given that the grid has only 800 points, 1600 forward simulations run in parallel on an 8‑core CPU take about 1‑2 minutes – entirely acceptable. Why the perturbation step size is 0.01: | eps value | Issue | | :--- | :--- | | Too small (e.g., 1e-8) | \(L{+\epsilon} - L{-\epsilon}\) approaches the floating‑point round‑off level, so the gradient is drowned by numerical noise | | Too large (e.g., 0.1) | The perturbation goes beyond the local linear regime, and the central‑difference truncation error becomes excessive | | 0.01 (this project) | Balances truncation and round‑off errors, and has shown stable convergence in validation | 5.8 RMSprop + Gradient Clipping – Why This Combination Why not plain SGD: With 800 parameters, the gradient magnitudes vary enormously. The α at the heat‑source centre is highly sensitive to loss (large gradient), while α far from the source is almost unaffected (tiny gradient). Plain SGD with a single learning rate causes the centre to oscillate and the corners to barely move. RMSprop solves this: If a parameter's gradients are consistently large, is also large, so the normalised effective step size shrinks automatically. Conversely, if gradients are consistently small, the effective step size grows. This makes the optimiser "agnostic" to the parameter's identity – whether you are at the heat‑source centre or a far‑away corner, your update magnitude stays in the same ballpark. The role of gradient clipping: Even with RMSprop, occasional single‑point gradient anomalies can occur (e.g., numerical noise causing a gradient 100× larger than normal). Without handling this, that point's α jumps from 0.5 to near 0.001 or 1.0, ruining the entire training run. Clipping to [-1,1] acts as a "safety fuse". 5.9 Parallelisation Strategy – Why OpenMP Was Chosen There are 800 grid points, each requiring 2 forward simulations, each with 8000 steps. Total workload = 800 × 2 × 8000 = 12.8 million grid updates. Running this serially on a 3 GHz CPU would take several minutes. OpenMP can distribute this work across 8 cores, reducing the wall‑clock time to around 30 seconds. Why OpenMP instead of more complex alternatives: | Solution | Advantages | Disadvantages | Suitability | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | OpenMP | Minimal code changes (a few #pragma), cross‑platform, low shared‑memory communication cost | Only for single‑node multi‑core, no cluster support | ✅ Selected | | MPI | Can scale across multiple machines, theoretically unlimited | Major code changes, high communication overhead | ❌ Overkill for 800 points | | CUDA | Extremely fast on GPUs (thousands of cores) | Requires an NVIDIA GPU, completely different programming model | ❌ Avoided to keep no GPU dependency | The cost‑benefit of OpenMP:** Cost: requires compiler support ( ), and adds "non‑standard" directives. Benefit: training time drops from ~7 minutes to ~1 minute. For this 800‑point × 2‑perturbation × 8000‑step problem, this is an extremely attractive "bang for the buck". 5.10 Complete Mapping from Paper to Code | Paper / Mathematical Concept | Engineering Implementation | Code Location | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | PDE definition \(Tt = \alpha\Delta T + S\) | Explicit Euler update formula | | | Spatial discretisation | Five‑point Laplacian stencil | variable computation | | Temporal discretisation | Forward Euler \(T^{n+1}=T^n+\Delta t\cdot F\) | in the update formula | | CFL stability condition | , using 0.5× safety factor | | | Dirichlet boundary | after each step | End of | | Forward simulation (given parameters, compute temperature) | loop calling | function | | Inverse problem (infer parameters from temperature) | iterative loop | function | | Loss function (MSE) | computing mean squared error | | | Gradient descent | , combined with RMSprop | Update loop | | Gradient computation (numerical) | Central difference \((L{+ε}-L{-ε})/(2ε)\) | Gradient double loop | | Optimisation acceleration (RMSprop) | Per‑parameter moving average of | RMSprop normalisation loop | | Parallel computation (OpenMP) | | Gradient / update loops | | Physical constraints (parameter bounds) | | Post‑update projection |

title: StepbyStep
content: Section 6: From Minimum Viable Product to Complete Project I recommend reading Section 10 first – it contains my personal reflections on the journey. Quick Reference Table | Term | Plain Explanation | |------|-------------------| | Minimum Viable Product (MVP) | The simplest runnable version that keeps only core functionality and strips away all bells and whistles | | Incremental development | Add one small feature at a time, make sure it works, then add the next – prevents bugs from piling up | | Ground‑truth validation | Construct a problem with a known answer and see whether the algorithm can recover it – the standard way to validate inversion algorithms | | Identifiability | Whether the observed data can uniquely determine the parameter you're looking for – poor identifiability causes inversion to fail | | Separation of concerns | Data storage, physics computation, and optimisation are placed in different classes that don't interfere with each other | | Thread‑local data | Each thread gets its own copy of data to avoid data races during parallel execution | | Gradient clipping | Limits the maximum single‑step update magnitude to prevent numerical anomalies from crashing the training | | Physical projection | Forces parameters to stay within physically reasonable bounds, ensuring the CFL condition can always be satisfied | | Local effective model | Inversion can only recover parameter regions that "affect the observations" – insensitive regions stay unchanged | | Multi‑time loss | Uses temperatures at multiple time instants as supervisory signals, enhancing parameter identifiability | 6.1 Overall Principle: From "It Runs" to "It Works Well" Every scientific computing project should follow the principle of "get it working first, then make it better". This project is no exception. The entire development process can be clearly divided into three phases: Minimum Viable Product (MVP): Get the program to run – compute gradients, update parameters, and watch the loss decrease. This phase ignores performance, convergence speed, and code beauty. The only goal is to prove the idea works. Feature completion: Add multi‑time loss, RMSprop, gradient clipping, and physical projection to make convergence more stable and results more reasonable. Performance optimisation: Add OpenMP parallelism to shorten training time. Below, I'll walk through the code's growth process step by step, following this exact order. 6.2 MVP Step 1: The Data Container (Grid2D) Core requirement: I need something to store 2D grid data. It must allocate memory, allow reading/writing at any grid point, and ideally handle boundaries automatically. Three things are enough: constructor, member variables, access function. At this stage, I didn't write , didn't write a copy constructor – because I didn't need them yet. Only when boundary operations started appearing repeatedly did I move them into the class: Design rationale: A 1D vector plus row‑major storage provides both memory contiguity and cache friendliness. Add functionality only when actually needed – don't design a "perfect" class upfront. Boundaries are part of the physics problem; the data container is responsible for storing boundary values and zeroing operations. 6.3 MVP Step 2: The Forward Solver (HeatSolver) Core requirement: I need a function that takes the current temperature field and physical parameters, and produces the temperature field at the next time step. Why not implement advection in the MVP phase: The advection term ( ) requires handling upwind differencing, which introduces conditional branches. Although the code is short, it adds complexity. The MVP goal is "get it running", so I stripped away all non‑essential complexity. Only after verifying the diffusion term was correct did I add advection. Verification method: Run a forward simulation with uniform Alpha=0.5 and a central Gaussian heat source, and observe whether the temperature field spreads symmetrically outward. If yes, the Laplacian and explicit Euler implementations are correct. Verification method: Set and observe whether the temperature field drifts to the right as a whole. If yes, the upwind differencing is correct. 6.4 MVP Step 3: Generating Observations Core requirement: I need a set of "real observational data" to validate the inversion algorithm. The most straightforward way: construct a known Alpha field, run the forward simulation to produce a temperature field, and treat that as the "observation". Why "left low, right high": The simpler the answer, the better. Left half 0.1 (insulating), right half 0.8 (conducting), with a clear step in between. If the inversion can recover that step, the program works. Why place the heat source inside the low‑conductivity region: When the source is inside the low‑conductivity region, the effect of "trapping heat" is strongest, and the observational signal is most sensitive. If the source were far away, heat would never reach that region, and the inversion would have zero sensitivity there – the fundamental identifiability issue in inverse problems. 6.5 MVP Step 4: Gradient Computation Core requirement: I need to compute the partial derivative of the loss function with respect to each Alpha grid point. The loss is computed through an 8000‑step forward simulation, so there is no analytic expression – numerical perturbation is required. This version is very slow – 800 points × 2 perturbations × 8000 steps = 12.8 million grid updates – but it computes correctly. The sole goal of the MVP phase is to verify that "the gradient direction is correct and the loss decreases". Verification method: Run one full gradient computation, update Alpha once, and see if the loss decreases. If it does, the gradient direction is correct. Choosing the perturbation step size eps: . Any smaller and the loss difference is drowned by floating‑point round‑off error; any larger and it exceeds the linear approximation regime. This is an empirical value that proves stable for this problem. Why not use automatic differentiation: AD requires external frameworks (like PyTorch). Since the point of this project is to teach C++ syntax, I deliberately avoided them. 6.6 MVP Step 5: Optimisation Iteration Core requirement: With the gradient, I can update Alpha and gradually reduce the loss. This is the raw inversion loop. It does only four things: Compute the gradient (see Section 6.5) Update in the opposite direction of the gradient ( ) Physical projection ( to ) Report loss to monitor progress This version already converges. With the heat source placed inside the low‑conductivity region, after about 50 iterations you can see the left side of Alpha drop noticeably and the right side rise noticeably. 6.7 Feature Completion: From MVP to a Usable Version After the MVP ran, I started adding features to make convergence more stable and results more reasonable. 6.7.1 Adding Multi‑Time Loss When comparing only the final time, the solution space is too large – many different Alpha distributions produce similar final temperatures. Adding intermediate instants forces the optimiser to match the entire temperature evolution trajectory. This step dramatically improved inversion stability, because the gradient signal spread from "the final time" to "the entire time axis". 6.7.2 Adding RMSprop The problem with plain gradient descent is that Alpha near the heat source has large gradients and updates quickly, while Alpha far from the source has small gradients and updates slowly. RMSprop maintains a moving average of the squared gradients for each parameter, adaptively adjusting the step size. This ensures that the update step sizes at the heat‑source centre and in the far corners are of the same order, preventing centre oscillation and corner stagnation. 6.7.3 Adding Gradient Clipping Although RMSprop balances magnitudes, occasionally a single point's gradient may become abnormally large due to numerical issues (e.g., 1e3), causing that point's Alpha to jump from 0.5 to 0.001 or 1.0 in one step. Gradient clipping acts as a safety net. 6.7.4 Tuning the Learning Rate The MVP phase used , which converged quickly but oscillated near the optimum. The final version was tuned to , yielding smoother convergence. 6.8 Performance Optimisation: OpenMP Parallelism The MVP's serial gradient computation made 200 iterations take hours, which was impractical for debugging. Observation: Gradient computation for the 800 grid points is completely independent – the gradient at point does not depend on the result at point . This is a classic "embarrassingly parallel" problem. Key design points: Each thread creates its own and , with no interference. lets threads that finish early take on more tasks, balancing the load. preserves the baseline state, ensuring every perturbation starts from the same reference. Speedup is about 13‑15× (on a 16‑core CPU), cutting training time from several hours to under 15 minutes. 6.9 Interpreting Results: What Counts as a "Reasonable" Inversion Result The final inferred Alpha field will not perfectly reproduce the "0.1 on the left, 0.8 on the right" ground truth. A typical actual result is: Near the heat source (x≈0.3, y≈0.25): Alpha drops to 0.10–0.15 Most of the right region: rises to 0.75–0.85 Left region far from the source: stays around 0.4–0.5 (the initial guess) Near the boundaries: barely changes This is normal, not a failure. The essence of inversion is "only recover parameters that affect the observations". Changes near the heat source have a large impact on the temperature field, so they are recovered. Changes far away have little impact, so their gradient is near zero, and they keep their initial guess. This raises a deeper question in inversion: how should the observation scheme (heat‑source placement, boundary conditions, recording duration) be designed to make all target parameters identifiable? That is a more meaningful discussion than "tweak parameters to converge faster". 6.10 Development Process Summary If you were to reproduce this project from scratch, here is the recommended step‑by‑step sequence: | Order | Module | Validation Method | Phase | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | 1 | (access + boundaries) | Fill values, print, verify layout | MVP | | 2 | (diffusion only) | Central source spreads symmetrically | MVP | | 3 | (advection) | Temperature field shifts as a whole | Feature extension | | 4 | Generate ground truth + observations | Save CSV, visual inspection | MVP | | 5 | Gradient computation (serial) | Run once, confirm loss decreases | MVP | | 6 | Optimisation loop (plain SGD) | Observe Alpha field changes | MVP | | 7 | Multi‑time loss | Compare single‑time vs. multi‑time convergence | Feature completion | | 8 | RMSprop | Observe smoother convergence curves | Feature completion | | 9 | Gradient clipping | Prevent occasional numerical blow‑ups | Feature completion | | 10 | OpenMP parallelism | Compare single‑core vs. multi‑core runtime | Performance optimisation | Every step stays in a "compilable, runnable, verifiable" state, ensuring that issues are caught early rather than discovering non‑convergence after writing 500 lines of code.
